questions.question: A file's first generation trailer declares committed_file_length = 128. The file's owner then performs a second commit (an ordinary append, not a rewrite) to this same file. Under this specification's writer rules, what is the smallest committed_file_length value that this second commit's trailer may declare? Give the answer as an integer number of bytes.
questions.answer_form: a single integer (bytes)
questions.why_it_matters: Combines the explicit prior-first-generation floor (128) with the separately-stated 'strictly greater, by at least 128' rule; tests whether an edition keeps both the initial floor and the per-commit increment, and gets the arithmetic right.

questions.question: Consider a remote reader opening a TARN file whose total size is exactly 30,000 bytes, with trailer fields dir_offset = 20 and dir_length = 100 (so the directory region occupies file bytes [20, 120)). The reader's open begins by speculatively fetching, in a single range request, what it believes may be the file's final 40,000 bytes; because the file is only 30,000 bytes long, this single fetch actually returns the file's full contents, bytes [0, 30000). (a) How many total range requests does this reader's open cost, counting only requests needed to obtain the trailer and the directory? (b) Is this reader obligated to verify the 16-byte front signature block by byte equality as part of this open, and if so, why? Answer (a) as an integer count of requests, and (b) as yes/no plus the one governing requirement's identifier.
questions.answer_form: (a) an integer request count; (b) yes/no plus a requirement id
questions.why_it_matters: Combines the speculative-fetch/containment rule (which collapses two requests into one) with the separate, residency-triggered front-block verification rule, which is a carve-out keyed to whether bytes are already in hand rather than to transport type.

questions.question: A file's directory contains one top-level record that is not a layer record (for concreteness, a user-metadata record). Its extent slot has extent_offset = 2^63 − 5 and extent_length = 10. Each of these two field values, taken alone, lies within this specification's 0-to-(2^63−1) value domain for such fields. (a) Does this extent slot nonetheless constitute a validity error? (b) If so, which single requirement identifier is violated — the one governing an individual field's value domain, or the one governing a declaration-derived sum of two fields? (c) What outcome class and scope apply? Answer with yes/no, the requirement identifier, and the outcome class name.
questions.answer_form: yes/no; a requirement identifier; an outcome-class name
questions.why_it_matters: Tests the quantifier distinction between a plain per-field domain check and a 'declaration-derived sum' check the document names as a separate, express designation — an easy point for a rewording to blur.

questions.question: A TARN file's physical bytes end at some offset F. The final 64 bytes, [F−64, F), do not match the trailer magic. However, 64 bytes before that, at [F−128, F−64), sits a byte sequence that is a fully valid trailer: correct magic, a verifying trailer CRC, and a committed_file_length field equal to F−64. A conforming reader opens this file via its default read path (not a deliberate recovery operation). (a) What must this reader report about the file? (b) Is the reader permitted, on this default path, to fall back to using the earlier valid-looking trailer it could find 64 bytes back? Answer (a) in one phrase (the outcome the default path assigns) and (b) yes/no.
questions.answer_form: (a) a short verdict phrase; (b) yes/no
questions.why_it_matters: Tests the sharp, absolute 'MUST NOT scan backward' rule on the default path, kept strictly apart from the separately-described, deliberate recovery operation — a carve-out a looser rewording could accidentally merge.

questions.question: In the checksum coverage map, which single checksum's covered byte range includes the four bytes of a layer record's own crc_of_crc_array field (that is, what would catch bit-corruption of the crc_of_crc_array field's stored bytes themselves)? Separately, what does crc_of_crc_array itself serve to verify — that is, over what bytes is it the CRC-32C? Give two short answers: (a) the name of the covering checksum/structure, and (b) the name of the structure crc_of_crc_array is computed over.
questions.answer_form: two short named answers
questions.why_it_matters: Requires tracing the chain of trust two links at once: what protects an interior checksum field's own bytes, versus what that same field protects — a distinction the coverage map states generally but the reader must instantiate for this specific field.

questions.question: A layer is interleaved, rank 2, with dimensions declared in this order: first a dimension named 'y' with extent 10 and tile extent 4, then a dimension named 'x' with extent 13 and tile extent 5. Its channels are declared in this order: 'p' (type int16) then 'q' (type uint8). Consider the sample at coordinate (y, x) = (9, 11). (a) What is this tile's disk ordinal (i.e., the index of its entry in the layer's tile index)? (b) At what byte offset within this tile's decoded tile image does channel 'q'’s value begin? Answer both as integers.
questions.answer_form: two integers
questions.why_it_matters: Forces combining the linearization ordinal formulas (grid count, tile/in-tile coordinates, spatial ordinal) with the separate interleaved byte-offset formula, using fresh numbers rather than either of the document's own worked examples.

questions.question: A layer is planar with a single bool channel 'm' whose recorded fill value is true (0x01). One of its tiles has tile extents (3, 3) (so 9 sample positions per tile) and is stored, with its 9 values, in in-tile ordinal order, being: true, false, true, false, true, false, true, false, true. Give the tile's full decoded byte image as exactly two hexadecimal bytes, most-significant byte first (i.e., byte 0 then byte 1), including any pad bits.
questions.answer_form: two hex bytes, e.g. 'XX YY'
questions.why_it_matters: Combines the LSB-first bit-packing rule, the pad-bit-range rule (which depends on P mod 8, here giving 7 pad bits rather than the document's own 6-pad-bit example), and the rule that pad bits must carry the channel's fill bit.

questions.question: A planar layer has two channels: 'a' (uint8) and 'b' (float64), with tile extents (16384, 16384) along its two dimensions (so P = 16384 × 16384 sample positions per tile). The layer's record declares codec 4 (lz4). (a) What is the decoded size, in bytes, of one addressed tile's plane for channel 'b'? (b) Does this layer's codec-4 declaration satisfy this specification's decoded-size cap for that codec? Answer (a) as an integer and (b) as yes/no, naming which channel's plane is decisive if the answer is no.
questions.answer_form: (a) an integer; (b) yes/no plus a channel name
questions.why_it_matters: Applies the prose rule that 'the largest channel plane governs' a per-layer codec cap to a concrete planar layer where the two channels' plane sizes differ by 8x, requiring the reader to compute both and compare the larger to the stated hex cap.

questions.question: A file-scope user-metadata document, stored under encoding 1 (none, i.e. verbatim JSON), is a single JSON object containing two members whose keys are written, respectively, as the literal UTF-8 text 'café' and as the escaped text 'café'. No other members are present. (a) Does this document violate the duplicate-key rule? (b) If so, what outcome class results for this record, and which register row (by its stated condition, not asking for a label) describes it? Answer (a) yes/no and (b) the outcome class name.
questions.answer_form: yes/no; an outcome-class name
questions.why_it_matters: Applies the keyword-precise rule that key identity is the decoded string, not the JSON source bytes, to a fresh escape-collision instance different from the document's own 'a'/a example.

questions.question: A file-scope user-metadata document is stored under encoding 2 (zstd). Its decoded byte length is exactly 800 bytes. The compressed frame carrying it sets Single_Segment_Flag (so it has no separate Window_Descriptor), and its Frame_Content_Size field is present with the value 750. (a) Is this conforming? (b) If not, is the violation classified as a failure to decode the document, or as a broken frame constraint (name which)? (c) What quantity does this specification require the frame's content-size field to match here — and how does that differ from what the analogous rule requires for a tile's stored bytes under the same codec? Answer (a) yes/no, (b) the classification, and (c) a one-sentence statement of the matched quantity and the contrast.
questions.answer_form: yes/no; a classification name; a one-sentence contrast
questions.why_it_matters: Tests two carve-outs the metadata-encoding section states against an otherwise-identical tile-codec rule: metadata has no declared decoded size, so the content-size check runs against the document's actual decoded length instead.

questions.question: A planar layer has entry_count = 150,000 tile-index entries (so segment 0 covers entries [0, 65536), segment 1 covers [65536, 131072), and segment 2 covers [131072, 150000)). A single region-read request needs three entries: disk ordinal 5,000 (segment 0), disk ordinal 70,000 (segment 1), and disk ordinal 140,000 (segment 2). The reader successfully verifies and uses the entries in segments 0 and 1, returning their tiles' sample values as part of servicing this request, and only afterward attempts segment 2, whose stored segment CRC fails to verify. (a) What outcome class and scope apply to this failure? (b) Does this failure retroactively invalidate the sample values already returned from the segment-0 and segment-1 tiles within this same request? (c) Is the reader permitted to serve any further requests from this layer afterward? Answer (a) the outcome class name, (b) yes/no, (c) yes/no.
questions.answer_form: outcome-class name; yes/no; yes/no
questions.why_it_matters: Requires computing which segment a given ordinal falls in and then applying the 'prospective, not retroactive' rule that distinguishes an index-chain (layer-scope) failure from a tile-scope failure — a keyword that changes whether already-served data in the same request stands.

questions.question: A layer stored at least one tile in the generation that a particular commit supersedes (it is not an empty layer being freely re-declared). In that one commit, the writer wants to simultaneously (i) append one brand-new channel to the end of this planar layer's channel list, and (ii) remove from the channel list the channel that was last in the list before this commit. Is a single commit that does both (i) and (ii) at once permitted under this specification's rules for a layer that already stores a tile? If not, name the two alternatives available to the writer for accomplishing the equivalent net effect.
questions.answer_form: yes/no plus two named alternatives
questions.why_it_matters: Tests the quantifier 'not both in one commit' on planar channel-list edits, applied to the boundary case of extending and shortening at the very same end of the list in a single operation.

questions.question: A layer record carries exactly two sub-records: one user-metadata sub-record (governed by its registry-fixed flags), and one sub-record of an experimental-range type (type value ≥ 0x8000) that the updater in question does not implement, with that sub-record's stored MUST_UNDERSTAND bit set to 1. The updater wants to drop this entire layer in an otherwise-unremarkable commit. Is the updater permitted to drop the layer? Answer yes/no, and name the specific mechanism (which record's flag, and what it does to the operation) that determines the answer.
questions.answer_form: yes/no plus a short mechanism statement
questions.why_it_matters: Tests an exception that can block an operation the layer record's own flags would otherwise license — an unimplemented critical sub-record overriding the layer's droppability.

questions.question: A rewriter is compacting a file. Doing so relocates one stored tile of a particular layer, which requires the rewriter to regenerate that layer's entire tile-index region (since one of its entries' stored extents has moved). While classifying that region's entries for regeneration, the rewriter meets one entry whose offset field equals the all-ones sentinel value but whose length field does not equal it (so this entry classifies as reject-tile on a structural ground). (a) Can the rewriter reproduce this single entry unchanged at a new offset? (b) Can the rewriter instead write the true sentinel pattern in this entry's place and proceed? (c) What are the two courses of action actually available to the rewriter for the layer as a whole? Answer (a) and (b) yes/no, and (c) name both courses of action.
questions.answer_form: two yes/no answers plus two named courses of action
questions.why_it_matters: Tests that a structurally invalid index entry gives a rewriter no stored extent to relocate and no license to fabricate a replacement, leaving only two whole-layer-level dispositions — a fine distinction between repairing and disposing.

questions.question: A verifier examines a file containing two layers, A and B. During its walk it establishes one definite violation in layer A (two of its dimension entries share an identical name). Separately, layer B declares a codec the verifier is unable to execute due to a resource constraint, so the verifier cannot check layer B's decoded-content obligations at all. (a) What overall verdict — conforming, nonconforming, or cannot establish — must the verifier report for the file as a whole? (b) Must the verifier still say anything in its report about the requirement it could not check on layer B, even though the overall verdict is already decided by (a)? If so, name the two things that per-requirement report must state.
questions.answer_form: a verdict name; yes/no plus two named report contents
questions.why_it_matters: Tests the precedence rule that an established violation always yields nonconforming regardless of unrelated cannot-establish conditions, paired with the separate, unconditional duty to report each unchecked requirement by name and ground.

questions.question: A conforming-looking TARN file has a trailer whose magic, CRC, and version gate all validate correctly, whose file_id, reserved bytes, and flags are all valid, and whose committed_file_length field equals 320, matching the transport-reported physical file size exactly. The same trailer's dir_offset field is 200 and its dir_length field is 60. Under the trailer's remaining field-validation rules, does this trailer pass validation? If it fails, name the exact register-row identifier (e.g., "F12") for the specific defect, and state the reader outcome (name the outcome class).
questions.sections: Part I — §6.2 (trailer field-validation order and bounds), §21.2 (file-scope violation register)
questions.answer_form: A verdict (pass/fail) plus, if it fails, a single register-row ID (e.g. "F10") and an outcome-class name (e.g. "reject-file")
questions.why_it_matters: Requires computing dir_offset+dir_length against F-64 (260 vs 256) and then mapping that specific arithmetic failure to its own register row, distinguishing it from the several other trailer-gate rows a careless answerer might cite instead.

questions.question: A remote reader opens a TARN file by issuing a single speculative suffix-range request for the file's final 500 bytes of a much larger file; the response does not include byte offset 0 of the file. The fetched trailer and directory both validate successfully by every rule that applies to them. Is this reader obligated, before any other processing, to verify the 16-byte front signature block by byte equality? Answer yes or no, and name the requirement identifier that decides the answer.
questions.sections: Part I — §6.1 (front signature block / residency rule)
questions.answer_form: Yes/No plus a single requirement identifier (e.g. "[R-CNT-04]")
questions.why_it_matters: Tests the prose carve-out that the front-block check binds on residency, not on being a remote vs. local reader per se — a reader whose fetched window does not reach offset 0 may defer or omit the check, which a table alone does not state.

questions.question: A TARN file's directory contains a single top-level record whose type field is 0x0050 and whose MUST_UNDERSTAND flag bit is set to 1 (PRESERVE_ON_EDIT is also set to 1, so the flag combination itself is not separately defective). No record type 0x0050 is one this specification assigns. What reader outcome applies to this file (name the outcome class), and which register-row identifier documents this exact condition?
questions.sections: Part I — §7.2/§7.3 (unknown record types, MUST_UNDERSTAND gate), §10.2 (reserved numeric range for record types), §21.2 (register)
questions.answer_form: An outcome-class name plus a single register-row ID (e.g. "F35")
questions.why_it_matters: Requires combining the numeric-range table (0x0050 falls in the reserved, not experimental, range) with the MU=1 unknown-type rule to land on the correct one of several superficially similar register rows (F24, F35, F36 are all nearby but distinct).

questions.question: An appender opens an existing TARN file whose live trailer has flags = 0x00010000 (bit 16 set; every other bit, including every bit of the incompat lane, is 0). This specification's text defines no meaning for bit 16. The appender's commit adds no feature that requires any flag bit to be set. What exact 32-bit value, in hex, MUST the appender's new trailer's flags field carry?
questions.sections: Part I — §6.3 (version and flag gates, ignore-lane carry-forward)
questions.answer_form: A single 32-bit hex value
questions.why_it_matters: Tests the MUST-level keyword rule that an updater copies forward unknown ignore-lane bits unchanged and sets no other bit — a rule easy to conflate with a creator's flags=0 obligation, which does not apply here.

questions.question: A layer is declared with rank 3, dimensions of extents (500, 0, 10) and tile extents (64, 8, 4) respectively, interleaved channel layout, and 5 channels. What value MUST this layer's entry_count field equal?
questions.sections: Part II — §11.1 (zero-extent dimensions), §11.2 (grid arithmetic and addressed-tile count)
questions.answer_form: A single non-negative integer
questions.why_it_matters: Requires combining the general grid-count formula (ceiling division per dimension) with the specific carve-out that a zero extent forces that axis's grid count to 0, which zeroes the product regardless of the other two (non-trivial) dimensions' values.

questions.question: A layer has planar channel layout with 2 dimensions whose grid counts (number of tiles along each axis) are G0 = 5 and G1 = 3, and it has 4 channels (channel indices 0 through 3). Under linearization 1 (row-major), what is the disk tile ordinal — i.e., the zero-based tile-index entry number — of the tile carrying channel index 3 at tile coordinates (t0, t1) = (2, 1)?
questions.sections: Part II — §11.4 (spatial tile ordinal and disk tile ordinal formulas)
questions.answer_form: A single non-negative integer
questions.why_it_matters: Requires chaining two formulas from one section (spatial ordinal s from tile coordinates, then disk ordinal c·N+s for a planar layer) rather than reading either off a table alone.

questions.question: An interleaved layer has exactly two channels declared in order: channel `a` of type uint16, then channel `b` of type uint8. One tile of this layer has exactly two sample positions, with in-tile ordinals 0 and 1. Before any filtering, at in-tile ordinal 0 channel `a` has the bit pattern 0x0102 and channel `b` has the bit pattern 0xAA; at in-tile ordinal 1, channel `a` has 0x0304 and channel `b` has 0xBB. This layer declares filter 2 (byte-shuffle) and codec 1 (none). List the tile's stored bytes, in order, as a sequence of six uppercase hex byte-pairs separated by spaces.
questions.sections: Part II — §14.2 (byte layout, sample stride Q), §17.3 (byte-shuffle filter definition)
questions.answer_form: Six space-separated uppercase hex byte-pairs, in offset order
questions.why_it_matters: Combines the interleaved sample-stride byte layout with the byte-shuffle permutation formula on a concrete multi-channel, multi-position tile; getting the stride or the permutation direction wrong produces different bytes that a real implementation would disagree on.

questions.question: A layer record declares a nonzero per-tile alignment A = 1024 together with a nonzero slab run length S = 50 and a slab alignment A_slab = 4096 (itself a valid power of two in range). Is this combination of declarations a validity error? If so, name the register-row identifier and the resulting reader outcome (name the outcome class).
questions.sections: Part II — §16.1/§16.2 (alignment and slab declarations, mutual exclusivity), §21.3 (layer-scope register)
questions.answer_form: A verdict plus a single register-row ID (e.g. "L20") and an outcome-class name
questions.why_it_matters: Tests the keyword rule that per-tile alignment and slab declarations are mutually exclusive regardless of whether every individual field (A, S, A_slab) is independently well-formed — a case where a table-only reading would wrongly find nothing wrong.

questions.question: A layer declares a channel of sample type uint32 (a numeric type with a 4-byte element size). That channel's entry, as parsed from the layer record, gives a fill field with a length prefix of 2 (i.e., only 2 bytes of fill data follow). Is this a validity error? If so, name the register-row identifier and the resulting reader outcome.
questions.sections: Part II — §12.1 (sample-type element sizes), §7.4/§13.1 (fill field length constraint), §21.3 (register)
questions.answer_form: A verdict plus a single register-row ID (e.g. "L30") and an outcome-class name
questions.why_it_matters: Requires cross-referencing the sample-type table's element size against the fill-length constraint stated elsewhere, rather than reading either table alone.

questions.question: Under index_encoding 1, a layer record declares entry_count = 12 but an extent slot of (0, 0). Is this combination a validity error? If so, name the register-row identifier and the resulting reader outcome.
questions.answer_form: A verdict plus a single register-row ID (e.g. "L22") and an outcome-class name
questions.why_it_matters: Requires applying the extent_length = entry_count×20 + ⌈entry_count/2^16⌉×4 formula (giving 244) to notice that an extent slot of (0,0), meaning length 0, cannot match a nonzero entry_count — a mismatch invisible without doing the arithmetic.

questions.question: During an appender's commit, one of a layer's existing tile-index entries is not touched by the commit (the tile it addresses is neither superseded nor newly stored) — call it entry E. Entry E's own 20 bytes are well-formed under §15.3's classification (non-sentinel, offset ≥ 16, both fields in the valid domain, no overflow, extent within bounds), but the bytes at the extent entry E addresses fail entry E's own crc field. When the appender re-emits this layer's tile-index region, what MUST it do with entry E's 20 bytes? And separately, when a reader later requests the tile entry E addresses, what outcome does that read report (name the outcome class)?
questions.sections: Part III — §15.3 (entry validity: well-formed entry vs. failing stored-bytes CRC), §20.3 (append procedure, no repair of carried structures)
questions.answer_form: Two paired verdicts: what the appender does with the entry's bytes (an action), and the reader's outcome class for that tile
questions.why_it_matters: Tests the carve-out that an entry whose only defect is a failing stored-bytes CRC is itself well-formed, so an appender carries it forward byte-identically rather than repairing or dropping it, while a later read of that tile still reports reject-tile — two different actors, two different obligations, one concrete case.

questions.question: A reader issues one region request against an accessed planar layer, covering two channels (`temp`, channel index 0, and `mask`, channel index 1) across several spatial tiles. Of all the tile-index entries the request needs, exactly one — the entry for channel `temp`'s tile at one particular spatial tile — fails verification of its stored bytes against its crc field (a structurally well-formed entry; only its stored bytes' checksum fails); every other needed entry, across both channels and every other spatial tile the request covers, verifies and decodes without incident. Which of the following most narrowly and correctly describes what the reader is barred from returning: (a) only `temp` channel's data at that one spatial tile; (b) both channels' data at that one spatial tile; (c) all of `temp` channel's data across every spatial tile the request covers; (d) the entire request, including `mask` channel and every other spatial tile? Answer with the single letter.
questions.sections: Part III — §19.4 (tile-read algorithm, bounded failure), §2.4 (owning scope / tile vs. layer outcome)
questions.answer_form: A single letter (a, b, c, or d)
questions.why_it_matters: Tests that a tile-scope failure (reject-tile) is bounded to exactly the failing tile and does not propagate to the other channel at the same spatial location or to other tiles in the same multi-entry request — a scope-boundary rule stated in prose, not a table.

questions.question: A rewriter is compacting a TARN file. In doing so it must regenerate one layer's entire tile-index region, because some of that layer's stored extents are being relocated. Among that layer's existing tile-index entries is one entry that §15.3 classifies as reject-tile on a structural ground (for example, its offset and length fields are inconsistent with the sentinel pattern) — meaning the entry addresses no usable stored extent at all. List, as a short ordered list, the only two dispositions available to the rewriter for this situation (i.e., the only two things it is permitted to do), per the specification's own text.
questions.sections: Part III — §20.4 (drop licence for PE=0 records), §20.5 (rewriting, region regeneration)
questions.answer_form: An ordered list of exactly two named dispositions
questions.why_it_matters: Tests a specific carve-out: a structurally invalid entry has no stored extent for the rewriter to re-point when regenerating the region, so the rewriter cannot simply relocate it like every other entry, leaving only two named outs — drop the layer, or refuse to rewrite.

questions.question: An interleaved layer declares two channels, both int32 (4-byte element size each), and tile extents (128, 128) — so P = 16,384 sample positions per tile. This layer declares codec 3 (zstd). One of its stored tiles' zstd frame header declares (via a Window_Descriptor) a Window_Size of 1,048,576 bytes. Is this tile's frame a validity error under the codec's declared-window rule? If so, name the register-row identifier, the resulting outcome class, and whether the detecting actor is the reader or the verifier.
questions.sections: Part II/III — §14.2 (decoded size arithmetic), §17.2 (zstd frame window constraint), §21.4 (tile-scope register), §21.9 (the separate, non-violation resource-limit case)
questions.answer_form: A verdict plus a single register-row ID (e.g. "T21"), an outcome-class name, and a detector name (reader/verifier)
questions.why_it_matters: Requires computing the tile's decoded size from geometry (P×Q = 131,072 bytes) to see the declared window (1 MiB) exceeds it, and tests the quantifier distinction the document draws between ‘exceeds the tile's own decoded size’ (always a violation) versus ‘exceeds a reader's own resource bound’ (never one) — a distinction a rewording could easily blur.

questions.question: A layer's tile index has entry_count = 131,072, giving two segments: segment 0 (entries 0 through 65,535) and segment 1 (entries 65,536 through 131,071) — each covering exactly 65,536 entries. Every entry in segment 0 is the sentinel. In segment 1, every entry is the sentinel except for exactly one, which is a non-sentinel (stored-tile) entry. May the writer, for segment 1, emit the stored constant 0xEECB3BB2 as its segment-CRC-array value instead of computing the real CRC-32C over segment 1's actual entry bytes? Answer yes or no, and name the requirement identifier that decides the answer.
questions.sections: Part II — §15.4 (segment CRC, the all-sentinel shortcut constant)
questions.answer_form: Yes/No plus a single requirement identifier (e.g. "[R-IDX-05]")
questions.why_it_matters: Tests a conjunctive quantifier easy to half-read: the shortcut constant applies only where a segment is BOTH full (covers exactly 2^16 entries) AND entirely sentinels — segment 1 here is full but not all-sentinel, so the real CRC must still be computed, unlike segment 0.

findings.title: version_minor floor-and-carry rule for appenders is a SHOULD, not a MUST
findings.detail: While drafting a Part I question, I tried to build one around [R-CNT-26]'s appender version_minor rule: given an appender's input trailer version_minor and a commit that needs no new minor-gated feature, what value MUST the output's version_minor carry (the natural candidate answer being max(feature floor, prior minor))? On close reading, the rule is stated as a SHOULD, not a MUST: 'A writer SHOULD emit the lowest version_minor that defines every feature present in the file ... and an appender the maximum of that floor and the prior trailer's minor.' Because writer/updater conformance is semantic ([R-CNF-05]: two conforming writers given identical input MAY produce different conforming files) and this specific sub-rule is advisory, an appender that emits some other version_minor value is not thereby shown nonconforming by anything I can find in the text — there is no register row for it, and it is not listed among [R-ERR-05]'s hard limits. That means a question asking 'what value MUST the output carry' has no single answer this specification actually forces as a file-conformance matter, only a recommended one. I did not include this question in the final slate (I substituted a genuinely MUST-level question about ignore-lane flag carry-forward, [R-CNT-08]) precisely because of this softness. I am not confident this rises to a defect in the document — the SHOULD appears to be a deliberate, clearly-marked choice consistent with the document's general semantic-conformance stance — but it is a real trap for anyone trying to build a determinate byte-level conformance question on this specific rule, so I am reporting it rather than silently discarding it.
findings.quotation_a: A writer SHOULD emit the lowest version_minor that defines every feature present in the file — for a file expressible under this text, 0 — and an appender the maximum of that floor and the prior trailer's minor
findings.quotation_b: absent
findings.byte_level_rationale: This is not a two-edition divergence (I read only one edition) and not itself a byte-level defect in the specification; it is an observation about the difficulty of turning one specific SHOULD-level rule into a determinate byte-level quiz question, made in the course of building the slate.

answers.decisive_quote: A commit's committed_file_length is strictly greater than the prior trailer's, by at least 128
answers.reasoning: R-LIF-02 fixes the minimum strict increase per commit at 128 bytes (and a §9.2 Note derives the same 128-byte floor independently from the 64-byte trailer, the >=4-byte directory CRC, and the 64-alignment rule). Prior F = 128, so the smallest legal second-commit F is 128 + 128 = 256.

answers.reasoning: The single speculative suffix fetch returned the full file [0,30000), which contains both the trailer [29936,30000) and the directory [20,120); by R-CNT-09's containment rule the second (directory) request is unnecessary, and the same response discloses the transport-authoritative size per R-CNT-10, so open costs exactly 1 request. Because that fetch made bytes [0,16) resident, R-CNT-04 obliges byte-equality verification of the front signature block.

answers.reasoning: extent_offset (2^63-5) and extent_length (10) are each within [0,2^63-1] individually (so R-ENC-03 is not violated), but their declaration-derived sum is 2^63+5, exceeding the domain -- exactly register row F3's condition, governed by R-ENC-04, not R-ENC-03. Since this is a non-layer top-level record, §7.2 assigns the file as the governing scope, so the outcome is reject-file (confirmed by F3's table row, whose outcome per the §21.2 header is reject-file).

answers.reasoning: The final 64 bytes fail the trailer-magic check (register row F8, reject-file, detected at open). R-LIF-05 fixes the default read path as trailer-at-end-or-fail and forbids scanning backward; finding the earlier valid trailer is exclusively §9.6's deliberate recovery-scan operation, explicitly 'not a reader behavior' on the default path, so the reader may not fall back to it.

answers.reasoning: crc_of_crc_array's own 4 stored bytes sit inside the layer record's inline payload, which is part of the directory's record sequence; §8.1's map states the directory region's terminal checksum covers 'the preceding dir_length - 4 bytes (the raw record sequence)', which is what would catch corruption of crc_of_crc_array's stored bytes. Separately, §7.4's layout table defines crc_of_crc_array itself as 'CRC-32C over the index's segment-CRC array (§15)'.

answers.reasoning: Gy=ceil(10/4)=3, Gx=ceil(13/5)=3. (y,x)=(9,11) -> tile coords (2,2), in-tile position (1,1). Spatial/disk ordinal (interleaved) s = ty*Gx+tx = 2*3+2 = 8. In-tile ordinal u = uy*Tx+ux = 1*5+1 = 6. Sample stride Q = B_p+B_q = 2+1 = 3; channel q's in-sample offset F_q = B_p = 2 (p declared first). Byte offset = u*Q+F_q = 6*3+2 = 20. Verified by local Python computation.

answers.decisive_quote: the tile's pad bits ... MUST carry the plane's channel's fill bit
answers.reasoning: P=9, decoded size = ceil(9/8)=2 bytes, LSB-first packing. Byte0 packs ordinals 0-7 (true,false,true,false,true,false,true,false) -> bits 1,0,1,0,1,0,1,0 (LSB first) = 0x55. Byte1 bit0 = ordinal 8 (true) = 1; bits 1-7 are pad bits (P mod 8 = 1, so positions 1-7 are pad), fixed to the channel's fill bit (true=1) by R-SER-05, giving byte1 = 0xFF.

answers.decisive_quote: in a planar layer each channel's plane carries its own decoded size ... and the largest governs
answers.reasoning: P = 16384*16384 = 268,435,456; channel b is float64 (8 bytes/element), so its planar decoded size = P*8 = 2,147,483,648 bytes. R-COD-07's lz4 cap is 0x7E000000 = 2,113,929,216 bytes, and in a planar layer 'the largest [channel plane] governs'. Channel b's plane (2,147,483,648) exceeds the cap by 33,554,432 bytes; channel a's plane (268,435,456, uint8) does not. So the codec-4 declaration is nonconforming, decisively because of channel b.

answers.decisive_quote: "a" and "a" are the same key, and a document in which any one object carries that key twice is unreadable
answers.reasoning: Key identity under R-MTA-04 is the decoded string, not source bytes; a literal 'café' key and an escaped 'café' key decode to the identical string, so the object carries the same key twice -- register row R9's exact condition. R9's outcome class, per the §21.5 header ('Outcome: ignore-record'), is ignore-record, and the row's own condition text is 'Two members of one object in a user-metadata document carry the same key, identity being the decoded string and not the JSON source bytes'.

answers.reasoning: §18.2 states the content-size field, when present, 'MUST equal the byte length of the decoded document' (800 here, not the declared 750), and explicitly routes such a mismatch to R4 (a broken frame constraint) rather than R3 (a failure to decode), since the bytes do decode successfully. This is R-MTA-09's document-level transposition of R-COD-06's tile rule, where the compared quantity is the layer's declared decoded size rather than a measured decode output.

R-RDR-04 states that a layer-scope failure within a request 'bars the request's remaining entries and all further service from the layer' but is prospective only, so values already returned (segment 0 and 1's tiles) stand unaffected, while no further requests may be served from the layer afterward.

answers.reasoning: §20.3 step 4 expressly forbids extending and shortening a planar layer's channel list in the same commit: 'a commit that shortens a planar layer's channel list appends no channel to it and one that extends it removes none, whatever the counts'. The stated equivalent-effect alternatives are exactly two: perform it as two separate commits, or perform a whole-file rewrite (§20.5).

answers.reasoning: §20.4 states that for a type the updater does not implement, the record's stored flags (not a registry) are authoritative; here that sub-record's stored MU bit is 1. The table's MU=1 row: 'Retain byte-identical. The updater MUST NOT modify the scope the record governs. At layer scope an unknown critical record blocks modification of that layer, its drop included.' The user-metadata sub-record (registered type, registry-fixed MU=0,PE=1) is irrelevant to this block; it is the unimplemented experimental-range sub-record's MU=1 status that forbids the drop.

answers.answer: (a) no; (b) no; (c) drop the layer, or refuse to rewrite
answers.decisive_quote: it can neither reproduce the entry nor invent a replacement: drop the layer ... or refuse
answers.reasoning: §20.5 states that an entry §15.3 classifies reject-tile on a structural ground (here: offset=sentinel, length!=sentinel) has no stored extent for regeneration to target, so it cannot be reproduced unchanged (a); and the rewriter cannot 'invent a replacement' such as writing the true sentinel pattern either (b), since that would be repairing rather than carrying forward a detected violation (barred by R-WRT-01/R-LIF-01's no-repair principle). R-WRT-06 then leaves exactly two disposals for the layer: drop it (licensed by §20.4's table for the layer record) or refuse to rewrite.

answers.citations: §9.2 [R-LIF-02] (steps and closing clause); §9.2 Note 2 (the derivation from R-LIF-01/R-CNT-06/R-CNT-27)
answers.decisive_quote: A commit's committed_file_length is strictly greater than the prior trailer's, by at least 128, so the committed file length orders a file's generations (§9.3).
answers.reasoning: The first generation's trailer declares F0 = 128. R-LIF-02 fixes the minimum step between successive commits' committed_file_length at strictly greater, by at least 128 (forced by the 64-byte trailer, the >=4-byte directory, the >=16 dir_offset floor and the 64-alignment requirement, as §9.2's second Note derives). The second commit is an ordinary append (not a rewrite, so file_id and the increasing-F rule both apply), so the smallest legal F1 is 128 + 128 = 256.

answers.citations: §6.4 [R-CNT-09] (speculative suffix + containment), [R-CNT-10] (transport-authoritative size in the range response); §6.1 [R-CNT-04] (front-block residency); §19.1 step 1
answers.decisive_quote: A reader MAY instead speculatively fetch a suffix window in one request and use containment: if the fetched buffer contains the directory region, request 2 is unnecessary.
answers.reasoning: The single speculative fetch, though aimed at the final 40,000 bytes, actually returns bytes [0,30000) — the entire file — because the file is shorter than the requested suffix. That response necessarily carries the transport-authoritative file size (R-CNT-10) and contains both the trailer [F-64,F) and the directory [20,120), so by R-CNT-09's containment rule no second request is needed: total cost is 1 request for trailer+directory. Because this same fetch also makes bytes [0,16) resident (it reached offset 0), R-CNT-04 obliges the reader to verify the 16-byte front signature block by byte equality before other processing — residency, not transport, is the test, and this reader's open happens to leave those bytes resident.

answers.citations: §7.2 [R-CNT-13] (extent-slot validity, non-layer top-level record scope = file); §4.2 [R-ENC-04] (declaration-derived sum overflow); §2.4 [R-CNF-08]; register row F3
answers.decisive_quote: Any other combination with either half zero, an extent_offset < 16, an extent extending past F − 64, or an overflowing sum — extent_offset + extent_length is a declaration-derived quantity under `[R-ENC-04]` — is a validity error at the scope the record governs (§7.3): the layer for a layer record and for sub-records, the file for other top-level records
answers.reasoning: extent_offset = 2^63-5 and extent_length = 10 each lie in [0, 2^63-1] individually, so R-ENC-03 (the per-field domain rule) is not violated. But their declaration-derived sum, 2^63+5, exceeds 2^63-1, which is exactly R-ENC-04's overflow condition (matching register row F3: 'A sum of a u64 offset and length taken from the file exceeds 2^63-1 although each field alone is in domain', instanced for a non-layer top-level record). The record is a user-metadata record (not a layer record), so per §7.2 its extent slot is governed at file scope, giving outcome reject-file.

answers.citations: §9.5 [R-LIF-05] (default read path); §9.6 [R-LIF-06] (recovery scan is a separate, deliberate operation, not a reader behavior)
answers.decisive_quote: The default read path is trailer-at-end-or-fail: a reader that finds no valid trailer in the final 64 bytes MUST report the file torn or invalid and MUST NOT scan backward.
answers.reasoning: The final 64 bytes fail the trailer-magic check (an F8-type failure). Under the default open path (not a deliberate recovery operation, §9.6), R-LIF-05 requires the reader to report the file torn or invalid and forbids scanning backward — so the earlier, byte-valid trailer 64 bytes further back is never consulted on this path, even though it would satisfy every check §9.6's recovery scan applies. Falling back to it is exactly the recovery-scan behavior §9.6 reserves for recovery tools and verifiers, 'never conforming readers on the default path.'

answers.answer: (a) the directory region's terminal checksum; (b) the layer's segment-CRC array
answers.citations: §8.1 coverage map (Directory region row); §7.4 (crc_of_crc_array field definition); §7.1
answers.decisive_quote: Directory region | final 4 bytes of the region | the preceding dir_length − 4 bytes (the raw record sequence) ... crc_of_crc_array | u32 | CRC-32C over the index's segment-CRC array (§15)
answers.reasoning: crc_of_crc_array is a field inside a layer record's inline payload, and every layer record's header+inline payload lies inside the directory's raw record sequence (the dir_length-4 covered bytes). Per §8.1's coverage map, that whole record sequence is covered by the directory region's own terminal 4-byte CRC-32C — so bit-corruption of crc_of_crc_array's stored bytes is caught by that directory-region checksum. Separately, and unrelated to what covers it, crc_of_crc_array's own defined purpose (§7.4) is to be the CRC-32C over the index's segment-CRC array (the tile index's per-segment CRC array, §15.1/§15.4), which crc_of_crc_array itself covers as the next link in the §8.2 chain of trust.

answers.decisive_quote: the disk tile ordinal, which orders tile-index entries (§15), is s for an interleaved layer ... channel c's value at in-tile ordinal u sits at byte u · Q + Fᶜ
answers.reasoning: Grid counts: G_y = ceil(10/4) = 3, G_x = ceil(13/5) = 3. Tile coordinates for (y,x)=(9,11): t_y = 9 div 4 = 2, t_x = 11 div 5 = 2. Spatial ordinal s = t_y*G_x + t_x = 2*3+2 = 8 (§11.4's s = Σ tᵢ·∏_{j>i}Gⱼ, with x last-declared so its coefficient is 1). Interleaved layer's disk ordinal is s itself: 8. For the byte offset: in-tile position u_y = 9 mod 4 = 1, u_x = 11 mod 5 = 1; in-tile ordinal u = u_y*T_x + u_x = 1*5+1 = 6 (row-major, last dimension x fastest, tile extent T_x=5). Channels 'p' (int16, size 2) then 'q' (uint8, size 1): sample stride Q = 2+1 = 3; q's in-sample offset F_q = size(p) = 2. Channel q's byte offset at in-tile ordinal u is u·Q + F_q = 6·3 + 2 = 20.

answers.citations: §14.3 [R-SER-03] (packed boolean plane bit layout); §14.5 [R-SER-05] (pad-bit content = channel's fill bit)
answers.decisive_quote: value k occupies bit k mod 8 of byte k div 8 (§4.4) ... Every pad bit (§14.3) MUST carry the plane's channel's fill bit.
answers.reasoning: P=9 values (true,false,true,false,true,false,true,false,true at ordinals 0-8), LSB-first packing. Byte 0 holds ordinals 0-7: bit0=1(T),bit1=0(F),bit2=1(T),bit3=0(F),bit4=1(T),bit5=0(F),bit6=1(T),bit7=0(F) -> value = 1+4+16+64 = 85 = 0x55. Byte 1 holds ordinal 8 in bit0 (true=1) plus 7 pad bits (bit positions 1-7, since P mod 8 = 1); the fill value is recorded true (0x01), so every pad bit is 1, giving byte1 = 0b11111111 = 0xFF. Byte order requested is byte0 then byte1: 55 FF.

answers.citations: §14.2 [R-SER-02] (planar decoded size = P·Bᶜ); §17.2 [R-COD-07] (lz4 decoded-size cap, largest plane governs)
answers.decisive_quote: Writers MUST NOT declare this codec for a layer any of whose addressed tiles' decoded size exceeds 0x7E000000 bytes — the block format's practical interoperability bound; in a planar layer each channel's plane carries its own decoded size (§14.2, §14.3), and the largest governs
answers.reasoning: P = 16384*16384 = 268,435,456 sample positions per tile. Channel b is float64 (element size 8), planar decoded size = P·B_b = 268,435,456*8 = 2,147,483,648 bytes. Channel a is uint8 (size 1): P·B_a = 268,435,456 bytes, well under the cap. R-COD-07's lz4 cap is 0x7E000000 = 2,113,929,216 bytes, and the largest channel plane governs in a planar layer. Channel b's plane (2,147,483,648) exceeds that cap, so the codec-4 declaration does not satisfy R-COD-07 for this layer; channel b is the decisive (governing) channel.

answers.decisive_quote: Key identity is the *decoded* string, not its JSON source bytes: "a" and "a" are the same key, and a document in which any one object carries that key twice is unreadable, since which member wins would otherwise be a parser's choice.
answers.reasoning: Under encoding 1 (verbatim JSON), the document is decoded as ordinary JSON text; key identity for the duplicate-key rule is the decoded UTF-8 string, not the source bytes. A literal 'café' key and an escaped-but-equivalent 'café' key (e.g. one written with a \uXXXX escape for the accented character) decode to the identical string, so the object carries that key twice — a violation of R-MTA-04's no-duplicate-keys restriction (register row R9). Every R9-type violation takes the ignore-record outcome under the user-metadata quarantine (R-CNT-25), which R9's own row confirms (detector: reader, detected: extent use, outcome ignore-record per §21.5's heading).

answers.answer: (a) no; (b) broken frame constraint (R4); (c) the field must equal the decoded document's actual byte length (800), whereas the analogous tile-scope rule under the same codec requires the field to match the tile's decoded size as derived purely from the layer's structural declarations (geometry/layout/channel types), never from what the stored bytes actually decode to.
answers.citations: §18.2 [R-MTA-09] (content-size field pinned to decoded document length) and its contrast with §17.2 [R-COD-06] (tile content-size field pinned to declared decoded size); §21.5 rows R3/R4
answers.decisive_quote: The frame's content-size field, unlike the decoded size and the window, is *not* left to the reader: it MAY be present, and when present it MUST equal the byte length of the decoded document. A mismatch is one of the frame constraints R4 registers, not a failure to decode under R3: the bytes decode, and what is wrong is what the header said about them.
answers.reasoning: The document decodes to 800 bytes, but the frame's Frame_Content_Size field (present, since Single_Segment_Flag makes it double as Window_Size) declares 750 — a mismatch against R-MTA-09's rule that a present content-size field must equal the decoded document's byte length. This is explicitly routed to R4 ('a broken frame constraint'), not R3 ('failure to decode'), because the bytes still decode; what's wrong is what the header asserted about them. Every register row (R4 included) is a file-conformance violation regardless of its ignore-record blast radius, so the file as a whole is not conforming. The contrast with the tile rule (R-COD-06): for a tile, the frame's content-size field (when present) must match the tile's decoded size, a quantity fixed by the layer's declarations alone and known before any decode; a user-metadata document has no such declared size, so §18.2 substitutes the document's actual decoded byte length as the quantity the field must match.

answers.citations: §15.4 [R-IDX-04] (segment CRC verification, cross-check failure outcome); §19.4 step 3/step 8 [R-RDR-04] (prospective bar, already-returned values stand)
answers.decisive_quote: To use entry k, a reader MUST verify, in dependency order, crc_of_crc_array over the fetched CRC array and the segment CRC over the fetched segment containing k ... any mismatch or cross-check failure (`[R-CNT-17]`) is reject-layer. ... the bar is prospective, so values the reader has already returned under §19.2's timing stand
answers.reasoning: Segment 2's stored CRC failing verification is an index-chain (segment CRC) failure, which R-IDX-04 assigns reject-layer — a layer-scope outcome, unlike a stored tile's own CRC failure (which would be tile-scope). Per §19.4 step 8 / R-RDR-04, a failure that takes layer scope 'bars the request's remaining entries and all further service from the layer,' but 'the bar is prospective... values the reader has already returned under §19.2's timing stand' — so the segment-0/segment-1 sample values already returned within this same request are not retroactively invalidated (answer to (b): no), while the reader may serve no further requests from this layer afterward (answer to (c): no).

answers.answer: no; two commits, or a rewrite
answers.citations: §20.3 step 4 [R-WRT-04] (planar channel-list extend/shorten exclusivity within one commit)
answers.decisive_quote: a commit that shortens a planar layer's channel list appends no channel to it and one that extends it removes none, whatever the counts, so replacing the last channel, or any run of channels at the end, is two commits or a rewrite.

probe_answers.answer: Two requests, in order, before the record sequence can be parsed. (1) Suffix range [F-64, F) = [4032, 4096) for a 4,096-byte file -- 64 bytes. Its response also discloses the transport-authoritative complete length F where the transport supports it, so this single request supplies both step 1 (obtain F) and step 2 (trailer bytes) of the open algorithm. Validate in this fixed order: trailer magic; trailer CRC; version gate; then (all three passed) the remaining field gates as a set: flags, committed_file_length=transport size and multiple of 64, dir_offset>=16, dir_length>=4, dir_offset+dir_length<=F-64, file_id!=0, reserved bytes zero. Any failure is reject-file before the directory is ever touched. (2) [dir_offset, dir_offset+dir_length) -- the directory region; verify its trailing 4-byte CRC-32C over the preceding dir_length-4 bytes before any other use, then parse the record sequence. Total bytes fetched before the trailer+directory are both validated: 64 + dir_length. The document's baseline is exactly these two requests (a reader MAY instead speculatively fetch one larger suffix window and use containment to avoid request 2, but that is an alternative, not part of the counted baseline). The field bounding the second range before it is read is the trailer's own dir_offset (start) together with dir_length (extent) -- both obtained from request 1 and gated by [R-CNT-06]'s own-field checks, and neither may be acted on until the trailer CRC covering them has verified, per [R-ENC-10]/[R-ENC-05].
probe_answers.decisive_quote: The baseline remote open is two requests, each with an exact target: (1) fetch the final 64 bytes ... (2) fetch [dir_offset, dir_offset + dir_length)

probe_answers.answer: 0x00000004 sets bit 2 (bit 0 = LSB). Bits 0-15 are the trailer's incompat lane; bit 2 lies inside it. Format major 1's text defines no flag bits at all, so every incompat-lane bit is unimplemented by definition, and a reader MUST reject-file on any set incompat-lane bit (register row F19, governing [R-CNT-08]). The file is NOT conforming: the trailer layout table's own valid-values column for flags requires bits 0-15 'all zero,' so a set bit violates the field's stated valid range under [R-CNT-06] independent of which reader opens it -- every conforming reader rejects this file, and it is nonconforming under the file-conformance predicate itself.

probe_answers.decisive_quote: Flags: a reader MUST reject-file on any set bit it does not implement in the incompat lane (bits 0-15) ... In this specification's text no flag bits are defined

findings.location_a: §19.1 ("The open algorithm"), step 1, vs. §2.3 ("Conformance classes") and its worked Note on row F5, and [R-CNF-11]'s definition of a verifier's cannot-establish verdict
findings.title: Open-algorithm step 1 applies the 128-byte floor before the major is known; §2.3 says it must not reach a foreign-major file
findings.detail: §19.1 step 1 instructs a reader, as the very first step of opening any file: 'Obtain the transport-authoritative file size F ...; an F below 128 is a validity error at file scope decided from F alone and needing no other byte of the file ([R-CNT-27], F5).' This is unconditional and precedes step 2 (fetching the trailer), so it is applied before version_major -- which lives inside the trailer -- is ever read. Separately, §2.3's format-major 'reach' doctrine ([R-CNF-13]) states a condition reaches a file declaring another major only when it asserts an invariant [R-CNT-24] fixes in every major, and its own worked Note names F5 by row number as a condition that does NOT reach: 'F5 does not reach although its subject is the physical file size, which no major can redefine: the 128-byte floor it asserts is derived from a directory of at least 4 bytes at an offset of at least 16 and a 64-aligned F ([R-CNT-27]), and those are format major 1's.' The accompanying general rule is explicit that a non-reaching condition 'is not assessed against a file declaring another major, no violation of it is established there' -- which can only be honored by first determining (or ruling out) the declared major, an operation §19.1's step ordering forecloses for any file under 128 bytes, since that determination needs trailer bytes step 1 has not yet fetched. Concretely: for a file with, say, 80<=F<128 whose trailer (once read) validates magic, CRC and a version_major the reader does not implement, §19.1 prescribes an immediate, trailer-blind reject-file on F5/[R-CNT-27] grounds, while §2.3 prescribes that F5 must not be established against this file at all, leaving only the capability-refusal ground of [R-CNT-07]. This is not cosmetic: [R-CNF-11] defines a verifier's nonconforming and cannot-establish verdicts as mutually exclusive and priority-ordered ('An established violation takes priority: a verifier that has established any violation reports nonconforming ... and cannot establish is available only to a traversal that established no violation'), and separately names exactly this situation -- 'the file names a format major version it does not implement' -- as a canonical ground for cannot-establish. Whether this file's verdict is nonconforming (F5 established, per §19.1's literal, major-blind ordering) or cannot-establish (F5 does not reach, per §2.3, and only the major is the obstacle) is left genuinely undetermined by the document as written, even though the distinction is MUST-level and consequential.
findings.quotation_a: an F below 128 is a validity error at file scope decided from F alone and needing no other byte of the file (`[R-CNT-27]`, F5)
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: It decides a verifier's MUST-level verdict for one and the same input: nonconforming (an established file-conformance violation, F5) versus cannot-establish (no violation established, only an unimplemented major, per [R-CNF-11]'s own example of that verdict). [R-CNF-11] states these outcomes are mutually exclusive and that an established violation takes strict priority, so an implementer who codes the literal, sequential reading of §19.1 and one who codes §2.3's reach doctrine will certify or refuse to certify the identical bytes differently, and will report different grounds to a caller -- exactly the reader-vs-corruption diagnostic distinction §6.3 itself says SHOULD be kept separate.

findings.location_a: §17.4 ([R-COD-11]) and §2.3 ([R-CNF-03]), read against §21.6's closing paragraph and §21.9 ([R-ERR-04])
findings.title: No outcome class describes a reader that has simply not yet implemented a core codec/filter/type
findings.detail: The document names exactly two licensed cases in which a conforming reader refuses an otherwise-acceptable, possibly-conforming file: an unimplemented format major ([R-CNT-07]) and an experimental-range top-level record type carrying MU=1 ([R-CNT-15]), which §21.6's closing paragraph explicitly enumerates as 'the two capability refusals.' Everything else a conforming reader must be able to do -- every codec, every filter, every sample type, both channel layouts, both user-metadata encodings, both registered record types -- is instead made a precondition of being a 'conforming reader' at all ([R-CNF-03]), and §17.4/[R-COD-11] is explicit that software lacking one of these is simply 'not a conforming reader,' full stop, with no register row, no outcome class, and no described behavior for what such software does when it meets, e.g., a zstd-coded layer. This is a foreseeable situation for anyone using this document as an implementation order (build codec 1 first, add zstd later), yet the conformance vocabulary -- which otherwise gives every other capability boundary (format major, MU=1 record type, resource limits under [R-ERR-04]) an explicit, licensed, reportable disposition -- has nothing to say about it beyond 'that software is out of scope.'
findings.quotation_a: software unable to execute an assigned codec or filter is not a conforming reader (`[R-CNF-03]`)
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: A genuinely conforming reader, by [R-CNF-03]'s own definition, can never be in this state, so resolving the question changes nothing about which bytes a conforming implementation may emit or must accept/reject. The gap is in what the document tells a partial implementation to do while it is still being built, not in what a finished conforming reader does, so it fails the byte-level test and is reported as a documentation-completeness observation rather than a conformance-affecting ambiguity.

probe_answers.answer: In order: (1) new tile payload, 100,000 bytes; (2) the layer's full new tile-index region, 644 bytes (32 entries × 20 + 4-byte segment CRC — one entry re-pointed, 31 byte-identical); (3) new complete directory + CRC (every record byte-identical except the modified layer's); (4) pre-trailer pad to the next 64-byte boundary; (5) new 64-byte trailer. Prior bytes that become slack: the superseded tile's old payload and the layer's entire prior 644-byte index region (not just the changed entry), plus the old directory/pad/trailer being superseded.
probe_answers.citations: §20.3's worked example immediately following R-WRT-04; R-CNT-17's general index-size formula (§7.4); R-LIF-02's fixed commit step order (§9.2).
probe_answers.decisive_quote: "Superseding one 100,000-byte stored tile of a 32-tile interleaved layer appends: the new payload (100,000 bytes), the layer's full new index region (32 · 20 + 4 = 644 bytes — one entry re-pointed, 31 byte-identical), the new directory (every record byte-identical except the modified layer's), the pad, and the 64-byte trailer. The prior index region and the superseded payload become slack, reclaimable only by a rewrite."

probe_answers.answer: An appender MUST NOT append at all — the file is reject-file for the appender as a reader first, so no commit is available on it under any target. A rewriter MUST refuse to rewrite the file outright, on the ground that such a type may define references it cannot safely relocate.
probe_answers.citations: §20.4 preservation table, MU=1 row; R-CNT-15 (§7.2); R-WRT-06 (§20.5).
probe_answers.decisive_quote: "At file scope no commit is available at all: the updater is a reader of the file first (§2.3), and [R-CNT-15] makes an unimplemented top-level MU = 1 record reject-file... At either scope a rewriter MUST refuse to rewrite the file, on [R-WRT-06]'s own ground."

probe_answers.answer: Yes, an appender MAY drop it in a commit whose only effect is the drop (explicitly licensed). Yes, a rewriter MAY drop it in any rewrite. Neither is required (MUST) to report the loss; the keyword is SHOULD.
probe_answers.citations: §20.4 preservation table, MU=0/PE=0 row.
probe_answers.decisive_quote: "an appender MAY drop the record in any commit it is otherwise free to make — one whose only effect is the drop included — and a rewriter MAY drop it in any rewrite. An updater that drops such a record SHOULD report the loss."

probe_answers.answer: (a) Appender's commit: flags unchanged — bit 20 remains set, no other ignore-lane bit set. (b) Rewrite: same as (a) — bit 20 copied forward, no other bit set. (c) A creator writing a new file from decoded input content: flags = 0 — bit 20 is NOT carried over, because a plain creator undertakes nothing toward its input regardless of what it read or decoded.
probe_answers.citations: R-CNT-08 (§6.3); §20.5's restatement for rewriters; §20.1's three-tier taxonomy (creator vs. appender vs. rewriter) and §20.2/§6.3's flags=0 rule for creators.
probe_answers.decisive_quote: "An updater MUST copy forward unknown ignore-lane bits of its input file, MUST NOT clear them, and MUST NOT set any other... As a creator it undertakes nothing toward its input, whatever it read: §20.2 binds it, it writes flags = 0."

probe_answers.answer: Not permitted as an appender operation (fill is a fixed declaration once a layer stores a tile). Operations offered instead: create a new layer with the desired fill, or a rewrite that re-declares the layer under a fresh file_id. Whether the resulting file (if such a commit were nonetheless made) is nonconforming is conditional: the bar itself is a conduct rule that does not by itself make the file nonconforming, but if the layer has any tile with padding positions, the stale padding bytes now mismatch the new fill, which IS a detectable violation (T4, reject-tile, verifier-detected) and the file is nonconforming; if the layer has no padding at all, the change is unwitnessed and the file is not made nonconforming by it.
probe_answers.citations: §20.3 step 4 fixed-declarations list and its 'own terms' paragraph; §14.5/R-SER-05; §21.4 row T4; §21.7's witnessed/unwitnessed test.
probe_answers.decisive_quote: "This bar binds the commit as an actor: no file is nonconforming by virtue of its violation... a file such a commit leaves can be nonconforming on its own terms... but for a stored tile's decoded size, a padding position or pad bit, or a boolean byte the register witnesses (T3, T14, T21, T22, T4, T5, T2)... no check any actor owes able to see it."

probe_answers.answer: The next reader, on the default read path, finds no valid trailer in the final 64 physical bytes (the old trailer trailₙ is no longer at the file's end) and MUST report the file torn/invalid, and MUST NOT scan backward. The physical byte sequence as a whole is not a conforming file (fails the trailer gates at file scope), but the committed prefix ending at the old F is fully intact and recoverable. The next appender MUST NOT append; it must run the deliberate recovery scan (§9.6), which finds trailₙ as the nearest surviving candidate, re-verifies it whole-file, truncates the physical file to that old F (or overwrites from F and truncates no later than its own trailer-durability step), reports the candidate settled on and how many were rejected, and then commits afresh from there.
probe_answers.citations: §9.2's own 'what a crash sees' worked example, row 2 (mid-commit); R-LIF-05 (§9.5); R-LIF-04 (§9.4); R-LIF-06 (§9.6).
probe_answers.decisive_quote: "mid-commit ... trailₙ intact, but no longer at the file's end ... a reader on the default path reports the file torn and MUST NOT scan backward."

probe_answers.answer: It must verify, for each stored tile it copies, the full structural checksum chain — crc_of_crc_array over the fetched segment-CRC array, the segment CRC over the segment containing the entry, and the entry's own crc field against the tile's stored bytes — never a decode of the tile's content (Part I/Part II independence). When a checksum fails, this is a detected violation the rewriter may not silently carry forward; its only two options are to refuse the whole rewrite, or drop the entire layer (its record's registry-fixed flags being MU=0/PE=0, which licenses the drop) — there is no finer-grained 'drop just this tile' disposal in the document's carry/re-create/drop framework. It may NOT instead re-create the layer, because re-creation requires decoding the layer's content under §20.2's creator rules, which by hypothesis this rewriter cannot do for this sample type.
probe_answers.citations: §3.3 Note (Part I/Part II independence); R-WRT-09 (§20.5); §20.5's general refuse/drop-or-refuse rule; §20.4's registry-fixed layer flags (§7.3); §20.5's re-creation definition.
probe_answers.decisive_quote: "it relies structurally on every structure it copies, so it MUST verify each link of the chain... before emitting that structure's bytes... A rewriter MUST refuse to rewrite when any check [R-WRT-09] obliges fails... Dropping is the one disposal that answers, and only where §20.4's table licenses it... A layer the rewrite re-creates is new output... written... from content the rewriter decoded."

probe_answers.answer: No, the commit may not drop the layer. The layer's own registry-fixed PE=0 would ordinarily license dropping it, but that license is overridden the instant it carries an unimplemented MU=1 sub-record, because dropping the layer necessarily modifies away that sub-record's governed scope, which the MU=1 row forbids. I checked §20.4's table (MU=1 row), §20.4's very next paragraph (explicit statement about this exact case), and §7.2's Note — all three agree; no disagreement found.
probe_answers.citations: §20.4 preservation table MU=1 row; §20.4's paragraph beginning 'A commit MAY therefore drop a layer record'; §7.2's Note.
probe_answers.decisive_quote: "One sub-record blocks the drop, a sub-record of a type the updater does not implement with MU = 1, the drop being a modification of the scope it governs (the table's first row)."

probe_answers.answer: The append procedure's own steps (step 2 and step 5) do not state an independent rule; they explicitly delegate to §20.4 ('MUST NOT drop the record save where §20.4 licenses the drop'; 'Re-emit the directory per §20.4'). §20.4's MU=0/PE=0 row licenses exactly this drop. The two sections agree completely — they are one rule stated once with an explicit cross-reference, not two independent rules that happen to align.
probe_answers.citations: §20.3 step 2; §20.3 step 5; §20.4 preservation table MU=0/PE=0 row.
probe_answers.decisive_quote: "MUST NOT drop the record save where §20.4 licenses the drop." / "Re-emit the directory per §20.4, followed by its CRC."

probe_answers.answer: The preservation table obliges only retain-or-drop (the table's PE=0 row), not MU=1's mandatory retention, because the MU=1 row is expressly scoped to types the updater does NOT implement. Since the updater implements this type (from its own definition), only the PE bit selects the governing row, and PE=0 licenses the drop. So the updater MAY drop this unmodified record (SHOULD report the loss). The deciding sentence is explicit and singular.
probe_answers.citations: §20.4's paragraph immediately following the three-row table.
probe_answers.decisive_quote: "Its MU = 1 row reaches only a type the updater does not implement — an updater implements both registered types and understands an unregistered type it implements from its definition, modifying their records as §20.3 and that definition provide — so for an implemented type only the PE bit bites."

findings.title: MU=1 table row is easy to misread as unconditional for an implemented-but-unregistered type
findings.detail: The three-row preservation table's rows are captioned by MU/PE value, and its MU=1 row reads as an unconditional 'retain byte-identical, never drop' rule. But the paragraph immediately following the table states this row 'reaches only a type the updater does not implement,' so for a type the updater implements (even an unregistered one whose private definition fixes MU=1), only the PE bit governs and PE=0 licenses a drop. An implementer reading only the table's row captions, without this connecting sentence, would very plausibly conclude the opposite: that this record must always be retained. This changes which bytes a conforming updater may legitimately emit (record present vs. record dropped) for the identical input state.
findings.quotation_a: "Its MU = 1 row reaches only a type the updater does not implement... so for an implemented type only the PE bit bites."
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: Directly determines whether a conforming updater's output directory may omit this record: reading only the table row, an implementer would forbid the drop; reading the connecting sentence, the drop is licensed. Two implementations could diverge on this exact byte (presence/absence of the record) for identical input and identical operation.

findings.title: An ignore-lane flag bit survives an appender/rewriter but is silently dropped by a plain creator that read the same input
findings.detail: A tool that opens an existing file, decodes its content, and writes a brand-new file from that content is, per §20.1's own taxonomy, a 'creator' unless it either extends the input (appender) or explicitly undertakes §20.4/§20.5's preservation obligations (rewriter). A creator 'undertakes nothing toward its input, whatever it read' and MUST write flags=0. So the identical starting trailer bit (an unknown ignore-lane bit) is preserved byte-for-byte by an appender or a rewriter, but is zeroed by a creator that happens to have read and decoded the very same file — a divergence driven entirely by which of the three named tiers the tool is classified as, not by anything about the bit or the content.
findings.quotation_a: "As a creator it undertakes nothing toward its input, whatever it read: §20.2 binds it, it writes flags = 0, and it answers for every byte of its output."
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: Directly determines one bit's value in the output trailer's flags field for otherwise-identical processing of identical input content, depending solely on which writer tier the tool self-identifies as.

findings.title: Whether an impermissible fill-only change makes the resulting file byte-level nonconforming depends on the layer's own padding geometry, not on the change itself
findings.detail: §20.3 step 4 bars an appender from changing a stored layer's fill, framing the bar as a conduct rule that does not itself make a file nonconforming. But the same passage identifies T4 (padding-position content mismatching the declared fill) as one of the specific register rows such a change CAN trigger. Since padding positions exist only in tiles at the high edge of a dimension whose extent is not a multiple of its tile extent, the very same forbidden fill-only commit produces a byte-level nonconforming file (via T4) for a layer with any padding, and produces a file with no detectable defect at all for a layer with none — an outcome that turns entirely on unrelated geometry fields, not on the fill change's own severity.
findings.quotation_a: "a file such a commit leaves can be nonconforming on its own terms... but for a stored tile's decoded size, a padding position or pad bit, or a boolean byte the register witnesses (T3, T14, T21, T22, T4, T5, T2)... no check any actor owes able to see it."
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: Directly determines whether a conforming verifier must reject the output file (T4, reject-tile) or accept it, for byte-identical fill-declaration edits, depending solely on whether the layer's tile-extent-vs-dimension-extent arithmetic produces any padding position.
