probe_answers.answer: 128 bytes total. [0,16) front signature block (magic 89 54 41 52 4E 0D 0A 1A + 8 zero bytes). [16,20) directory region: 0 records + CRC-32C of zero bytes = 00000000. [20,64) pre-trailer pad, 44 bytes, slack. [64,128) trailer: magic at [64,72)=8A 4E 52 41 54 0D 0A 1A; version_major [72,74)=1; version_minor [74,76)=0; flags [76,80)=0 (no incompat, no ignore-lane bits); dir_offset [80,88)=16; dir_length [88,96)=4; committed_file_length [96,104)=128; file_id [104,112)=any nonzero value (writer's own random draw, e.g. Appendix A's EF CD AB 89 67 45 23 01); reserved [112,124)=0; trailer CRC [124,128)=CRC-32C over trailer bytes [0,60) (0x402F157E for Appendix A's exact file_id choice, but this value depends on file_id). This file has zero layers, which section 21.6 records as a conforming, defined condition.
probe_answers.citations: Section 5.1's Example ('The smallest conforming file is exactly 128 bytes...'); R-CNT-27 (128-byte floor); section 6.2's trailer layout table; Appendix A's byte table and hex dump.
probe_answers.decisive_quote: The smallest conforming file is exactly 128 bytes: front block [0, 16); an empty directory — zero records, so 4 bytes holding the CRC-32C of zero bytes, 0x00000000 — at [16, 20); 44 bytes of slack, zeroed by advice; trailer at [64, 128).

probe_answers.answer: In commit order: (1) new stored-tile payload, 100,000 bytes; (2) the layer's full new tile-index region, 644 bytes (32 x 20 = 640 entry bytes + one 4-byte segment CRC, since entry_count=32 fits one segment); (3) the new directory + its 4-byte CRC, size unspecified in the document (every record byte-identical except the touched layer's extent slot, which now points at the new 644-byte region); (4) pad to the next 64-byte boundary; (5) the 64-byte trailer. Prior bytes becoming slack: the superseded (also 644-byte) old tile-index region, the superseded old stored-tile payload, and the entire prior generation's directory, pad, and trailer.
probe_answers.citations: Section 20.3's own worked example (immediately following R-WRT-04); R-WRT-04's six ordered steps; section 5.2/R-CNT-21 on what becomes slack.
probe_answers.decisive_quote: Superseding one 100,000-byte stored tile of a 32-tile interleaved layer appends: the new payload (100,000 bytes), the layer's full new index region (32 · 20 + 4 = 644 bytes — one entry re-pointed, 31 byte-identical), the new directory (every record byte-identical except the modified layer's), the pad, and the 64-byte trailer. The prior index region and the superseded payload become slack, reclaimable only by a rewrite.

probe_answers.answer: The appender may do nothing to the file at all: an unimplemented top-level record with MU=1 is reject-file at the open step that precedes every commit, so no commit is available - the appender is a reader of the file first and must refuse before writing anything. A rewriter must likewise refuse to rewrite the file outright, on its own separate ground (such an unimplemented critical type can define references this specification does not, so its bytes cannot be safely relocated).
probe_answers.citations: R-CNT-15 (unknown top-level type, MU=1 -> reject-file); section 20.3 step 2 ('reject-file bars every commit'); section 20.4's table MU=1 row ('At file scope no commit is available at all... R-CNT-15 makes an unimplemented top-level MU = 1 record reject-file'); R-WRT-06's closing sentence for rewriters.
probe_answers.decisive_quote: At either scope a rewriter MUST refuse to rewrite the file, on `[R-WRT-06]`'s own ground: such a type can define references this specification does not (§7.2), so its bytes cannot be safely relocated.

probe_answers.answer: Yes to both: an appender MAY drop the record in a commit whose only effect is the drop, and a rewriter MAY drop it in any rewrite - the licence is the PE=0 bit's own. Neither is obliged to report the loss under a MUST; the keyword is SHOULD ('An updater that drops such a record SHOULD report the loss'), not MUST.
probe_answers.citations: Section 20.4's table, MU=0/PE=0 row; R-WRT-08 (updater must not re-encode/modify save by relocation).
probe_answers.decisive_quote: Retain byte-identical, or drop it — its extent becoming slack. The licence is the bit's own... so an appender MAY drop the record in any commit it is otherwise free to make — one whose only effect is the drop included — and a rewriter MAY drop it in any rewrite. An updater that drops such a record SHOULD report the loss; unreported, application state disappears with no diagnostic.

probe_answers.answer: (a) Appender's commit: output flags carry the input's bit 20 unchanged (still set), and no other bit is set or cleared - an updater MUST copy forward unknown ignore-lane bits, MUST NOT clear them, and MUST NOT set any other. (b) Rewrite: identical outcome - the output trailer MUST copy the input's unknown ignore-lane bits forward and set no other, in place of the flags=0 a creator writes. (c) A creator that read the input and writes a new file from what it decoded: output flags = 0 entirely - bit 20 is NOT carried forward, because a creator 'undertakes nothing toward its input, whatever it read' and 'writes flags = 0.'
probe_answers.citations: R-CNT-08 (updater copy-forward obligation, appender and rewriter alike); R-WRT-06 (rewriter trailer flags rule, section 20.5); section 20.1's creator/rewriter contrast (R-WRT-01).
probe_answers.decisive_quote: As a creator it undertakes nothing toward its input, whatever it read: §20.2 binds it, it writes flags = 0, and it answers for every byte of its output (`[R-CNF-05]`), bytes it copied from another file included.

probe_answers.answer: Not permitted as an appender commit: fill value is one of the declarations fixed for as long as a layer stores a tile, so a commit changing only it is barred; the operations offered instead are declaring a new layer (a different identity under a different name) or performing a whole-file rewrite under a fresh file_id that re-declares the layer. Whether the resulting file is nonconforming: the bar itself is a writer-conduct rule whose violation alone creates no register row and does not by itself make the file nonconforming (it 'states no condition a file can exhibit'), BUT the document explicitly allows that 'a file such a commit leaves can be nonconforming on its own terms' - concretely, if the layer has any edge-tile padding, the already-stored tiles' padding positions were fill-encoded under the old fill value, so they now fail the padding-content rule (T4, reject-tile, verifier-detected) against the newly declared fill. Where a layer has no padding positions at all and every addressed tile stays stored, I found no other byte-level distinguisher for this specific violation - a genuine instance of an unwitnessed condition under the document's own test.
probe_answers.citations: Section 20.3 step 4's fixed-declarations paragraph (R-WRT-04); R-ERR-01/R-CNF-02 (conduct rules vs. file conformance); section 14.5/R-SER-05 (padding content fixed to the channel's fill); section 21.4 row T4; section 21.7 (the unwitnessed-condition test).
probe_answers.decisive_quote: This bar binds the commit as an actor: no file is nonconforming by virtue of its violation, and no register row records the violation itself... a file such a commit leaves can be nonconforming on its own terms, as the paragraph below sets out.

probe_answers.answer: The next reader sees no valid trailer at the physical end of the file (the new trailer was never appended), so under the default read path it MUST report the file torn or invalid and MUST NOT scan backward. The file, as physical bytes, is not a conforming file in that state (it fails the trailer gates at open). The next appender, per the recovery-before-re-append rule, finds that validating the trailer at the physical end fails, so it MUST NOT append; it must instead run the deliberate recovery scan, which finds the prior trailer (trail-n) intact at its old offset (protected by committed-prefix immutability), re-verifies it whole-file, and truncates to it, restoring the file exactly to its last fully committed generation before resuming normal appends.
probe_answers.citations: Section 9.2's own worked 'Example - what a crash sees,' row 2 ('mid-commit'); R-LIF-05 (default read path, no backward scan); R-LIF-04 (appender must establish F, torn file blocks append); R-LIF-06 (deliberate recovery scan and re-verification).
probe_answers.decisive_quote: Mid-commit the physical tail is not a trailer, so a reader on the default path reports the file torn and MUST NOT scan backward (`[R-LIF-05]`). What makes that recoverable rather than fatal is that trail-n and everything it reaches are still byte-intact: §9.6's deliberate scan finds trail-n and truncating to it restores the file exactly.

probe_answers.answer: The rewriter must verify each carried stored tile's checksum (the crc field of its tile-index entry, per section 8.1's coverage map) before emitting that tile's bytes forward - this is a purely structural check and requires no decode of the unimplemented sample type at all, since a rewriter only decodes what it re-creates, never what it merely carries. If a carried tile's checksum fails, the rewriter has detected a violation it may not emit; since it cannot decode-and-recreate the layer (the sample type is unimplemented) and cannot patch just the one entry without modifying the layer record's crc_of_crc_array (which is not one of the document's three sanctioned dispositions - carry forward verbatim, re-create, or drop), its only licensed options are to drop the entire layer record (licensed by the layer type's registry-fixed PE=0) or to refuse to rewrite the file altogether. It may NOT instead re-create the layer, because re-creation requires decoding the layer's content as a reader first, which an unimplemented sample type precludes.
probe_answers.citations: R-WRT-09 (rewriter's verification depth over carried structures: checksum only, no decode); section 20.5 ('What it re-creates it decodes as a reader first... and writes as a creator'); section 20.5's refuse-or-drop paragraph; section 20.4's table (layer PE=0 licenses the drop); R-CNF-06 ('without necessarily understanding all of its content').
probe_answers.decisive_quote: A rewriter MUST refuse to rewrite when any check `[R-WRT-09]` obliges fails, and MUST NOT emit a file carrying a violation it has detected: it can neither re-emit the structure corrected (`[R-WRT-05]`), nor keep it and call the output clean. Dropping is the one disposal that answers, and only where §20.4's table licenses it... Where the table does not license a drop the rewriter MUST refuse.

probe_answers.answer: No, the commit may not drop the layer: an unimplemented MU=1 sub-record blocks any modification of the layer that carries it, dropping included, regardless of the layer record's own PE=0 status - the layer's PE=0 only licenses its drop when nothing else blocks it. I checked every sentence in section 20.4 bearing on this (the table's MU=1 row, and the body-text sentences on dropping a layer and on sub-record flags) and found full agreement, not disagreement: the 'whatever their PE bits' sentence covers retained sub-records' PE bits, while a separate, explicit sentence carves out the MU=1-unimplemented case as the one thing that blocks the drop.
probe_answers.citations: Section 20.4's table, MU=1 row ('At layer scope an unknown critical record blocks modification of that layer, its drop included'); section 20.4's body text on dropping a layer record (R-WRT-05's surrounding paragraph); R-CNT-18 (layer-scope treatment of an unimplemented critical sub-record).
probe_answers.decisive_quote: A commit MAY therefore drop a layer record, and the drop takes the layer whole: a sub-record's flags govern it within a layer the updater keeps, so a dropped layer's sub-records and their extents go with it whatever their PE bits. One sub-record blocks the drop, a sub-record of a type the updater does not implement with MU = 1, the drop being a modification of the scope it governs (the table's first row).

probe_answers.answer: Yes, the appender may drop it: section 20.3's append procedure explicitly defers to section 20.4 as its own named exception ('MUST NOT drop the record save where section 20.4 licenses the drop'), and section 20.4's MU=0/PE=0 row licenses exactly this drop, 'in any commit it is otherwise free to make - one whose only effect is the drop included.' The two sections fully agree; section 20.3 states the general bar and names its own carve-out, and section 20.4 is that carve-out.
probe_answers.citations: Section 20.3 step 2 (append procedure, carry-forward and drop rules); section 20.4's table, MU=0/PE=0 row; section 20.4's preamble on stored flags being authoritative for an unimplemented type.
probe_answers.decisive_quote: Against any other structure the appender carries forward, it MUST NOT repair the defect — `[R-LIF-01]` freezes the committed prefix — and MUST NOT drop the record save where §20.4 licenses the drop.

probe_answers.answer: The preservation table obliges the updater to retain the record byte-identically or drop it (the MU=0/PE=0 row's obligation), because the deciding sentence establishes that the MU=1 row 'reaches only a type the updater does not implement' - since this updater implements the type from its own definition, the MU bit does not block modification and 'for an implemented type only the PE bit bites'; with PE fixed at 0 by that definition, the PE=0 row governs a record the updater does not modify. The updater MAY drop it (SHOULD report the loss if it does).
probe_answers.citations: Section 20.4's preamble ('For a type the updater implements that this specification does not register, the definition it implements the type from supplies the flags, and the stored bits never do'); the deciding sentence on the MU=1 row's scope; the MU=0/PE=0 row's obligation and licence.
probe_answers.decisive_quote: Its MU = 1 row reaches only a type the updater does not implement — an updater implements both registered types and understands an unregistered type it implements from its definition, modifying their records as §20.3 and that definition provide — so for an implemented type only the PE bit bites.

findings.location_a: section 20.3 step 4 (fixed-declarations paragraph, governed by R-WRT-04) and section 14.5/R-SER-05 (padding content) and section 21.4 row T4
findings.title: A fill-only commit on a stored-tile layer is a conduct violation that is byte-witnessed only when the layer has edge-tile padding
findings.detail: The document bars an appender from changing a stored-tile-bearing layer's fill value in place, and frames that bar as a pure writer-conduct rule whose violation alone creates no register row and does not by itself make the resulting file nonconforming (R-ERR-01/R-CNF-02: 'no file is nonconforming by virtue of its violation... the bar stating no condition a file can exhibit'). The same passage then says the file such a commit leaves 'can be nonconforming on its own terms.' Tracing that through: if the layer has any edge-tile padding, the already-stored tiles' padding positions were fill-encoded under the layer's old fill value (R-SER-05), so after the commit they no longer match the newly declared fill and a verifier finds a T4 violation (reject-tile) - a genuine byte-level, register-backed consequence. But if the layer has no padding at all (extents exactly divide tile extents) and every addressed tile remains stored, I could find no other rule in the document that a byte-level check could use to detect this specific violation: the stored tile bytes are unchanged, the checksums still verify, and the change is confined to a channel-entry field with no other structural fingerprint. An implementer building a verifier from this document alone, and reasoning that 'the fixed-declaration bar has consequences,' would need to independently discover that those consequences are conditional on padding shape, since the document states the general bar and its unwitnessed classification but does not spell out this particular padding-dependent split explicitly in one place - a reader has to assemble it from R-WRT-04, R-SER-05, and section 21.7's general test. This is not a contradiction (the document's own framework predicts and licenses exactly this kind of split-detectability outcome, and section 21.7 explicitly discusses an analogous case, an undisclosed compression dictionary), but it is a real seam worth naming for an implementer auditing what a verifier can and cannot actually catch here.
findings.quotation_a: This bar binds the commit as an actor: no file is nonconforming by virtue of its violation, and no register row records the violation itself, the register enumerating file-conformance violations (§21.1) and the bar stating no condition a file can exhibit (§21.7, `[R-ERR-01]`, `[R-CNF-02]`); a file such a commit leaves can be nonconforming on its own terms, as the paragraph below sets out.
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: Resolving this does change what a conforming verifier must do with the resulting bytes, but only conditionally: where the layer has edge-tile padding, a verifier MUST reject the affected tiles under T4/R-SER-05 once the fill value changes underneath already-stored tiles: a directly byte-level, testable consequence. Where the layer has no padding, no byte-level check in the document distinguishes the violating file from a legitimate one, so in that instance the condition is unwitnessed and changes nothing any implementation may accept or reject. I flag byte_level=true because the general case does have byte-level teeth (via T4) even though a specific sub-case does not, and I record that split explicitly rather than picking one answer for the whole condition.

probe_answers.answer: Three verdicts. (1) conforming: no violation established anywhere, and every file-level requirement was actually checkable and checked (e.g. a file where the coverage walk completes clean and every layer's codec/filter is executable). (2) nonconforming: the verifier establishes at least one violation anywhere in §21.2-21.4 (e.g. the trailer CRC at F-4 fails to match, F14) - this verdict is reported 'however many requirements it was unable to check,' i.e. it takes priority over any capability/resource gap. (3) cannot establish: no violation was established, but some requirement was unable to be checked on a capability or resource ground - e.g. the file names a format major the verifier does not implement, a top-level record carries MU=1 with a type not implemented, the verifier cannot execute a layer's codec or filter (R-COD-11), it declines a layer's/tile's decode on resource grounds, or it declines to decode a user-metadata document (R-MTA-09). Note: 'unexamined' (used when a verifier elects to stop at the first violation and does not examine remaining scopes) is a report qualifier, not a fourth verdict, and is explicitly distinguished from cannot-establish.
probe_answers.citations: §2.3 (definition of Conforming verifier, R-CNF-11): the three-verdict sentence and its list of cannot-establish grounds; §2.3's priority sentence ('An established violation takes priority...'); §2.3's closing sentences on 'unexamined' being neither a verdict nor cannot-establish.
probe_answers.decisive_quote: "A verifier reports one of three verdicts: *conforming*, *nonconforming*, or *cannot establish* — the last where some requirement is one it is unable to check on a capability or resource ground..."

probe_answers.answer: Depends on which numeric range the unimplemented type value falls in, and the document is explicit that this is the whole of the distinction: (a) If the type value is in the RESERVED range (0x0003-0x7FFF): emitting it with MU=1 is itself a registered violation (F35, reader-detected at open, reject-file; also F36, verifier-detected, since emitting any reserved-range type at all is a violation whatever its MU bit) - the verdict is NONCONFORMING, and the fixing requirement is R-CNT-15 (F35's governing rule) together with R-CNT-15's general 'emitting one is a violation' clause (F36). (b) If the type value is in the EXPERIMENTAL range (≥0x8000): R-CNT-15 still obliges the reader/verifier to reject-file, but this is one of §21.6's 'conforming files a reader nevertheless refuses' - the file itself is not a violation (R-CNF-02), so the verdict is CANNOT ESTABLISH (per §2.3's own listed ground: 'a record carries MUST_UNDERSTAND = 1 with a type it does not implement'), fixed only if no other violation is established, and the requirement to report as unchecked is the layer's/record's content obligations that the unread type might have governed. §2.3 states the bifurcation directly: a conforming file carrying such a type 'is necessarily from the experimental range, since a reserved-range type carrying MU = 1 is itself a violation.'
probe_answers.citations: §2.3 (R-CNF-03's parenthetical: '...in a conforming file such a type is necessarily from the experimental range, since a reserved-range type carrying MU = 1 is itself a violation'); §2.3's cannot-establish list (R-CNF-11); §21.2 rows F35 and F36 (R-CNT-15); §21.6's closing paragraphs on the two 'conforming files a reader nevertheless refuses' and on what is registered in each case.
probe_answers.decisive_quote: "in a conforming file such a type is necessarily from the experimental range, since a reserved-range type carrying MU = 1 is itself a violation"

probe_answers.answer: Assuming minimal 64-byte-alignment padding at every commit (pad1=20, pad2=20, pad3=36 bytes; F1=4,480, F2=13,120, F3=14,528), a completed coverage walk over generation 3 reports a live-state byte total of 12,816 bytes (front 16 + A's live tiles 4,096 [3,072 retained + 1,024 new] + A's re-emitted 84-byte index + B's tiles 8,192 + B's 164-byte index + directory3 200 + trailer3 64) and a slack total of 1,712 bytes (14,528 - 12,816), cross-checked as the sum of: A's superseded gen-1 index region (84) + the superseded 1,024-byte tile + generation-1's directory/pad/trailer superseded in gen 2 (200+20+64=284) + generation-2's directory/pad/trailer superseded in gen 3 (200+20+64=284) + generation-3's own pre-trailer pad (36) = 1,712.

probe_answers.answer: Verdict on the file: cannot establish (fixed to that verdict only if the verifier established no violation elsewhere in the file; if it did, nonconforming takes priority regardless). What the report says about that layer: the verifier reports that it was unable to check that layer's decoded-content obligations (R-SER-05 padding-fill content, R-SER-08 boolean-byte content, and any codec-specific framing checks), naming the requirement it could not check and the ground (inability to execute the declared codec/filter), per R-CNF-11's per-requirement reporting duty - it must NOT report the layer as violating anything, since the inability is a capability limit on the verifier, not a finding about the bytes.
probe_answers.citations: §17.4 (R-COD-11): 'A verifier that cannot execute a layer's codec or filter cannot establish that layer's conformance and MUST NOT certify the file. That inability is not a finding that the file is nonconforming, and it fixes the file's verdict as cannot establish only where the verifier established no violation elsewhere.' §9.7: 'A verifier that certifies decodes every stored tile... one that declines a tile's decode on resource grounds reports that check unmade and cannot certify.' §2.3/R-CNF-11's per-requirement reporting duty.
probe_answers.decisive_quote: "A verifier that cannot execute a layer's codec or filter cannot establish that layer's conformance and MUST NOT certify the file."

probe_answers.answer: In general, no: §20.3's bar on changing a fixed declaration of a layer that stored a tile binds the commit as an actor, and 'no register row records the violation itself' - §21.7 states plainly that, absent a side effect on decoded size, padding/pad-bit content, boolean-byte content, or codec/filter framing, 'no check any actor owes [is] able to see it.' The verifier can see it only indirectly, and only for certain kinds of fixed-declaration changes: a change disturbing decoded size fails T3 (or T14 under codec 1); a change to codec or filter generically fails that codec's own framing/consumption checks (T17, T23, T24, T25); a change disturbing what a padding position or boolean byte must hold fails T4/T5/T2. A change that reshuffles meaning without breaking any of these (e.g. certain dimension-order or name-adjacent changes) is invisible to any check the document obliges. Since the probe does not specify which fixed declaration changed, the document does not determine a single yes/no answer.
probe_answers.citations: §20.3 step 4 (the bar itself, its 'no register row records the violation itself' sentence, and the worked list of fixed declarations - layout, linearization, index encoding, codec, filter, rank, dimension order, tile extents, channel type/fill, interleaved channel list, planar channel position); §21.7 ('under new [fixed declarations] the same bytes would denote values, coordinates or padding the writer did not store, with every checksum in §8 certifying the result and, but for a stored tile's decoded size, a padding position or pad bit, or a boolean byte the register witnesses (T3, T14, T21, T22, T4, T5, T2) and a decode that fails outright, or a codec's framing check that precedes it, under a changed codec or filter (T17, T24, T25), no check any actor owes able to see it').
probe_answers.decisive_quote: "no check any actor owes able to see it (§21.7)"

probe_answers.answer: At the record's own governing scope (file scope if the record is a non-layer top-level record; layer scope if it is a layer record or one of its sub-records). Two separate things happen: (1) as a matter of behavior, every reader/updater MUST treat the record as PE=1 regardless of the stored PE=0 bit - it is never silently deletable, and (for an implemented type) is processed under that type's normal semantics unchanged; this is not itself flagged as wrong by ordinary readers. (2) A verifier MUST additionally treat the stored MU=1/PE=0 combination itself as a validity error at that governing scope - registered as F25 (top-level record, reject-file) or L46 (layer record or sub-record, reject-layer) - making the file nonconforming even though no reader behavior differs.
probe_answers.citations: §7.2 (R-CNT-12: 'Writers MUST NOT emit the combination MU = 1 with PE = 0; a reader or updater encountering it MUST treat the record as PE = 1 (never silently deletable)... a verifier MUST treat a nonzero reserved flag bit or the MU = 1 with PE = 0 combination as a validity error at the record's governing scope.'); §20.4's re-emission table (the MU=1 row: 'whose PE bit is read as 1 whatever is stored'); §21.2 row F25 and §21.3 row L46.
probe_answers.decisive_quote: "a verifier MUST treat a nonzero reserved flag bit or the MU = 1 with PE = 0 combination as a validity error at the record's governing scope"

findings.title: Pre-trailer pad length is bounded below but not fixed, so verifier-reported slack totals are not unique across conforming writers
findings.detail: §6.2 requires only that the pad reach the next 64-byte boundary, and states 'a longer gap is conforming, and no conforming commit produces one' - i.e. minimal padding is the expected case but any longer, 64-byte-aligned pad remains conforming. An implementer building a writer may therefore legally emit any pad length at or above the minimum for each commit. An implementer building a verifier must accept all such files and, per §9.7/R-CNT-21, report the resulting slack total exactly as it stands in that file - so two conforming writers given the identical layer history can produce files whose reported slack totals differ by any multiple of 64 bytes, purely as a matter of writer discretion the specification declines to pin down, even though nothing else about the files differs.
findings.quotation_a: Writers MUST place the directory so that no structure lies between its end and the trailer. Those bytes — the pre-trailer pad — are slack (§5.2): a writer that ends its directory on a 64-byte boundary leaves none, this specification does not constrain their content, and bounds their number only through step 5 of the commit protocol, which pads to the next 64-byte boundary (`[R-LIF-02]`) — a longer gap is conforming, and no conforming commit produces one.
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: This changes which bytes a conforming implementation may emit (any writer may legally over-pad by additional 64-byte multiples) and, correspondingly, changes the exact numeric slack total a conforming verifier must accept and report for two files with byte-identical layer content and commit history - the divergence is a real difference in accepted file bytes and in the verifier's own reported output, not merely a difference in wording or emphasis.

result.walk_summary:
I implemented, on paper, a conforming verifier for TARN format major 1 from edition C alone. The certification procedure is: open (trailer→directory→record walk, reject-file on failure) → per-layer full record validation (reject-layer) → per-segment index-chain verification (reject-layer) → per-entry classification into sentinel/structural-invalid/well-formed (reject-tile for the invalid cases) → payload CRC + codec decode + decoded-size check for every stored tile, which a verifier (unlike an ordinary reader) must do for all of them to certify → verifier-only decoded-content checks (padding fill, pad bits, interleaved-bool bytes, filter stride) → verifier-only layer/file structural checks (overlap, alignment, slab packing) → verifier-only flag/record checks (reserved bits, MU=1/PE=0, registered-type mismatch, reserved-range type, metadata ordering) → coverage walk (disjointness, checksum-per-map, slack total, exact or partial) → capability/resource-ground reporting. The verdict vocabulary is conforming / nonconforming / cannot-establish, with an unconditional priority rule: any established violation forces nonconforming regardless of how much else went unchecked, and cannot-establish is reserved for a traversal that established nothing else.

I built a concrete three-generation file for the coverage-walk arithmetic (creation of layer A, addition of layer B, supersession of one of A's tiles) and derived byte-exact offsets, pads, F, live totals and slack from the document's own commit-protocol and re-emission rules, cross-checking the slack figure two independent ways (F−live vs. itemized superseded structures) to the same 1,712 bytes. I also built a second, non-completing walk (an L18 intra-layer overlap) and applied §5.2's explicit rule that a layer whose overlap the walk itself discovered has its already-enumerated claimants discarded, giving a partial slack figure and naming the stopping violation, as the register requires.

For the six probes I cited every passage bearing on each act and reported where the document's own conditional structure (not a defect) makes an answer depend on which numeric range a value falls in (V2), where the document's own priority rule makes a superficially plausible verdict path (V4's "cannot establish" for codec inexecutability) actually unreachable for a genuinely conforming verifier, and where a cross-generation writer-conduct bar is explicitly undetectable from the live state by design (V5). probe_answers.answer: Three verdicts. conforming: the verifier checks every requirement at every scope and establishes zero violations (and has no unresolved capability/resource gap it needs to report as blocking certification) — "a verifier certifies only violation-free files" (§2.4). nonconforming: it establishes at least one register-row violation anywhere, e.g. the trailer CRC at offset 60 not matching CRC-32C of trailer bytes [0,60) (F14, governing rule R-CNT-06/R-CNT-20/R-ENC-09) — "An established violation takes priority: a verifier that has established any violation reports nonconforming, however many requirements it was unable to check" (R-CNF-11). cannot establish: some requirement is one it cannot check on a capability or resource ground and it has established no violation elsewhere, e.g. the file names a format major version this verifier does not implement, so the non-reaching requirements of that major are simply unknowable to it (R-CNT-07, R-CNF-13, listed as an example ground in §21.6's closing paragraph and R-CNF-11).
probe_answers.citations: R-CNF-11 (§2.3); §2.4; F14 register row and its governing R-CNT-06 (§6.2); R-CNT-07 and R-CNF-13 (§2.3); §21.6 closing paragraphs.
probe_answers.decisive_quote: "An established violation takes priority: a verifier that has established any violation reports *nonconforming*, however many requirements it was unable to check, and *cannot establish* is available only to a traversal that established no violation."

probe_answers.answer: Depends on the type value's numeric range, which the probe does not state, so I give both: (a) If the type is in the RESERVED range (0x0003-0x7FFF, not yet registered): the file already carries an established violation regardless of the MU bit — emitting any reserved-range value is itself a violation (register row F36, verifier-detected, governing R-CNT-15/R-EXT-03) — and MU=1 additionally makes an ordinary reader's open-time behavior reject-file (register row F35, reader-detected, governing R-CNT-15). Verdict: nonconforming (R-CNF-11's priority rule fires on F36/F35 alone). (b) If the type is in the EXPERIMENTAL range (>=0x8000): the file is conforming on its own terms ("an unrecognized... MU = 0" case is explicitly non-violating per §21.6, and the MU=1 case is one of the two named "conforming files a reader nevertheless refuses": R-CNT-15 obliges the reader/verifier to reject-file, but R-CNF-02 keeps the bytes conforming). Verdict: cannot establish, contingent on no other violation being found (R-CNF-11, listed by name in §21.6's closing paragraphs as one of the cannot-establish grounds). The fixing requirement in both branches is R-CNT-15 (the MU-bit outcome rule) read together with R-CNF-11 (which fixes the verdict word), and in the reserved-range branch also R-EXT-03 (the reserved-range emission prohibition that F36 registers).
probe_answers.citations: R-CNT-15 (§7.2); F35, F36 register rows (§21.2); R-EXT-03 (§10.3); §21.6 ("conforming files a reader nevertheless refuses", second bullet); R-CNF-11 (§2.3); R-CNF-02 (§2.3).
probe_answers.decisive_quote: "the second is an experimental-range top-level record type carrying MU = 1 (§10.2, §10.3): [R-CNT-15] obliges the reader to reject, and [R-CNF-02] makes the file conforming all the same."

probe_answers.answer: Pads assumed: only the mandatory pre-trailer pad each commit needs to reach a 64-byte-aligned trailer offset (R-LIF-02 step 5); no per-tile alignment or slab is declared, so no other gap is required (R-SLB-05). Generation 1: pad1=20 B, F1=4,480 B. Generation 2 (adds B, A untouched): pad2=20 B, F2=13,120 B. Generation 3 (A's index re-emitted whole, entry_count unchanged at 4 so index stays 84 B, one entry re-pointed to the new 1,024-B payload, three entries byte-identical): pad3=36 B, F3=14,528 B. Live-state byte total at generation 3 = 12,816 B (front 16 + A's tiles 4,096 + A's re-emitted index 84 + B's tiles 8,192 + B's index 164 + directory3 200 + trailer3 64). Slack total a completing coverage walk reports = F3 - live = 1,712 B, independently confirmed as: generation-1's superseded directory+pad+trailer (284 B) + generation-2's superseded directory+pad+trailer (284 B) + A's superseded 1,024-B tile plus its superseded 84-B old index (1,108 B) + generation-3's own 36-B pre-trailer pad = 1,712 B.
probe_answers.citations: R-LIF-02 (§9.2, creation and commit steps); R-CNT-06 (64-byte trailer alignment, F mod 64=0); R-WRT-04 (§20.3 step 4, whole-index re-emission on a stored-tile-set change, byte-identical untouched entries); R-WRT-05 (untouched layer's record/extent slot carried byte-identically); R-CNT-17 (index-region size formula, entry_count x 20 + ceil(entry_count/2^16) x 4); R-CNT-21 (slack definition and the verifier's duty to sum and report it); R-SLB-05 (no alignment/slab declared -> no layout promise beyond the forced pad).
probe_answers.decisive_quote: "Every layer whose stored-tile set or index content this commit changes has its tile-index region re-emitted in full ... with entries for tiles this commit stores or supersedes written to their new state ... and every other entry byte-identical at its disk-ordinal position."

probe_answers.answer: R-COD-11/§17.4's literal answer: cannot establish (verifier must not certify), contingent on no violation established elsewhere. But for a genuinely conforming verifier this scenario is only reachable at a reserved-or-experimental codec/filter value (every assigned codec 1-4 and filter 1-2 being core/mandatory per R-CNF-03), and that value is independently a layer-scope violation established at layer access -- before any decode is attempted -- by register row L43 (codec) or L45 (filter), both reader-detected. R-CNF-11's own priority rule then forces the actual verdict to nonconforming, not cannot establish, in every case a conforming verifier can actually reach (see Finding verifierb-01). Either way, the report on that layer is: reject-layer, naming the invalid codec/filter value (L43/L45), and noting per R-CNF-11's naming duty that the layer's decode/content obligations (padding fill, bool-byte legality, etc.) were never checked.
probe_answers.citations: R-COD-11 and §17.4 in full; R-CNF-03 (§2.3, codecs/filters are core); L43, L45 register rows (§21.3) and their governing R-COD-03/R-COD-09; R-CNF-11 (§2.3, priority rule).
probe_answers.decisive_quote: "For a conforming reader that position arises only at a reserved or experimental value, every assigned codec and filter being core: it rejects the layer ([R-COD-03], [R-COD-09]); software unable to execute an assigned codec or filter is not a conforming reader ([R-CNF-03])."

probe_answers.answer: The verifier cannot see it, and cannot report any verdict traceable to that specific act: coverage verification and the open/layer-access/tile-use checks all "walk the live state only" (R-LIF-08 heading text; §9.7's Note: "Nothing here enumerates prior commits"), the superseded prior generation's directory is slack with no content constraint a reader/verifier may interpret (R-CNT-21, R-LIF-08), and §20.3 step 4 states expressly that this bar "binds the commit as an actor: no file is nonconforming by virtue of its violation, and no register row records the violation itself." The new generation is evaluated entirely on its own current declarations; no verdict follows from the act of changing a fixed declaration per se, unless the resulting new declaration independently trips an ordinary check against currently-live bytes it did not trip before (e.g. a re-typed channel whose new decoded size no longer matches a still-live stored tile's byte length -> T3/R-SER-07 reject-tile, or a newly-applied lz4 cap violation -> L44).
probe_answers.citations: §20.3 step 4 (the fixed-declaration list and its binding text); R-CNT-21 and R-LIF-08 (§5.2, §9.7 -- slack unconstrained, live-state-only walk); §9.7's Note ("Nothing here enumerates prior commits"); T3/R-SER-07 and L44/R-COD-07 as examples of independent, coincidental detection.
probe_answers.decisive_quote: "This bar binds the commit as an actor: no file is nonconforming by virtue of its violation, and no register row records the violation itself, the register enumerating file-conformance violations (§21.1) and the bar stating no condition a file can exhibit."

probe_answers.answer: Two things happen at once. Every reader/updater (verifier included, acting as a reader) treats the record as PE=1 regardless of what is stored -- "never silently deletable" -- so ordinary processing is unaffected. Separately, the verifier flags the stored MU=1/PE=0 combination itself as a validity error at the record's own governing scope: file scope (reject-file, register row F25) if it is a non-layer top-level record, or layer scope (reject-layer, register row L46) if it is a layer record or one of its sub-records. Both rows are detector=verifier, detected=certification.
probe_answers.citations: R-CNT-12 (§7.2, both the reader-normalization clause and the verifier-detection clause); F25 register row and L46 register row (§21.2, §21.3); §2.4 (owning-scope -> outcome mapping).
probe_answers.decisive_quote: "Writers MUST NOT emit the combination MU = 1 with PE = 0; a reader or updater encountering it MUST treat the record as PE = 1 (never silently deletable). Both writer violations make the file nonconforming ([R-CNF-05]) while leaving conforming behavior unchanged, so their detection is a verifier's: a verifier MUST treat a nonzero reserved flag bit or the MU = 1 with PE = 0 combination as a validity error at the record's governing scope."

findings.title: R-COD-11's 'cannot establish' branch for an inexecutable codec/filter is unreachable by a conforming verifier as a final verdict
findings.detail: R-COD-11 opens by saying a verifier that cannot execute a layer's codec or filter 'cannot establish that layer's conformance and MUST NOT certify the file,' fixing the verdict as cannot-establish only where no other violation was established. Its own next sentence confines this, for any conforming reader, to a reserved-or-experimental codec/filter value, since every assigned codec (1-4) and filter (1-2) is core and mandatory (R-CNF-03). But a reserved/experimental codec/filter value is independently and unconditionally a layer-scope violation (register rows L43/L45), detected by an ordinary reader at layer access -- before any decode is attempted. Under R-CNF-11's own priority rule, an established violation forces the verdict to nonconforming regardless of unchecked items, so whenever the premise of R-COD-11's opening sentence is actually true for a conforming verifier, L43/L45 has already fired and the verdict is nonconforming, never cannot-establish. The described consequence is real language in the document but does not correspond to any reachable end state.
findings.quotation_a: "A verifier that cannot execute a layer's codec or filter cannot establish that layer's conformance and MUST NOT certify the file... For a conforming reader that position arises only at a reserved or experimental value, every assigned codec and filter being core: it rejects the layer ([R-COD-03], [R-COD-09]); software unable to execute an assigned codec or filter is not a conforming reader ([R-CNF-03])."
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: Under either reading of R-COD-11, a conforming verifier facing this scenario produces the identical bytes-level result: reject-layer is reported for the offending layer (via L43/L45), and the file's final verdict is nonconforming either way, since L43/L45 alone already forces that outcome regardless of what the verifier says about decode-inability. Only the internal justification differs, not any accept/reject/emit decision.

findings.title: The step-4 no-register-row bar cites R-ERR-01's 'no condition a file can exhibit' category, but fits §21.7's own 'unwitnessed condition' test instead
findings.detail: Section 20.3 step 4 says a commit that changes a fixed declaration of a layer that stored a tile leaves 'no register row' because 'the bar stat[es] no condition a file can exhibit,' citing R-ERR-01 by name. But R-ERR-01/§21.7 defines that category narrowly, via the R-ENC-06 fixed-field-width example: a structure written at the wrong width is not 'the same file with a hidden defect' but simply a different byte sequence evaluated on its own terms. The step-4 case does not fit that shape -- the changed declaration (a new fill value, a new type, etc.) is, taken alone, a perfectly legal value under every structural rule, so there is no 'different file, conforming or not on its own terms' story. What actually makes it a violation is a cross-generation fact (old directory's declaration versus the new live one) that the physical bytes do genuinely encode (the old directory survives as slack) but that no check this specification obliges anyone to perform ever compares, since coverage verification 'walks the live state only' and does not reconstruct history (§9.7's Note). That is precisely the document's own definition of an unwitnessed condition, developed one paragraph earlier in the same section -- yet step 4 invokes the other category.
findings.quotation_a: "This bar binds the commit as an actor: no file is nonconforming by virtue of its violation, and no register row records the violation itself, the register enumerating file-conformance violations (§21.1) and the bar stating no condition a file can exhibit (§21.7, [R-ERR-01], [R-CNF-02])."
findings.quotation_b: "A condition this specification names is unwitnessed where, for every file exhibiting it, some file that does not exhibit it cannot be told apart from it by any check this specification obliges a reader or a verifier to perform... Distinguish an unwitnessed condition from a requirement that states no condition a file can exhibit."
findings.byte_level_rationale: Both categorizations reach the same stated practical conclusion -- no register row is owed and no reader/verifier behavior is prescribed for this act -- so no conforming implementation's accept, reject, or emit behavior differs depending on which category is correct. This is a finding about which of the document's own two named exemption doctrines correctly describes the same underlying fact, not about validity of any bytes.

I ran mkdir -p on my scratch directory and on the out/ directory (creation only, not a listing), wc -l on the four named files, and then only sed -n, diff <(sed...) <(sed...), and grep -n against those same four files -- no ls, find, git, or network call, and no directory was listed at any point. My scratch directory (.../fidelity-2/scratch/compare-reader/) was created but holds only the final transcript copy; every diff was consumed inline via process substitution rather than written to disk. result.summary: A full section-by-section diff of both editions (methodology: match section headers by line number in each file, then `diff` the whole section, confirmed by control greps) found the two texts byte-identical everywhere except inside Section 2.3 ("Conformance requirement") and one added tail paragraph in Section 21.6. Every section either walk's probes cite outside Section 2 -- Sections 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, 11 (bar one clause), 14, 15, 17, 19, 20.4, 21.1-21.5, 21.9 -- is identical, so R1, R2, R4, R5, R6, R7 and R8's agreement between the two walks reflects identical source text, not luck, and no LOSS/ADDITION exists at those probes. Inside Section 2.3, edition B reverses two MUST-level rules relative to edition A. First, [R-CNF-02]: edition A states a writer obligation that is either conduct-only or expressly declared not a file-conformance violation never makes the file nonconforming; edition B's rewrite says the opposite -- "a file that breaks one is nonconforming" -- which is also self-contradictory against edition B's own byte-identical Section 6.2 ("a longer gap is conforming") and Section 6.3 ("a set ignore-lane bit is not a file-conformance violation"). Second, [R-CNF-13]: edition A says a reaching condition's failure MUST be treated as ordinary reject-file, "rather than on capability grounds"; edition B says the opposite, "a capability refusal, not as reject-file" -- directly contradicting edition B's own byte-identical Section 21.2, whose reaching rows (F1/F6/F8/F14) are plain reject-file rows detected by the reader at open. Both reversals are byte-level: they flip whether a verifier reports "nonconforming" or "cannot establish" for identical bytes, a distinction [R-CNF-11] makes mutually exclusive and MUST-level. Two further LOSSes surface via broken cross-references: [R-CNF-03] drops "and both record types Section 7.3 registers" from the core-conformance list, while the byte-identical Appendix H checklist still cites [R-CNF-03] as requiring "both registered record types"; [R-CNF-11] drops "and updaters" from "Verifiers and updaters are readers... and inherit every reader obligation," while the byte-identical Section 20.4 table still cites Section 2.3 for "the updater is a reader of the file first." Two other Section 2.3 deletions (the version_major=0 carve-out sentence, and the F14/F5/F15 worked Note) and one Section 2.3/[R-CNF-06] clause drop were checked against the rest of the document and found EQUIVALENT: the same facts are stated, unchanged, in Section 21.2's identical preamble and Section 20.4's identical opening sentence, so nothing is actually lost from the document as a whole. Reader A's own CONTRADICTION finding (Section 19.1 step 1 vs. the reach doctrine over F5) rests on text identical in both editions and therefore applies equally to edition B; reader B did not surface it. Reader B's own AMBIGUITY/OBSERVATION findings (R1's request-count indeterminacy; F5's Instances-column redundancy) likewise rest on identical shared text and apply equally to edition A, which reader A did not surface. No additional rule, exception, quantifier, or figure difference was found in a further read of Sections 2.4, 10, 12-13, 16, 18, 20.1-20.3, 20.5, and 22-24, which are also byte-identical.

findings.title: Edition B reverses whether breaking a conduct-only/expressly-non-violation writer obligation makes the file nonconforming
findings.detail: Edition A states plainly that a file is never nonconforming for breaking a writer obligation that governs conduct rather than output, or that this specification expressly declares not a file-conformance violation -- naming as its own examples a set ignore-lane flag bit, a pre-trailer gap longer than the commit pad, and a layer's fixed declarations under Section 20.3 step 4. Edition B's rewrite of the same rule states the opposite: such a violation 'binds the writer, and a file that breaks one is nonconforming.' This also contradicts edition B's own Section 6.2 ('a longer gap is conforming') and Section 6.3 ('a set ignore-lane bit is not a file-conformance violation'), both byte-identical to edition A. An implementer following edition B's Section 2.3 alone, without cross-checking Section 6, would report nonconforming for files Section 6 (and edition A throughout) treats as conforming.
findings.quotation_a: A few obligations this specification places on writers govern their *conduct* rather than their output... and a file is never nonconforming by virtue of one: conduct rules bind the actor, the predicate binds the bytes. A writer obligation whose violation this specification expressly declares not to be a file-conformance violation binds the actor in the same way; Section 6.3's flags rules against a set ignore-lane bit..., Section 6.2's pre-trailer gap longer than [R-LIF-02] step 5's pad, and Section 20.3 step 4's bar on the fixed declarations of a layer that stores a tile are the cases this text states...
findings.quotation_b: A writer obligation that governs conduct rather than output, or whose violation this specification expressly declares not to be a file-conformance violation, binds the writer, and a file that breaks one is nonconforming. [R-CNF-02]
findings.byte_level_rationale: A verifier built strictly from edition B's Section 2.3 text would certify 'nonconforming' for a file with, e.g., a longer-than-pad pre-trailer gap and no other defect; a verifier built from edition A (or from edition B's own byte-identical Section 6.2) would certify the same file conforming. Different accept/reject verdicts on the identical file.

findings.title: Edition B reverses the disposition of a reaching condition's failure: reject-file becomes 'capability refusal'
findings.detail: Edition A requires a reader to treat a reaching condition's failure (e.g. trailer magic, trailer CRC) as ordinary reject-file under the requirement that states it, explicitly not as a capability-grounds refusal; the distinct capability diagnostic is reserved for the case where every reaching condition passes but the declared major is unimplemented. Edition B's rewrite says the opposite: treat the failure as a capability refusal, not as reject-file. This contradicts edition B's own Section 21.2 (byte-identical to edition A), whose opening paragraph derives exactly F8, F14, F6 and both of F1's instances as the reaching rows and whose table assigns all of them Detector=reader, Detected=open, under the section's stated 'Outcome: reject-file' -- none are marked as capability refusals.
findings.quotation_a: A reader MUST apply every reaching condition to a file whatever major it declares... and MUST treat its failure as reject-file on the ground of the requirement stating it rather than on capability grounds; the distinct diagnostic [R-CNT-07] asks for is owed where every reaching condition is satisfied and the declared major is one the reader does not implement.
findings.quotation_b: A reader MUST check every reaching condition whatever major the file declares, and MUST treat a failure as a capability refusal, not as reject-file under the requirement that states the condition...
findings.byte_level_rationale: Per [R-CNF-11] (identical in both editions), an established violation forces a verifier to report nonconforming, while a capability ground forces cannot-establish, and the two are mutually exclusive. Edition B's Section 2.3 text, taken alone, would route a reaching-condition failure (e.g. trailer-magic mismatch on a file declaring an unimplemented major) to cannot-establish; edition B's own Section 21.2 routes the identical bytes to nonconforming. Different MUST-level verdicts on the identical file.

findings.title: Edition B drops the requirement that a conforming reader implement both registered record types, breaking Appendix H's cross-reference
findings.detail: Edition A's [R-CNF-03] requires a conforming reader to handle, among other things, 'both record types Section 7.3 registers,' and its no-subset-profiles sentence disqualifies software that declines 'a registered record type.' Edition B drops both clauses; Section 7.3 itself never independently states this obligation. Edition B's Appendix H conformance checklist -- byte-identical to edition A's -- still credits [R-CNF-03] with requiring 'both registered record types,' so edition B now contains an internal citation to a rule its own cited section no longer states.

result.disclosure: Read exactly the four permitted files: edition A (scratch/cleanroom/editions/a/tarn.md, 4,981 lines), edition B (scratch/cleanroom/editions/c/tarn.md, 4,885 lines), and the two walk transcripts (transcript-writer-a.md, transcript-writer-b.md — the latter's Read-tool output overflowed inline and was saved by the harness to a tool-results file under my own session directory, which I then read in full; this is the same one permitted file's content, not a fifth file). No directory was listed. Working files (full.diff, this transcript) were written only to my assigned scratch directory, then the transcript was copied to the required out/ path. My context also contained a CLAUDE.md pointer, a user memory-index file with many prior-round TARN note titles, a git-status block, and skill/environment boilerplate, all supplied by the runtime before I began; none of it is part of either specification edition, I did not open any file it referenced, and none of my findings rely on it — disclosed per the brief's instruction, not repeated or treated as evidence.
result.summary:
The two editions are byte-identical outside exactly 6 diff hunks in a ~4,900-line document (confirmed by a whole-file `diff -u a/tarn.md c/tarn.md`, which is immune to the hard-wrap problem since it compares whole lines). Every passage either walker cited for probes W1–W5, W7, and W9–W11 falls inside the untouched majority of the text, so both walkers' answers to those probes are EQUIVALENT: correct because the source is identical, verified by direct diff rather than inferred from matching answers. W2's and W6's specific cited passages (§20.3's worked example, §20.3 step 4, §21.7) are likewise identical between editions.

Reading past the probes into the document's 6 actual diff hunks (per the charter's "go past the probes" instruction) found one substantive defect and two lesser internal-consistency issues, all specific to edition B (the "readable" rewrite), plus one purely expository loss.

The major finding: edition B's own §2.3 definition of `[R-CNF-02]` was rewritten to read "a file that breaks [a conduct-only obligation, or one this specification expressly declares not to be a file-conformance violation] is nonconforming" — the literal opposite of edition A's "a file is never nonconforming by virtue of one: conduct rules bind the actor, the predicate binds the bytes," and self-contradictory on its own terms (it names an obligation "this specification expressly declares not to be a file-conformance violation" and then says breaking it makes the file nonconforming). Edition B's own §20.3 step 4 — byte-identical to edition A there — still states edition A's polarity while citing the same `[R-CNF-02]` tag. This is a genuine CONTRADICTION internal to edition B, bearing directly on W6, that neither walker's transcript surfaces (neither quotes §2.3 for that probe).

Two lesser findings are internal-consistency defects rather than full rule losses: edition B's §2.3 "conforming reader" definition drops "registered record types" from its no-subset-profile list, and its "cannot establish" grounds (moved from §2.3 into a new §21.6 paragraph) arrive one ground short (the layer/tile-decode-decline case) — but in both cases the underlying rule is restated verbatim, identically, elsewhere in edition B (an unchanged appendix checklist, and §9.7 respectively), so a whole-document reading of B recovers the same rule as A. A fourth finding notes edition B has no counterpart to edition A's §3.3 "Part I/Part II independence" Note; since that Note was itself non-normative in A, and the operative rule it explains (`[R-WRT-09]`, §20.5) is byte-identical in both editions, this has no byte-level effect (confirmed by both walkers reaching identical W8 conclusions).

evidence.sweeps_run: `diff -u a/tarn.md c/tarn.md` → exactly 6 `@@` hunks (`grep -c "^@@"` on the diff = 6); this master sweep certifies everything outside those 6 spots is byte-identical. Targeted `diff <(sed -n ...) <(sed -n ...)` re-runs, each returning empty/exit 0: §5.1 in full, §20.3's worked example, §20.4 in full (the MU-flags table and its connecting sentences), §20.5 in full, §20.1–20.2, §9.2, §9.3–9.6, §6.2–6.3, §7.2–7.4, §14.5, §21.4, and the 'Conforming reader/writer/updater/verifier' appendix checklist near the end of both files. `grep -n "§3\.3"` → 0 hits in edition B (control: `grep -c "Part I" c/tarn.md` = 5, proving grep matches real content there). `grep -n "^#### 3\.3"` → 1 hit in A (line 435), 0 in B (control: `grep -n "^#### 3\."` finds 3.1/3.2 headers in both files). `grep -n "record types §7.3 registers"` → 1 hit in A, 0 in B (control: `grep -c "R-CNF-03"` in B = 11, nonzero). `grep -n "unable to check a requirement"` → 0 in A, 1 in B (the reverse-direction addition, corroborated by the diff hunk itself). `grep -n "resource ground"` (control sweep) → 6 hits in each file at a constant ~103-line offset, proving the rest of that phrase's occurrences (§9.7's coverage-walk text among them) are identical and only the two specific spots found by the diff actually differ.
evidence.derived_numbers: W2's index-region arithmetic (32 entries × 20 bytes = 640, + one 4-byte segment CRC since 32 ≤ 2¹⁶ = one segment per `[R-CNT-17]`'s ⌈entry_count/2¹⁶⌉ term = 644 bytes total) was checked against the document's own worked-example figure (644 bytes), which is character-for-character identical in both editions — no independent derivation was load-bearing since both editions state the same number. The two files' line counts (4,981 vs 4,885, a 96-line difference) were reconciled against the six hunks' net line deltas as a sanity check that no 7th silent hunk existed; the reconciliation is close enough (within the rounding of a header being relocated rather than deleted-and-reinserted) to trust the 6-hunk count as complete.
evidence.rejected_candidates: Suspected the missing §3.3 Note was a LOSS because writer-a's W8 answer cited it by name; closed once `[R-WRT-09]` and §20.5 (the actual operative rule) were confirmed byte-identical between editions and writer-b reached the identical conclusion without the Note, and once I noted the Note was already non-normative (inside a `> **Note.**` block) in edition A itself. Suspected the dropped 'registered record types' item and the dropped 'cannot establish' ground were full-strength LOSSes; closed to OBSERVATION-grade once I found both are restated verbatim, identically, in an unrelated but unchanged part of the same edition B (the appendix checklist, and §9.7 respectively) — the rule survives a whole-document reading of B even though its local defining text does not state it. Suspected W6's two matching walker answers might mask a real divergence given how extensively edition B's front matter was rewritten; closed for the probe itself (§20.3 step 4 and §21.7, which both walkers actually cite, are byte-identical) but this suspicion is what led to reading §2.3's general `[R-CNF-02]` definition side by side, which is where the one genuine CONTRADICTION (cmp-writer-01) was actually found.
evidence.confidence_empty: I ran the master `diff -u` sweep first, specifically so 'no other differences' would rest on a mechanical, complete comparison rather than my own reading coverage, and it returned only 6 hunks — I read all 6, including the two smallest (a one-line rewording near old-§12.1, and the two-clause split of the 'cannot establish' grounds), not just the large front-matter rewrite. Sections outside all 6 hunks (all of Part II's array-model chapters, Appendices B–H) needed no separate close reading pass to establish equivalence, since the master diff already certifies them byte-identical; I still spot-checked the appendix 'Conforming X' checklist directly because two of my findings depend on whether it does or does not restate content dropped from §2.3, and confirmed it does, identically in both editions.

findings.location_a: §2.3 Conformance definitions, "Conforming TARN file" bullet [R-CNF-02] (edition A only has this polarity; the identical text also appears, correctly, in both editions' §20.3 step 4)

findings.title: Edition B's [R-CNF-02] definition inverts edition A's conduct-rule polarity, contradicting edition B's own §20.3
findings.detail: Edition A states that a writer obligation governing conduct rather than output, or one this specification expressly declares not to be a file-conformance violation, never makes the file nonconforming by itself ("a file is never nonconforming by virtue of one: conduct rules bind the actor, the predicate binds the bytes"). Edition B's rewrite of the same [R-CNF-02] bullet says the opposite: "a file that breaks one is nonconforming" — asserted of the very category ("expressly declares not to be a file-conformance violation") that logically cannot make a file nonconforming, a self-contradiction within one sentence. Edition B's own §20.3 step 4 (byte-identical to edition A there) still states edition A's polarity under the same [R-CNF-02] tag ("no file is nonconforming by virtue of its violation... a file such a commit leaves can be nonconforming on its own terms" only where a separate, witnessed byte-level rule is also broken). An implementer building a verifier strictly from edition B's §2.3 text would reject files that a verifier built from §20.3 (or from edition A entirely) would accept — e.g. W6's no-padding case, a fill-value change on a layer with no edge-tile padding, which both walkers agree triggers no register row.
findings.quotation_a: A few obligations this specification places on writers govern their *conduct* rather than their output — where a value is published, which registry version a writer targets (§10.3, §18.3), or the barriers a commit performs (§9.2) — and a file is never nonconforming by virtue of one: conduct rules bind the actor, the predicate binds the bytes. A writer obligation whose violation this specification expressly declares not to be a file-conformance violation binds the actor in the same way...
findings.quotation_b: A writer obligation that governs conduct rather than output, or whose violation this specification expressly declares not to be a file-conformance violation, binds the writer, and a file that breaks one is nonconforming. `[R-CNF-02]`
findings.byte_level_rationale: A verifier implemented strictly from edition B's §2.3 [R-CNF-02] text would report NONCONFORMING for a file whose only defect is an unwitnessed writer-conduct violation (no register row triggered anywhere in §21); a verifier implemented from edition A's §2.3, or from either edition's §20.3 step 4, would report the identical file CONFORMING. That is a different accept/reject verdict on an identifiable file, arising from two internally inconsistent passages that exist only in edition B — edition A has no such tension anywhere in its text.

findings.location_b: §2.3, "Conforming reader" bullet [R-CNF-03] (edition B's shortened list); contrast with the unchanged "Conforming reader —" appendix checklist near the end of both editions, which still cites [R-CNF-03]/§2.3 for the full list

Edition B's rewrite of the same paragraph, under the same [R-CNF-03] tag, lists only five items, omitting record types from both the affirmative and negative forms. Both editions' unchanged "Conforming reader —" appendix checklist near the end of the document still reads "...implements all four codecs, both filters, both layouts, all thirteen sample types, both user-metadata encodings, and both registered record types ([R-CNF-03], §2.3)" — attributing the full six-item list to a definition that, in edition B, no longer states it.
findings.quotation_a: ...and MUST handle every codec and filter that §17 designates as core, both channel layouts (§14), every sample type that §12 designates as core, every user-metadata encoding §18.2 assigns, and both record types §7.3 registers. There are no subset profiles: software that declines to support a core codec, a core filter, either channel layout, a core sample type, an assigned user-metadata encoding, or a registered record type is not a conforming reader...
findings.quotation_b: ...and MUST handle every codec and filter that §17 designates as core, both channel layouts (§14), every sample type that §12 designates as core, and every user-metadata encoding §18.2 assigns. There are no subset profiles: software that declines any of those is not a conforming reader, even if it reads all other conforming files correctly.
findings.byte_level_rationale: An implementation built strictly from edition B's §2.3 paragraph alone could wrongly treat a reader that declines the layer/user-metadata record types as conforming; but edition B's own unchanged appendix checklist restates the full requirement verbatim, so a complete reading of edition B recovers the same rule as edition A, and the practical byte-level accept/reject outcome does not actually diverge for an implementation built from the whole of edition B.

findings.location_b: §2.3's shortened cross-reference plus the new closing paragraph of §21.6 in edition B (four grounds stated); contrast with §9.7, byte-identical in both editions, which independently states the missing ground's consequence
findings.title: Edition B's relocated "cannot establish" grounds list is one ground short of what it promises to enumerate
findings.detail: Edition A's [R-CNF-11] definition enumerates five grounds for a verifier reporting *cannot establish*, inline, including "when it declines a layer's or a tile's decode on resource grounds and so cannot check §14's decoded-content obligations ([R-ERR-04], [R-SER-05], [R-SER-08])". Edition B compresses this to a bare cross-reference, "(§21.6 names the grounds)," and adds a new paragraph to the end of §21.6 (absent from edition A) that enumerates only four grounds, omitting the layer/tile-decode-decline case entirely. Both editions' §9.7 (byte-identical) separately states that a verifier declining a tile's decode on resource grounds "reports that check unmade and cannot certify ([R-CNF-11], [R-ERR-04])", so the underlying rule survives in edition B, just not inside the paragraph its own §2.3 says is where "the grounds" are named.
findings.quotation_a: ...*cannot establish* — the last where some requirement is one it is unable to check on a capability or resource ground, as when the file names a format major version it does not implement, when a record carries MUST_UNDERSTAND = 1 with a type it does not implement (§21.6), when it cannot execute a codec or filter ([R-COD-11]), when it declines a layer's or a tile's decode on resource grounds and so cannot check §14's decoded-content obligations ([R-ERR-04], [R-SER-05], [R-SER-08]), or when it declines to decode a user-metadata document ([R-MTA-09]).
findings.quotation_b: A verifier is unable to check a requirement on a capability or resource ground, and so reports *cannot establish* ([R-CNF-11]), as when the file names a format major version it does not implement, a record carries MUST_UNDERSTAND = 1 with a type it does not implement, it cannot execute a codec or filter ([R-COD-11], §17.4), or it declines to decode a user-metadata document ([R-MTA-09]).
findings.byte_level_rationale: A reader of edition B who trusts its own promise ("§21.6 names the grounds") and stops there would build an incomplete list of cannot-establish triggers; but §9.7, unchanged in edition B, independently states the missing ground's operative consequence, so a whole-document implementation of edition B still reaches the same accept/reject/cannot-establish behavior as edition A.

The Note was itself non-normative in edition A (inside a `> **Note.**` block), so its removal does not remove a rule, only removes rationale/exposition.
