findings.title: B inverts A's rule that a conduct-only writer violation never makes the file nonconforming
findings.detail: A states that a handful of writer obligations govern the writer's conduct rather than the file's output (naming examples: which registry version a writer targets per §10.3/§18.3, the barriers a commit performs per §9.2, §6.3's ignore-lane-bit rule, §6.2's pre-trailer-gap pad, §20.3 step 4's bar), and says explicitly 'a file is never nonconforming by virtue of one: conduct rules bind the actor, the predicate binds the bytes.' B's rewritten [R-CNF-02] says the opposite: 'a file that breaks one is nonconforming,' and drops the enumerated examples entirely. This is not just a divergence from A -- it self-contradicts B's own unchanged §9.2 text (identical in both editions), which still says of a writer that omits a commit barrier: 'the file it produces is never nonconforming by virtue of it, as [R-CNF-02] says of every conduct rule.' A verifier implemented strictly from B's §2.3 would certify such a file as nonconforming; one implemented from B's own §9.2 (or from A) would certify it as conforming -- a direct byte-level verdict conflict.
findings.quotation_a: A few obligations this specification places on writers govern their *conduct* rather than their output — where a value is published, which registry version a writer targets (§10.3, §18.3), or the barriers a commit performs (§9.2) — and a file is never nonconforming by virtue of one: conduct rules bind the actor, the predicate binds the bytes. [R-CNF-02]
findings.quotation_b: A writer obligation that governs conduct rather than output, or whose violation this specification expressly declares not to be a file-conformance violation, binds the writer, and a file that breaks one is nonconforming. [R-CNF-02]
findings.byte_level_rationale: A verifier built from A (or from B's own untouched §9.2) reports 'conforming' for a file where only a conduct-only obligation was violated (e.g. a missing commit barrier, or a set ignore-lane bit); a verifier built strictly from B's rewritten §2.3 text alone would report 'nonconforming' for the identical bytes -- a different verdict on the same file.

findings.title: B drops the requirement that a conforming reader handle both registered record types
findings.detail: A requires a conforming reader to 'handle ... every user-metadata encoding §18.2 assigns, and both record types §7.3 registers,' and lists 'a registered record type' among the things whose declination disqualifies 'conforming reader' status under the no-subset-profiles rule. B's corresponding sentence ends at 'every user-metadata encoding §18.2 assigns' and the no-subset-profiles sentence is compressed to 'software that declines any of those' -- silently dropping the record-type item from both the requirement and the disqualification list. §7.3 itself (byte-identical in both editions) never independently frames declining a record type as disqualifying conforming-reader status, so this is not restated elsewhere.
findings.quotation_a: and MUST handle every codec and filter that §17 designates as core, both channel layouts (§14), every sample type that §12 designates as core, every user-metadata encoding §18.2 assigns, and both record types §7.3 registers. There are no subset profiles: software that declines to support a core codec, a core filter, either channel layout, a core sample type, an assigned user-metadata encoding, or a registered record type is not a conforming reader, even if it reads all other conforming files correctly.
findings.quotation_b: and MUST handle every codec and filter that §17 designates as core, both channel layouts (§14), every sample type that §12 designates as core, and every user-metadata encoding §18.2 assigns. There are no subset profiles: software that declines any of those is not a conforming reader, even if it reads all other conforming files correctly.
findings.byte_level_rationale: A reader implemented strictly from B's §2.3 alone would not know that declining to support the registered (0x0002) user-metadata record type disqualifies it from 'conforming reader' status; software built to that reading of B could correctly reject that record type entirely while still calling itself conforming, a classification an implementation built from A would refuse.

findings.title: B's replacement for A's five cannot-establish grounds and its experimental-encoding carve-out states only four grounds and drops the carve-out
findings.detail: A enumerates five grounds for a verifier's *cannot establish* verdict: (1) file names an unimplemented format major, (2) a record carries MUST_UNDERSTAND=1 with an unimplemented type, (3) verifier cannot execute a codec or filter, (4) verifier declines a layer's or a tile's decode on resource grounds and so cannot check §14's decoded-content obligations [R-ERR-04, R-SER-05, R-SER-08], (5) verifier declines to decode a user-metadata document [R-MTA-09]; and adds a carve-out that a user-metadata document under an experimental-range encoding is explicitly *not* such a ground (nothing is left unchecked, certification unaffected, R-MTA-10), while encoding 0 and a reserved value are violations (§21.5, R1). B compresses this whole passage in §2.3 to '(§21.6 names the grounds)' and adds a new paragraph to §21.6 that lists only grounds (1),(2),(3),(5) -- omitting ground (4) entirely -- and carries neither the experimental-encoding carve-out nor the R-MTA-10 citation.
findings.quotation_a: ...as when the file names a format major version it does not implement, when a record carries MUST_UNDERSTAND = 1 with a type it does not implement (§21.6), when it cannot execute a codec or filter ([R-COD-11]), when it declines a layer's or a tile's decode on resource grounds and so cannot check §14's decoded-content obligations ([R-ERR-04], [R-SER-05], [R-SER-08]), or when it declines to decode a user-metadata document ([R-MTA-09]). A user-metadata document under an experimental-range encoding — one this specification does not assign and a conforming file can carry (§21.6) — is not such a ground: no content rule attaches there, so nothing is left unchecked, and certification is unaffected ([R-MTA-10]); encoding 0 and a reserved value are violations (§21.5, R1).
findings.quotation_b: ...on a capability or resource ground (§21.6 names the grounds). [in §21.6, B adds:] A verifier is unable to check a requirement on a capability or resource ground, and so reports *cannot establish* ([R-CNF-11]), as when the file names a format major version it does not implement, a record carries MUST_UNDERSTAND = 1 with a type it does not implement, it cannot execute a codec or filter ([R-COD-11], §17.4), or it declines to decode a user-metadata document ([R-MTA-09]).
findings.byte_level_rationale: A verifier implemented strictly from B alone, on declining a layer's or tile's decode on resource grounds, has no textual basis for reporting the distinct *cannot establish* verdict A requires for that case (ground 4) -- it could instead report an ordinary rejection or an unclassified failure, a different reported verdict than one built from A. Separately, a verifier built from B alone could misapply ground (5)'s 'declines to decode a user-metadata document' to an experimental-range-encoded document and report *cannot establish* / decline certification, whereas A explicitly requires it to certify normally in that case (R-MTA-10) -- a different certification outcome for the same file.

findings.location_a: §2.3, reach paragraph (between the class list and §2.4), [R-CNF-13]
findings.title: B inverts the required outcome for a failing reaching condition (reject-file vs. capability refusal)
findings.detail: A requires a reader to treat a failing reaching condition (one asserting an invariant [R-CNT-24] fixes for every format major) as reject-file under the requirement stating it, explicitly 'rather than on capability grounds'; the distinct capability-refusal diagnostic ([R-CNT-07]) is reserved for the separate case where every reaching condition is satisfied but the declared major itself is unimplemented. B's rewrite says the reader must treat such a failure 'as a capability refusal, not as reject-file' -- the exact opposite -- while still going on, in the very next sentence, to describe [R-CNT-07]'s diagnostic as reserved for the 'every reaching condition satisfied' case, which is internally inconsistent with having just called reaching-condition failure itself a capability refusal. This also contradicts B's own unchanged §21.9 text, which names exactly two capability refusals (a foreign format major, and an unimplemented top-level MU=1 type) and does not include a reaching-condition failure as a third.
findings.quotation_a: A reader MUST apply every reaching condition to a file whatever major it declares — an exemption the condition's governing requirement grants on a ground other than the declared major applies unchanged, [R-CNT-04]'s residency exemption among them — and MUST treat its failure as reject-file on the ground of the requirement stating it rather than on capability grounds; the distinct diagnostic [R-CNT-07] asks for is owed where every reaching condition is satisfied and the declared major is one the reader does not implement.
findings.quotation_b: A reader MUST check every reaching condition whatever major the file declares, and MUST treat a failure as a capability refusal, not as reject-file under the requirement that states the condition; an exemption that the condition's own requirement grants for a reason other than the declared major lapses, [R-CNT-04]'s residency exemption among them. [R-CNT-07]'s distinct diagnostic is given where every reaching condition is satisfied and the declared major is one the reader does not implement.
findings.byte_level_rationale: For a file that declares a foreign format major and also fails a reaching condition (e.g. a corrupt trailer CRC, F14, which reaches under [R-CNT-24]), an implementation built from A reports reject-file with a diagnostic tied to the failing requirement; an implementation built strictly from B's rewritten text alone would report a capability refusal instead -- a different outcome class and a different diagnostic for the identical bytes, which §21's conformance vectors (§21.8) would distinguish.

findings.title: B redefines "addressed" as generation-relative where A treats it as an unconditional per-layer property
findings.detail: A's glossary entry says 'every tile of a layer is *addressed*' -- an unconditional, layer-level property -- before separately defining 'stored in a generation' as generation-relative. B's entry instead makes addressing itself generation-relative: 'a tile is *addressed* in a generation if that generation's tile index has an entry for it: the tiles of the layer's grid under the geometry that generation declares.' This introduces the idea that a layer's geometry (and hence its set of addressed tiles) can vary by generation, which the unchanged §11.2 text (defining 'addressed-tile count' as a fixed function N or C·N of the layer's declared grid, with no per-generation variability mentioned) and §15.1 (speaking simply of 'a layer's tile index') do not clearly support either way. I could not fully resolve, from these two files alone, whether layer geometry is in fact fixed for the life of a layer (which would make B's added generation-qualifier an undecided-elsewhere addition) or genuinely variable across generations (which would make A's simpler wording an oversimplification) without re-deriving §20.3/§20.5's full rewriting rules from scratch.
findings.quotation_a: **addressed tile / stored tile** — every tile of a layer is *addressed*. A tile is *stored in a generation* if and only if that generation's tile-index entry for it is not the sentinel (§15); unqualified *stored* means stored in the live generation.
findings.quotation_b: **addressed tile / stored tile** — a tile is *addressed* in a generation if that generation's tile index has an entry for it: the tiles of the layer's grid under the geometry that generation declares (§11.2, §15). It is *stored in a generation* if and only if that entry is not the sentinel (§15); unqualified *stored* means stored in the live generation.
findings.byte_level_rationale: I flag this as an ambiguity rather than a confirmed byte-level divergence because I was not able to determine, within the two-file access rule, whether a layer's declared geometry can ever differ between two generations of the same file; if it cannot, both wordings pick out the identical set of tiles and no implementation would differ; if it can, B's version is the more correct one and A's glossary entry would itself be the imprecise one. Either reading leaves an implementer of the other document with a definition of 'addressed' that does not obviously track the fuller one.

findings.title: Section 3.3, a Note on Part I/Part II independence, is deleted outright in B with no replacement
findings.detail: A carries a short subsection, entirely a `> **Note.**` block, stating that Part I (container) is independent of Part II (array model) by construction, and that this independence is load-bearing for the updater rules of §7 and §20 (i.e. why appenders and rewriters can carry a layer forward without being able to decode its samples). B's outline has no §3.3 at all -- grepping 'Container and array model' and '3.3' across the whole of B returns no match apart from unrelated numeric coincidences (e.g. an RFC version number). Because the block was already non-normative (a `Note`) under [R-CNF-01] in edition A, its outright removal cannot itself change what a strictly-conforming implementation built from B does, so it fails this task's byte-level LOSS test and is reported as an observation rather than a LOSS. It is nonetheless the starkest instance in this pair of content that existed only inside a Note in A now not appearing anywhere in B at all, which the charter asks me to flag.
findings.quotation_a: > **Note.** Part I (container) is independent of Part II (array model) by construction: no Part I structure requires decoding sample payloads, so appenders, and rewriters that carry a layer forward, operate on files whose layers they cannot decode — that independence is load-bearing for the updater rules of §7 and §20.
findings.quotation_b: absent
findings.byte_level_rationale: The removed text was itself non-normative (a Note) in edition A, so no implementation is built from it in either edition and no accept/reject verdict or emitted byte can differ because of its removal.

findings.title: B reverses both the diagnostic for a failed reaching condition and whether its governing exemptions still apply
findings.detail: A: a reader MUST treat a reaching condition's failure as an ordinary reject-file violation of the requirement stating it, 'rather than on capability grounds' - the distinct capability diagnostic ([R-CNT-07]) is reserved for the separate case where all reaching conditions pass but the declared major is simply unimplemented; and an exemption a condition's own requirement grants on another ground (R-CNT-04's residency exemption is A's own example) 'applies unchanged' when the file declares a non-1 major. findings.quotation_a: A reader MUST apply every reaching condition to a file whatever major it declares — an exemption the condition's governing requirement grants on a ground other than the declared major applies unchanged, `[R-CNT-04]`'s residency exemption among them — and MUST treat its failure as reject-file on the ground of the requirement stating it rather than on capability grounds; the distinct diagnostic `[R-CNT-07]` asks for is owed where every reaching condition is satisfied and the declared major is one the reader does not implement.
findings.quotation_b: A reader MUST check every reaching condition whatever major the file declares, and MUST treat a failure as a capability refusal, not as reject-file under the requirement that states the condition; an exemption that the condition's own requirement grants for a reason other than the declared major lapses, `[R-CNT-04]`'s residency exemption among them.
findings.byte_level_rationale: Take a reader relying on R-CNT-04's residency exemption (not holding certain bytes resident) that encounters a file declaring a non-1 major whose reaching condition fails. Per A, the exemption still applies (unchanged) and the failure is reported as an ordinary reject-file violation under the stated requirement. Per B, the exemption lapses (the reader must now perform the check it was previously exempt from) and, if it fails, the outcome is labelled a capability refusal rather than a reject-file violation of that requirement. Different obligations and a different diagnostic/verdict label on the same bytes and the same reader configuration.

result.summary:
A heading-aligned full-document sweep (every heading common to both editions, matched both directions) shows that of roughly 140 sections, only ~10 differ at all between A and C; everything else — all of Part I (container, §4-§10), all of Part II (array model, §11-§18), Part III's algorithms (§19-§20 bodies), the entire error register (§21.1-§21.5, §21.7-§21.9), Security, Privacy, Test Vectors, and every Appendix — is byte-identical. The rewrite's only real surface area is the front matter, §1 Introduction, §2.3-2.4 (conformance classes and outcome classes), §3.1-3.3 (terms), the §12 intro clause, and one added paragraph at the end of §21.6.

Within that narrow surface, §2.3 (Conformance classes) contains three genuine, high-confidence divergences, each independently confirmed via a cross-reference elsewhere in the same document (so the contradiction does not depend on trusting a paraphrase): (1) the "Conforming TARN file" bullet's rule for writer-conduct obligations is stated with the opposite conclusion in C ("a file that breaks one is nonconforming") from A ("a file is never nonconforming by virtue of one"), and C's own §6.3 (byte-identical to A's) contradicts C's own §2.3 conclusion on the worked example (a set ignore-lane bit); (2) the "reaching condition" paragraph has two MUST-level clauses each flipped to their antonym — "applies unchanged" becomes "lapses" for R-CNT-04's residency exemption, and "reject-file ... rather than on capability grounds" becomes "capability refusal ... not reject-file" — producing a concrete divergence in which bytes a conforming remote reader must fetch and how it must classify a genuine, unfixable defect on a file declaring an unimplemented format major; (3) the "Conforming reader" bullet's no-subset-profiles list drops "both record types §7.3 registers" (and the parallel disjunct "or a registered record type") from the set of things whose non-support disqualifies a reader, while C's own Appendix H checklist (byte-identical to A's) still cites "both registered record types" under the same requirement ID and section number — C disagrees with itself about what its own requirement 03 requires.

I closed seven other candidate divergences after checking whether the apparently-dropped content survives, verbatim and normatively, in an unchanged numbered section elsewhere in the same document (§20.1, §20.4, §9.7, §17.4, §6.4/§19.4/§9.5/§9.6/§20.3, or §4.7) — in every one of those cases it does, so I classify them as EQUIVALENT reorganization of exposition rather than LOSS, and list the closing sentence for each in the transcript rather than reporting them as findings.

findings.location_a: §2.3 Conformance classes, "Conforming TARN file" bullet, [R-CNF-02] (line 156, conduct clause ~168-179)
findings.title: C reverses A's conduct/predicate rule for writer obligations, contradicting C's own §6.3
findings.detail: A states that a writer obligation governing conduct (or one this spec expressly declares not a file-conformance violation) never makes the file nonconforming: 'conduct rules bind the actor, the predicate binds the bytes,' and names §6.3's ignore-lane-bit rule as a worked example. C's rewritten sentence keeps the same category of obligation but flips the conclusion to 'a file that breaks one is nonconforming.' §6.3 is byte-identical in both editions and states outright that a set (undefined) ignore-lane bit 'is not a file-conformance violation' — so edition C's §2.3 now contradicts edition C's own §6.3 on the very case A cites. Concretely: a minimal conforming file with trailer flags bit 16 set (an undefined ignore-lane bit) and a correctly-recomputed trailer CRC is CONFORMING under A (and under C's §6.3), but a verifier applying only C's rewritten §2.3 general rule at face value must call the identical bytes NONCONFORMING, since writing flags=0 is exactly the kind of writer obligation the sentence now says makes the file nonconforming when broken.
findings.quotation_a: a file is never nonconforming by virtue of one: conduct rules bind the actor, the predicate binds the bytes. A writer obligation whose violation this specification expressly declares not to be a file-conformance violation binds the actor in the same way; §6.3's flags rules against a set ignore-lane bit ... are the cases this text states
findings.quotation_b: A writer obligation that governs conduct rather than output, or whose violation this specification expressly declares not to be a file-conformance violation, binds the writer, and a file that breaks one is nonconforming.
findings.byte_level_rationale: A verifier built strictly from edition C's §2.3 sentence classifies the described file (valid trailer, one set undefined ignore-lane bit, correct CRC) as nonconforming; a verifier built from edition A's §2.3 (or from either edition's byte-identical §6.3) classifies the identical byte sequence as conforming. Same bytes, opposite certification verdict depending on which passage of C is applied — and C's two passages disagree with each other on the identical file.

findings.title: Two MUST-level clauses on reaching-condition failures are each flipped to their antonym in C
findings.detail: A: an exemption a condition's own requirement grants on a non-major ground (R-CNT-04's residency exemption is the named example) 'applies unchanged' when the condition reaches a file of another major, and a reader 'MUST treat its failure as reject-file on the ground of the requirement stating it rather than on capability grounds.' C: the same exemption 'lapses,' and the reader 'MUST treat a failure as a capability refusal, not as reject-file under the requirement that states the condition.' Both editions frame these as MUST-level rules; C's wording is the antonym of A's at both points while the surrounding sentence structure and even the R-CNT-04/R-CNT-07 citations are otherwise unchanged — this is not paraphrase or reflow. Concretely, for a remote reader (§6.4-style, not holding the front signature block resident) opening a file that declares an unimplemented major and whose front signature block (a reaching condition per §6.3, byte-identical in both editions: 'the front signature block ... is constant ... permanently') is actually corrupted: under A the exemption still lets that reader skip fetching bytes [0,16) and, having every reaching condition it did check pass, report the case as a capability-only refusal ([R-CNT-07]'s diagnostic), never fetching the corrupted bytes at all. Under C the exemption 'lapses,' so the same reader is now required to fetch and check those bytes for reach purposes — an extra byte range A never requires — and, on finding them corrupted, C's parallel clause tells it to report even that discovered, non-major-specific defect as a mere 'capability refusal' rather than the corruption it is (exactly the misdiagnosis §6.3 itself warns readers against, since no future major fixes an invariant [R-CNT-24] fixes for every major).
findings.quotation_a: an exemption the condition's governing requirement grants on a ground other than the declared major applies unchanged, `[R-CNT-04]`'s residency exemption among them — and MUST treat its failure as reject-file on the ground of the requirement stating it rather than on capability grounds
findings.quotation_b: an exemption that the condition's own requirement grants for a reason other than the declared major lapses, `[R-CNT-04]`'s residency exemption among them ... MUST treat a failure as a capability refusal, not as reject-file under the requirement that states the condition
findings.byte_level_rationale: The two editions require different reader I/O and different mandatory diagnostic categorization for the identical file (declared unimplemented major + corrupted, non-resident front signature block): A permits the remote reader to never fetch bytes [0,16) and to report a pure capability refusal; C requires fetching those bytes for reach purposes and then requires labeling the resulting defect the same way A reserves for the no-defect case. An implementation built from A alone and one built from C alone perform different byte-range fetches and emit different mandatory diagnostic classifications for the same input file.

quizDivergences.title: Slate A quiza-04: the editions' takers answer differently
quizDivergences.detail:
QUESTION: A TARN file's physical bytes end at some offset F. The final 64 bytes, [F−64, F), do not match the trailer magic. However, 64 bytes before that, at [F−128, F−64), sits a byte sequence that is a fully valid trailer: correct magic, a verifying trailer CRC, and a committed_file_length field equal to F−64. A conforming reader opens this file via its default read path (not a deliberate recovery operation). (a) What must this reader report about the file? (b) Is the reader permitted, on this default path, to fall back to using the earlier valid-looking trailer it could find 64 bytes back? Answer (a) in one phrase (the outcome the default path assigns) and (b) yes/no.
FROM A: (a) reject-file (reported as torn/invalid); (b) no [high] cites §9.5 [R-LIF-05]; §21.2 row F8 [R-CNT-06]; §9.6
FROM B: (a) file torn or invalid; (b) no [high] cites §9.5 [R-LIF-05] (default read path); §9.6 [R-LIF-06] (recovery scan is a separate, deliberate operation, not a reader behavior)
A's reasoning: The final 64 bytes fail the trailer-magic check (register row F8, reject-file, detected at open). R-LIF-05 fixes the default read path as trailer-at-end-or-fail and forbids scanning backward; finding the earlier valid trailer is exclusively §9.6's deliberate recovery-scan operation, explicitly 'not a reader behavior' on the default path, so the reader may not fall back to it.
B's reasoning: The final 64 bytes fail the trailer-magic check (an F8-type failure). Under the default open path (not a deliberate recovery operation, §9.6), R-LIF-05 requires the reader to report the file torn or invalid and forbids scanning backward — so the earlier, byte-valid trailer 64 bytes further back is never consulted on this path, even though it would satisfy every check §9.6's recovery scan applies. Falling back to it is exactly the recovery-scan behavior §9.6 reserves for recovery tools and verifiers, 'never conforming readers on the default path.'

quizDivergences.quotation_b: The default read path is trailer-at-end-or-fail: a reader that finds no valid trailer in the final 64 bytes MUST report the file torn or invalid and MUST NOT scan backward.
quizDivergences.byte_level_rationale: Mechanically detected divergence; the quiz comparator decides whether it is the same answer, a taker error, or a difference between the editions.

quizDivergences.title: Slate A quiza-05: the editions' takers answer differently
quizDivergences.detail:
QUESTION: In the checksum coverage map, which single checksum's covered byte range includes the four bytes of a layer record's own crc_of_crc_array field (that is, what would catch bit-corruption of the crc_of_crc_array field's stored bytes themselves)? Separately, what does crc_of_crc_array itself serve to verify — that is, over what bytes is it the CRC-32C? Give two short answers: (a) the name of the covering checksum/structure, and (b) the name of the structure crc_of_crc_array is computed over.
FROM A: (a) the directory region's checksum; (b) the segment-CRC array [high] cites §4.5; §7.4; §8.1 coverage map
FROM B: (a) the directory region's terminal checksum; (b) the layer's segment-CRC array [high] cites §8.1 coverage map (Directory region row); §7.4 (crc_of_crc_array field definition); §7.1
A's reasoning: crc_of_crc_array's own 4 stored bytes sit inside the layer record's inline payload, which is part of the directory's record sequence; §8.1's map states the directory region's terminal checksum covers 'the preceding dir_length - 4 bytes (the raw record sequence)', which is what would catch corruption of crc_of_crc_array's stored bytes. quizDivergences.title: Slate A quiza-10: the editions' takers answer differently
quizDivergences.detail:
QUESTION: A file-scope user-metadata document is stored under encoding 2 (zstd). Its decoded byte length is exactly 800 bytes. The compressed frame carrying it sets Single_Segment_Flag (so it has no separate Window_Descriptor), and its Frame_Content_Size field is present with the value 750. (a) Is this conforming? (b) If not, is the violation classified as a failure to decode the document, or as a broken frame constraint (name which)? (c) What quantity does this specification require the frame's content-size field to match here — and how does that differ from what the analogous rule requires for a tile's stored bytes under the same codec? Answer (a) yes/no, (b) the classification, and (c) a one-sentence statement of the matched quantity and the contrast.
FROM A: (a) no; (b) broken frame constraint; (c) The document's content-size field must equal the document's actual decoded byte length (there being no independently declared document size), whereas a tile's content-size field under the same codec must equal the tile's decoded size derived purely from the layer's structural declarations, fixed before any decoding occurs. [high] cites §18.2 [R-MTA-09]; register row R4 vs R3
FROM B: (a) no; (b) broken frame constraint (R4); (c) the field must equal the decoded document's actual byte length (800), whereas the analogous tile-scope rule under the same codec requires the field to match the tile's decoded size as derived purely from the layer's structural declarations (geometry/layout/channel types), never from what the stored bytes actually decode to. [high] cites §18.2 [R-MTA-09] (content-size field pinned to decoded document length) and its contrast with §17.2 [R-COD-06] (tile content-size field pinned to declared decoded size); §21.5 rows R3/R4
A's reasoning: §18.2 states the content-size field, when present, 'MUST equal the byte length of the decoded document' (800 here, not the declared 750), and explicitly routes such a mismatch to R4 (a broken frame constraint) rather than R3 (a failure to decode), since the bytes do decode successfully. This is R-MTA-09's document-level transposition of R-COD-06's tile rule, where the compared quantity is the layer's declared decoded size rather than a measured decode output.
B's reasoning: The document decodes to 800 bytes, but the frame's Frame_Content_Size field (present, since Single_Segment_Flag makes it double as Window_Size) declares 750 — a mismatch against R-MTA-09's rule that a present content-size field must equal the decoded document's byte length. This is explicitly routed to R4 ('a broken frame constraint'), not R3 ('failure to decode'), because the bytes still decode; what's wrong is what the header asserted about them. Every register row (R4 included) is a file-conformance violation regardless of its ignore-record blast radius, so the file as a whole is not conforming. The contrast with the tile rule (R-COD-06): for a tile, the frame's content-size field (when present) must match the tile's decoded size, a quantity fixed by the layer's declarations alone and known before any decode; a user-metadata document has no such declared size, so §18.2 substitutes the document's actual decoded byte length as the quantity the field must match.

A mismatch is one of the frame constraints R4 registers, not a failure to decode under R3: the bytes decode, and what is wrong is what the header said about them.

quizDivergences.title: Slate A quiza-13: the editions' takers answer differently
quizDivergences.detail:
QUESTION: A layer record carries exactly two sub-records: one user-metadata sub-record (governed by its registry-fixed flags), and one sub-record of an experimental-range type (type value ≥ 0x8000) that the updater in question does not implement, with that sub-record's stored MUST_UNDERSTAND bit set to 1. The updater wants to drop this entire layer in an otherwise-unremarkable commit. Is the updater permitted to drop the layer? Answer yes/no, and name the specific mechanism (which record's flag, and what it does to the operation) that determines the answer.
FROM A: no; the experimental sub-record's stored MUST_UNDERSTAND=1 bit governs (since the updater does not implement that type) and blocks any modification of the layer, drop included [high] cites §20.4; [R-CNT-15]; [R-CNT-22]
FROM B: no; the sub-record's stored MUST_UNDERSTAND=1 bit, for an experimental-range type the updater does not implement, makes those stored flags authoritative (per record framing / R-CNT-15) and blocks any modification of the layer it governs, including dropping the layer, under §20.4's MU=1 row [high] cites §20.4 table (MU=1 row) [R-WRT-08]; §7.3/§7.2 [R-CNT-15], [R-CNT-18] (stored flags authoritative for an unimplemented type)
A's reasoning: §20.4 states that for a type the updater does not implement, the record's stored flags (not a registry) are authoritative; here that sub-record's stored MU bit is 1. The table's MU=1 row: 'Retain byte-identical. The updater MUST NOT modify the scope the record governs. At layer scope an unknown critical record blocks modification of that layer, its drop included.' The user-metadata sub-record (registered type, registry-fixed MU=0,PE=1) is irrelevant to this block; it is the unimplemented experimental-range sub-record's MU=1 status that forbids the drop.
B's reasoning: The sub-record is of an experimental-range type (>=0x8000) the updater does not implement; for a type the updater does not implement, the stored flags are authoritative (§20.4's preamble, §7.3/R-CNT-15), and here MUST_UNDERSTAND is stored as 1. §20.4's table row for MU=1 states that such a record must be retained byte-identical and that 'the updater MUST NOT modify the scope the record governs,' explicitly naming that at layer scope this 'blocks modification of that layer, its drop included.' The co-present user-metadata sub-record (registry-fixed MU=0, PE=1) is independently retained but does not change this outcome — one MU=1 unimplemented sub-record is sufficient to block the drop of the whole layer.

quizDivergences.title: Slate A quiza-15: the editions' takers answer differently
quizDivergences.detail:
QUESTION: A verifier examines a file containing two layers, A and B. During its walk it establishes one definite violation in layer A (two of its dimension entries share an identical name). Separately, layer B declares a codec the verifier is unable to execute due to a resource constraint, so the verifier cannot check layer B's decoded-content obligations at all. (a) What overall verdict — conforming, nonconforming, or cannot establish — must the verifier report for the file as a whole? (b) Must the verifier still say anything in its report about the requirement it could not check on layer B, even though the overall verdict is already decided by (a)? If so, name the two things that per-requirement report must state.
FROM A: (a) nonconforming; (b) yes; the requirement (its identity/name), and the ground (the capability or resource reason it could not be checked) [high] cites §2.3 [R-CNF-11]
FROM B: nonconforming; yes; the requirement it could not check, and the capability/resource ground it could not check it on [high] cites §2.3 [R-CNF-11] (verdict priority and mandatory per-requirement reporting)
A's reasoning: Layer A's duplicate dimension name is an established violation, and R-CNF-11 makes 'cannot establish' available only where no violation has been established anywhere in the file; an established violation forces the overall verdict to nonconforming regardless of what else is unchecked. R-CNF-11 nonetheless separately requires: 'A verifier MUST report each requirement it was unable to check on a capability or resource ground, naming the requirement and the ground, whichever of the three verdicts it reports' -- so the codec-execution failure on layer B must still be reported, naming the unchecked requirement and the resource ground.
B's reasoning: Layer A's duplicate dimension names is an established, definite violation (L9), so R-CNF-11's priority rule fixes the overall verdict at nonconforming regardless of how many other requirements (such as layer B's decoded-content obligations) the verifier could not check — 'cannot establish' is only available where no violation was established at all. Independently of the overall verdict, R-CNF-11 obliges the verifier to report every requirement it was unable to check on a capability or resource ground, 'naming the requirement and the ground,' whichever of the three verdicts is reported — so the verifier must still state, for layer B's uncheckable codec, both the specific requirement it could not check and the capability/resource ground that prevented checking it.

quizDivergences.quotation_b: An established violation takes priority: a verifier that has established any violation reports *nonconforming*, however many requirements it was unable to check, and *cannot establish* is available only to a traversal that established no violation. A verifier MUST report each requirement it was unable to check on a capability or resource ground, naming the requirement and the ground, whichever of the three verdicts it reports.

quizDivergences.title: Slate B quizb-q8: the editions' takers answer differently
quizDivergences.detail:
QUESTION: A layer record declares a nonzero per-tile alignment A = 1024 together with a nonzero slab run length S = 50 and a slab alignment A_slab = 4096 (itself a valid power of two in range). FROM B: fail; L20; reject-layer [high] cites §7.4 (alignment/slab mutual exclusion note); [R-CNT-16]; §21.3 row L20

quizDivergences.title: Slate B quizb-q11: the editions' takers answer differently
quizDivergences.detail:
QUESTION: During an appender's commit, one of a layer's existing tile-index entries is not touched by the commit (the tile it addresses is neither superseded nor newly stored) — call it entry E. Entry E's own 20 bytes are well-formed under §15.3's classification (non-sentinel, offset ≥ 16, both fields in the valid domain, no overflow, extent within bounds), but the bytes at the extent entry E addresses fail entry E's own crc field. When the appender re-emits this layer's tile-index region, what MUST it do with entry E's 20 bytes? And separately, when a reader later requests the tile entry E addresses, what outcome does that read report (name the outcome class)?
FROM A: carry the 20 bytes forward byte-identically (unchanged); reject-tile [high] cites §15.3 [R-IDX-03]; §20.3 step 4 [R-WRT-04], step 2 [R-WRT-01]; §21.4 row T1 [R-CNT-20]
FROM B: carry the entry's 20 bytes forward byte-identically (unchanged) at its disk-ordinal position; reject-tile [high] cites §20.3 step 2 and step 4, [R-WRT-04]; §15.3 entry-validity table; §21.4 row T1
A's reasoning: §15.3 makes such an entry well-formed (not structurally defective), so §20.3 step 4's default applies to an untouched entry: it is re-emitted byte-identical at its disk-ordinal position, and step 2 bars the appender from repairing what it carries forward. For a subsequent read, the stored bytes still fail the entry's crc, which is register row T1, whose outcome (§21.4 header, [R-CNT-20]) is reject-tile.
B's reasoning: Entry E is untouched by the commit and its own 20 bytes are well-formed under §15.3's structural classification, so it is neither superseded nor newly written; step 4's rule that 'every other entry [is] byte-identical at its disk-ordinal position' applies, and the step-2 note makes explicit that even a defective (here, crc-failing) entry an appender meets is reproduced byte-identically, not repaired. Separately, §15.3's table states that an entry whose stored bytes fail its own crc field is reject-tile (the entry itself remains well-formed and its extent stands) -- matching register row T1, whose detector is the reader at tile use.
quizDivergences.quotation_a: An entry whose only defect is that its stored bytes fail its crc is well-formed: the defect lies in the bytes it addresses, not in the entry, so its extent stands
quizDivergences.quotation_b: a malformed index entry an appender meets while re-emitting a region is carried forward byte-identically at its disk-ordinal position under step 4, not repaired to a sentinel
quizDivergences.byte_level_rationale: Mechanically detected divergence; the quiz comparator decides whether it is the same answer, a taker error, or a difference between the editions.

quizDivergences.title: Slate B quizb-q13: the editions' takers answer differently
quizDivergences.detail:
QUESTION: A rewriter is compacting a TARN file. In doing so it must regenerate one layer's entire tile-index region, because some of that layer's stored extents are being relocated. Among that layer's existing tile-index entries is one entry that §15.3 classifies as reject-tile on a structural ground (for example, its offset and length fields are inconsistent with the sentinel pattern) — meaning the entry addresses no usable stored extent at all. List, as a short ordered list, the only two dispositions available to the rewriter for this situation (i.e., the only two things it is permitted to do), per the specification's own text.
FROM A: 1. Drop the layer 2. Refuse to rewrite [high] cites §20.5 [R-WRT-06]/[R-WRT-07] regenerating-region text
FROM B: Drop the layer; Refuse to rewrite [high] cites §20.5, [R-WRT-06]
A's reasoning: §20.5 states directly that meeting a structurally reject-tile entry while regenerating a region leaves the rewriter exactly two disposals: drop the whole layer (as §20.4's table licenses), or refuse to rewrite the file.
B's reasoning: When regenerating a tile-index region, an entry §15.3 classifies reject-tile on a structural ground has no stored extent to re-point (unlike a sentinel, which is simply re-emitted unchanged, or a crc-only-failing entry, which still has a real extent to relocate). §20.5 states explicitly and exhaustively that the rewriter's only two options are to drop the layer (licensed by §20.4's PE=0 disposal table, since a layer record has PE=0) or to refuse to rewrite the file entirely.
quizDivergences.quotation_a: since it can neither reproduce the entry nor invent a replacement: drop the layer, which §20.4's table licenses ..., or refuse
quizDivergences.quotation_b: `[R-WRT-06]` then leaves it two disposals, since it can neither reproduce the entry nor invent a replacement: drop the layer, which §20.4's table licenses and whose loss the rewriter SHOULD report as that table says, or refuse.

quizDivergences.title: Slate B quizb-q14: the editions' takers answer differently
quizDivergences.detail:
QUESTION: An interleaved layer declares two channels, both int32 (4-byte element size each), and tile extents (128, 128) — so P = 16,384 sample positions per tile. This layer declares codec 3 (zstd). One of its stored tiles' zstd frame header declares (via a Window_Descriptor) a Window_Size of 1,048,576 bytes. Is this tile's frame a validity error under the codec's declared-window rule? If so, name the register-row identifier, the resulting outcome class, and whether the detecting actor is the reader or the verifier.
FROM A: yes, T21, reject-tile, reader [high] cites §14.2 decoded-size arithmetic; §17.2 [R-COD-06]; §21.4 row T21
FROM B: fail; T21; reject-tile; reader [high] cites §14.2 byte-layout table; §17.2, [R-COD-06]; §21.4 row T21
A's reasoning: P=128*128=16384, Q=4+4=8 (two int32 channels, interleaved), decoded size = P·Q = 131,072 bytes. The declared Window_Size (1,048,576) exceeds that, which is [R-COD-06]'s bar, register row T21, detector reader (per the row's own Detector column), outcome reject-tile (§21.4 header).
B's reasoning: Decoded size = P·Q = (128×128)·(4+4) = 16,384×8 = 131,072 bytes. The frame's declared Window_Size of 1,048,576 bytes exceeds this decoded size, which [R-COD-06] makes a validity error at tile scope, checkable purely from the frame header (a reader obligation, not one reserved to a verifier). Register row T21 documents this exact condition with Detector = reader and outcome reject-tile.

quizDivergences.quotation_b: MUST NOT declare a window size exceeding the tile's decoded size; a reader MUST treat either as a validity error at tile scope, both being header-checkable.

findings.title: Edition B reverses whether breaking a conduct-only/expressly-non-violation writer obligation makes the file nonconforming
findings.detail: Edition A states plainly that a file is never nonconforming for breaking a writer obligation that governs conduct rather than output, or that this specification expressly declares not a file-conformance violation -- naming as its own examples a set ignore-lane flag bit, a pre-trailer gap longer than the commit pad, and a layer's fixed declarations under Section 20.3 step 4. Edition B's rewrite of the same rule states the opposite: such a violation 'binds the writer, and a file that breaks one is nonconforming.' This also contradicts edition B's own Section 6.2 ('a longer gap is conforming') and Section 6.3 ('a set ignore-lane bit is not a file-conformance violation'), both byte-identical to edition A. An implementer following edition B's Section 2.3 alone, without cross-checking Section 6, would report nonconforming for files Section 6 (and edition A throughout) treats as conforming.
findings.quotation_a: A few obligations this specification places on writers govern their *conduct* rather than their output... and a file is never nonconforming by virtue of one: conduct rules bind the actor, the predicate binds the bytes. A writer obligation whose violation this specification expressly declares not to be a file-conformance violation binds the actor in the same way; Section 6.3's flags rules against a set ignore-lane bit..., Section 6.2's pre-trailer gap longer than [R-LIF-02] step 5's pad, and Section 20.3 step 4's bar on the fixed declarations of a layer that stores a tile are the cases this text states...
findings.quotation_b: A writer obligation that governs conduct rather than output, or whose violation this specification expressly declares not to be a file-conformance violation, binds the writer, and a file that breaks one is nonconforming. [R-CNF-02]
findings.byte_level_rationale: A verifier built strictly from edition B's Section 2.3 text would certify 'nonconforming' for a file with, e.g., a longer-than-pad pre-trailer gap and no other defect; a verifier built from edition A (or from edition B's own byte-identical Section 6.2) would certify the same file conforming. Different accept/reject verdicts on the identical file.

findings.title: Edition B reverses the disposition of a reaching condition's failure: reject-file becomes 'capability refusal'
findings.detail: Edition A requires a reader to treat a reaching condition's failure (e.g. trailer magic, trailer CRC) as ordinary reject-file under the requirement that states it, explicitly not as a capability-grounds refusal; the distinct capability diagnostic is reserved for the case where every reaching condition passes but the declared major is unimplemented. Edition B's rewrite says the opposite: treat the failure as a capability refusal, not as reject-file. This contradicts edition B's own Section 21.2 (byte-identical to edition A), whose opening paragraph derives exactly F8, F14, F6 and both of F1's instances as the reaching rows and whose table assigns all of them Detector=reader, Detected=open, under the section's stated 'Outcome: reject-file' -- none are marked as capability refusals.
findings.quotation_a: A reader MUST apply every reaching condition to a file whatever major it declares... and MUST treat its failure as reject-file on the ground of the requirement stating it rather than on capability grounds; the distinct diagnostic [R-CNT-07] asks for is owed where every reaching condition is satisfied and the declared major is one the reader does not implement.
findings.quotation_b: A reader MUST check every reaching condition whatever major the file declares, and MUST treat a failure as a capability refusal, not as reject-file under the requirement that states the condition...
findings.byte_level_rationale: Per [R-CNF-11] (identical in both editions), an established violation forces a verifier to report nonconforming, while a capability ground forces cannot-establish, and the two are mutually exclusive. Edition B's Section 2.3 text, taken alone, would route a reaching-condition failure (e.g. trailer-magic mismatch on a file declaring an unimplemented major) to cannot-establish; edition B's own Section 21.2 routes the identical bytes to nonconforming. Different MUST-level verdicts on the identical file.

findings.title: Edition B drops the requirement that a conforming reader implement both registered record types, breaking Appendix H's cross-reference
findings.detail: Edition A's [R-CNF-03] requires a conforming reader to handle, among other things, 'both record types Section 7.3 registers,' and its no-subset-profiles sentence disqualifies software that declines 'a registered record type.' Edition B drops both clauses; Section 7.3 itself never independently states this obligation. Edition B's Appendix H conformance checklist -- byte-identical to edition A's -- still credits [R-CNF-03] with requiring 'both registered record types,' so edition B now contains an internal citation to a rule its own cited section no longer states.
findings.quotation_a: ...and MUST handle every codec and filter that Section 17 designates as core, both channel layouts (Section 14), every sample type that Section 12 designates as core, every user-metadata encoding Section 18.2 assigns, and both record types Section 7.3 registers. There are no subset profiles: software that declines to support a core codec, a core filter, either channel layout, a core sample type, an assigned user-metadata encoding, or a registered record type is not a conforming reader...
findings.quotation_b: ...and MUST handle every codec and filter that Section 17 designates as core, both channel layouts (Section 14), every sample type that Section 12 designates as core, and every user-metadata encoding Section 18.2 assigns. There are no subset profiles: software that declines any of those is not a conforming reader, even if it reads all other conforming files correctly.
findings.byte_level_rationale: A reader implementation that supports only layer records (type 0x0001) and rejects every file containing a user-metadata record would fail edition A's [R-CNF-03] but, read literally, satisfies edition B's [R-CNF-03]; the two texts license different software as 'conforming' for the same input files.

findings.title: Edition B drops 'and updaters' from the sentence establishing that updaters inherit every reader obligation
findings.detail: Edition A states that verifiers and updaters are both readers of the files they process and inherit every reader obligation. Edition B narrows this to verifiers only. Section 20.4's step table -- byte-identical in both editions -- depends on this: its MU=1 row states 'the updater is a reader of the file first (Section 2.3),' citing back to exactly the sentence edition B has narrowed.
findings.quotation_a: Verifiers and updaters are readers of the files they process and inherit every reader obligation.
findings.quotation_b: Verifiers are readers of the files they process and inherit every reader obligation.
findings.byte_level_rationale: Edition B's Section 2.3, read alone, no longer establishes that an updater must satisfy every ordinary reader obligation (only that a verifier must); an updater built to satisfy only the obligations edition B's Section 2.3 assigns it, while still relying on Section 20.4's cross-reference, would be under-specified as to which reader-level checks (e.g. reject-file gates) it must still perform before writing.

findings.title: Reader A's CONTRADICTION about F5 vs. the reach doctrine applies unchanged to edition B; reader B did not surface it
findings.detail: Reader A's finding (readera-01) is that Section 19.1 step 1 rejects any file under 128 bytes on F5 grounds before the trailer, and hence version_major, is ever read, while Section 2.3's reach doctrine says F5 does not reach a file declaring another major and so must not be established against it -- leaving a file with 80<=F<128 whose (unread) trailer would validate an unimplemented major with an undetermined verdict. Section 19.1 is byte-identical between editions, and F5's exclusion from the reaching rows is stated identically in both editions' Section 21.2 preamble, so this exact tension exists in edition B as written, unchanged. Reader B's transcript and findings do not raise it. Edition B's separate reversal in [R-CNF-13] (cmp-reader-02) means edition B no longer even states clearly that a reaching condition's failure is ordinary reject-file rather than a capability refusal, which if anything sharpens the difficulty of resolving the tension from edition B's text alone.
findings.quotation_a: an F below 128 is a validity error at file scope decided from F alone and needing no other byte of the file ([R-CNT-27], F5)
findings.quotation_b: an F below 128 is a validity error at file scope decided from F alone and needing no other byte of the file ([R-CNT-27], F5)
findings.byte_level_rationale: The cited passages are byte-identical between editions, so this is not a fidelity difference between A and B; it is a finding that a defect readera-01 attributes to 'the document' is present equally in both texts and that reader B's walk omitted it, not that edition B resolves it.

findings.location_b: Section 21.2 (F5 Instances column); Section 21.1; Section 6.4 (R1 baseline)

Both conditions are therefore properties of the shared text and apply equally to edition A; reader A's transcript quotes the same Section 6.4 passages but does not tag its own R1 answer as underdetermined or raise either point as a finding.

findings.title: Dropped version_major=0 carve-out sentence and F14/F5/F15 worked Note: substance survives verbatim in Section 21.2
findings.detail: Edition A's Section 2.3 states that a file with version_major=0 declares no major at all and so raises no reach question (F18 applies instead), and carries a non-normative Note walking through why F14 reaches, F5 does not, and F15 does not despite citing [R-CNT-24]. Both are absent from edition B's Section 2.3. Section 21.2's opening paragraph, byte-identical in both editions, already states the version_major=0 point directly and, by deriving exactly F8/F14/F6/F1 as the reaching rows 'and no other row,' already establishes F5's exclusion without needing the deleted Note's worked reasoning.
findings.quotation_a: A file whose version_major is 0 declares no major at all (Section 6.3): it is not a file declaring a format major other than 1, no reach question arises for it, and [R-CNT-07] rejects it (Section 21.2, F18).
findings.quotation_b: absent
findings.byte_level_rationale: Both editions state, in byte-identical Section 21.2 text, that version_major=0 is outside the reach premise and that F5 is excluded from the reaching rows; no implementation decision changes between the editions on this point.

findings.title: Dropped 'governs every record type' clause restated verbatim at Section 20.4
findings.detail: Edition A's [R-CNF-06] notes that the preservation obligations of Section 20.4 govern every record type, not only those an updater does not understand. Edition B drops the appositive from [R-CNF-06], but Section 20.4's own opening sentence, byte-identical in both editions, states the same fact directly.
findings.quotation_a: An updater MUST satisfy every writer requirement for the bytes it produces, and additionally MUST honor the preservation obligations of Section 20.4 -- which govern every record type, not only those it does not understand.
findings.quotation_b: An updater MUST satisfy every writer requirement for the bytes it produces, and additionally MUST honor the preservation obligations of Section 20.4.
findings.byte_level_rationale: Section 20.4's identical opening sentence ('Persistence governs every record type; only the authoritative source of the flags differs') already states the dropped fact for any reader of the full document.

findings.title: Both walks answer R1 from byte-identical Section 6.4 text; the 'underdetermined' tagging difference is a reporting choice, not a text difference

Reader B additionally tags its structured R1 answer '[underdetermined]' and raises readerb-03 as an AMBIGUITY finding; reader A's transcript quotes the same material without either tag or finding. Since Section 6.4 is confirmed byte-identical between editions, this is not evidence the two editions differ on R1's determinacy.
findings.quotation_a: A reader MAY instead speculatively fetch a suffix window in one request and use containment: if the fetched buffer contains the directory region, request 2 is unnecessary.
findings.quotation_b: A reader MAY instead speculatively fetch a suffix window in one request and use containment: if the fetched buffer contains the directory region, request 2 is unnecessary.
findings.byte_level_rationale: The quoted sentence, and all of Section 6.4, is byte-identical between editions, so no implementation built from one edition alone would differ from one built from the other on R1's answer or its determinacy.

findings.title: R2, R5, R6, R7 and R8 are answered identically from confirmed byte-identical passages in both editions

findings.location_a: R3 (Section 17.2 [R-COD-03]; Section 17.4 [R-COD-11]; Section 2.3 [R-CNF-03] codec clause; Section 21.3 row L43)
findings.location_b: R3 (Section 17.2 [R-COD-03]; Section 17.4 [R-COD-11]; Section 2.3 [R-CNF-03] codec clause; Section 21.3 row L43)

The [R-CNF-03] clause requiring core-codec support and the no-subset-profiles disqualification for codecs (distinct from the separately-affected record-type clause covered by cmp-reader-03) are unchanged between editions, as are Section 17.2, Section 17.4 and Section 21.3's L43 row. findings.quotation_b: software unable to execute an assigned codec or filter is not a conforming reader ([R-CNF-03])

findings.location_a: §2.3 Conformance definitions, "Conforming TARN file" bullet [R-CNF-02] (edition A only has this polarity; the identical text also appears, correctly, in both editions' §20.3 step 4)
findings.location_b: §2.3 Conformance definitions, "Conforming TARN file" bullet [R-CNF-02] (edition B's rewritten text; contradicts edition B's own §20.3 step 4, which is byte-identical to edition A's)
findings.title: Edition B's [R-CNF-02] definition inverts edition A's conduct-rule polarity, contradicting edition B's own §20.3
findings.detail: Edition A states that a writer obligation governing conduct rather than output, or one this specification expressly declares not to be a file-conformance violation, never makes the file nonconforming by itself ("a file is never nonconforming by virtue of one: conduct rules bind the actor, the predicate binds the bytes"). Edition B's rewrite of the same [R-CNF-02] bullet says the opposite: "a file that breaks one is nonconforming" — asserted of the very category ("expressly declares not to be a file-conformance violation") that logically cannot make a file nonconforming, a self-contradiction within one sentence. Edition B's own §20.3 step 4 (byte-identical to edition A there) still states edition A's polarity under the same [R-CNF-02] tag ("no file is nonconforming by virtue of its violation... a file such a commit leaves can be nonconforming on its own terms" only where a separate, witnessed byte-level rule is also broken). An implementer building a verifier strictly from edition B's §2.3 text would reject files that a verifier built from §20.3 (or from edition A entirely) would accept — e.g. W6's no-padding case, a fill-value change on a layer with no edge-tile padding, which both walkers agree triggers no register row.
findings.quotation_a: A few obligations this specification places on writers govern their *conduct* rather than their output — where a value is published, which registry version a writer targets (§10.3, §18.3), or the barriers a commit performs (§9.2) — and a file is never nonconforming by virtue of one: conduct rules bind the actor, the predicate binds the bytes. A writer obligation whose violation this specification expressly declares not to be a file-conformance violation binds the actor in the same way...
findings.quotation_b: A writer obligation that governs conduct rather than output, or whose violation this specification expressly declares not to be a file-conformance violation, binds the writer, and a file that breaks one is nonconforming. `[R-CNF-02]`
findings.byte_level_rationale: A verifier implemented strictly from edition B's §2.3 [R-CNF-02] text would report NONCONFORMING for a file whose only defect is an unwitnessed writer-conduct violation (no register row triggered anywhere in §21); a verifier implemented from edition A's §2.3, or from either edition's §20.3 step 4, would report the identical file CONFORMING. That is a different accept/reject verdict on an identifiable file, arising from two internally inconsistent passages that exist only in edition B — edition A has no such tension anywhere in its text.

findings.location_b: §2.3, "Conforming reader" bullet [R-CNF-03] (edition B's shortened list); contrast with the unchanged "Conforming reader —" appendix checklist near the end of both editions, which still cites [R-CNF-03]/§2.3 for the full list
findings.title: Edition B's [R-CNF-03] list drops "registered record types" that an unchanged appendix still attributes to it
findings.detail: Edition A's [R-CNF-03] paragraph lists six things a conforming reader's no-subset-profile obligation covers, ending "...and both record types §7.3 registers," and restates the same six in its negative form ("...or a registered record type is not a conforming reader"). Edition B's rewrite of the same paragraph, under the same [R-CNF-03] tag, lists only five items, omitting record types from both the affirmative and negative forms. Both editions' unchanged "Conforming reader —" appendix checklist near the end of the document still reads "...implements all four codecs, both filters, both layouts, all thirteen sample types, both user-metadata encodings, and both registered record types ([R-CNF-03], §2.3)" — attributing the full six-item list to a definition that, in edition B, no longer states it.
findings.quotation_a: ...and MUST handle every codec and filter that §17 designates as core, both channel layouts (§14), every sample type that §12 designates as core, every user-metadata encoding §18.2 assigns, and both record types §7.3 registers. There are no subset profiles: software that declines to support a core codec, a core filter, either channel layout, a core sample type, an assigned user-metadata encoding, or a registered record type is not a conforming reader...
findings.quotation_b: ...and MUST handle every codec and filter that §17 designates as core, both channel layouts (§14), every sample type that §12 designates as core, and every user-metadata encoding §18.2 assigns. There are no subset profiles: software that declines any of those is not a conforming reader, even if it reads all other conforming files correctly.
findings.byte_level_rationale: An implementation built strictly from edition B's §2.3 paragraph alone could wrongly treat a reader that declines the layer/user-metadata record types as conforming; but edition B's own unchanged appendix checklist restates the full requirement verbatim, so a complete reading of edition B recovers the same rule as edition A, and the practical byte-level accept/reject outcome does not actually diverge for an implementation built from the whole of edition B.

findings.location_b: §2.3's shortened cross-reference plus the new closing paragraph of §21.6 in edition B (four grounds stated); contrast with §9.7, byte-identical in both editions, which independently states the missing ground's consequence
findings.title: Edition B's relocated "cannot establish" grounds list is one ground short of what it promises to enumerate
findings.detail: Edition A's [R-CNF-11] definition enumerates five grounds for a verifier reporting *cannot establish*, inline, including "when it declines a layer's or a tile's decode on resource grounds and so cannot check §14's decoded-content obligations ([R-ERR-04], [R-SER-05], [R-SER-08])". Edition B compresses this to a bare cross-reference, "(§21.6 names the grounds)," and adds a new paragraph to the end of §21.6 (absent from edition A) that enumerates only four grounds, omitting the layer/tile-decode-decline case entirely. Both editions' §9.7 (byte-identical) separately states that a verifier declining a tile's decode on resource grounds "reports that check unmade and cannot certify ([R-CNF-11], [R-ERR-04])", so the underlying rule survives in edition B, just not inside the paragraph its own §2.3 says is where "the grounds" are named.
findings.quotation_a: ...*cannot establish* — the last where some requirement is one it is unable to check on a capability or resource ground, as when the file names a format major version it does not implement, when a record carries MUST_UNDERSTAND = 1 with a type it does not implement (§21.6), when it cannot execute a codec or filter ([R-COD-11]), when it declines a layer's or a tile's decode on resource grounds and so cannot check §14's decoded-content obligations ([R-ERR-04], [R-SER-05], [R-SER-08]), or when it declines to decode a user-metadata document ([R-MTA-09]).
findings.quotation_b: A verifier is unable to check a requirement on a capability or resource ground, and so reports *cannot establish* ([R-CNF-11]), as when the file names a format major version it does not implement, a record carries MUST_UNDERSTAND = 1 with a type it does not implement, it cannot execute a codec or filter ([R-COD-11], §17.4), or it declines to decode a user-metadata document ([R-MTA-09]).
findings.byte_level_rationale: A reader of edition B who trusts its own promise ("§21.6 names the grounds") and stops there would build an incomplete list of cannot-establish triggers; but §9.7, unchanged in edition B, independently states the missing ground's operative consequence, so a whole-document implementation of edition B still reaches the same accept/reject/cannot-establish behavior as edition A.

findings.location_a: §3.3 "Container and array model" (a Note block, the entire subsection)
findings.location_b: absent — no §3.3 header or equivalent text exists in edition B
findings.title: Edition B has no counterpart to edition A's §3.3 Part I/Part II independence Note, with no byte-level effect found
findings.detail: Edition A's §3.3 is a single Note stating that Part I (container) is independent of Part II (array model) by construction, so appenders and rewriters that carry a layer forward operate on files whose layers they cannot decode. Writer-a's W8 answer cites this Note by name as its justification. Edition B has no §3.3 section at all (confirmed: zero hits for "§3.3", "cannot decode", or a "#### 3.3" header in edition B, against working controls proving grep matches real content in that file). However, the actual operative rule for W8 — [R-WRT-09]'s verification-depth statement and §20.5's carry/re-create/drop framework — is byte-identical between editions, and writer-b (reading the edition lacking this Note) reached the identical W8 conclusion citing only those passages. The Note was itself non-normative in edition A (inside a `> **Note.**` block), so its removal does not remove a rule, only removes rationale/exposition.
findings.quotation_a: **Note.** Part I (container) is independent of Part II (array model) by construction: no Part I structure requires decoding sample payloads, so appenders, and rewriters that carry a layer forward, operate on files whose layers they cannot decode — that independence is load-bearing for the updater rules of §7 and §20.
findings.quotation_b: absent
findings.byte_level_rationale: Both walkers reach the identical, correct W8 conclusion (structural checksum verification only, no decode required, for a rewriter carrying an unimplemented sample type forward) from [R-WRT-09] and §20.5 alone, which are byte-identical between editions; the missing Note supplies rationale for that rule, not the rule itself, so no accept/reject verdict or emitted byte differs.

findings.location_b: §2.3, "Conforming TARN file" bullet (R-CNF-02); contradicted by §9.2 (unchanged in B)
findings.title: B's §2.3 bullet says a conduct-rule-violating file 'is nonconforming', inverting A's 'never nonconforming by virtue of one'
findings.detail: Edition A states that a file breaking a writer conduct-only obligation (flags-lane bits, pre-trailer gap length, §20.3 step 4's fixed-declaration bar) 'is never nonconforming by virtue of one: conduct rules bind the actor, the predicate binds the bytes.' Edition B's parallel sentence says instead 'a file that breaks one is nonconforming' - the opposite rule, stated at the exact sentence carrying the R-CNF-02 tag. B's own §9.2 (byte-identical to A) still says a conduct violation means 'the file it produces is never nonconforming by virtue of it, as [R-CNF-02] says of every conduct rule' - directly contradicting B's own §2.3. An implementer built strictly from B's §2.3 would wrongly reject files A (and B's own §9.2) both certify.
findings.quotation_a: A few obligations this specification places on writers govern their conduct rather than their output ... and a file is never nonconforming by virtue of one: conduct rules bind the actor, the predicate binds the bytes.
findings.quotation_b: A writer obligation that governs conduct rather than output, or whose violation this specification expressly declares not to be a file-conformance violation, binds the writer, and a file that breaks one is nonconforming.
findings.byte_level_rationale: A verifier built from B's §2.3 alone would report NONCONFORMING for a file with, e.g., an over-minimal (but still 64-aligned) pre-trailer pad, or a set ignore-lane flag bit, or a §20.3-step-4 fixed-declaration change - all of which A (and B's own §9.2) certify as conforming. Different accept/reject verdict on identical bytes.

findings.title: B inverts a reaching condition's failure from reject-file to 'capability refusal', contradicting its own next sentence
findings.detail: A instructs: treat a reaching condition's failure AS reject-file, RATHER THAN on capability grounds. B instructs the opposite: treat it as a capability refusal, NOT as reject-file. Two sentences later, B (in text shared verbatim with A) says a verifier finding such a failure 'reports nonconforming' - which only follows if the failure is an established violation (reject-file), not a capability-ground gap, since R-CNF-11 (identical in both editions) ties capability/resource grounds to cannot-establish, never to nonconforming.
findings.quotation_a: MUST treat its failure as reject-file on the ground of the requirement stating it rather than on capability grounds
findings.quotation_b: MUST treat a failure as a capability refusal, not as reject-file under the requirement that states the condition
findings.byte_level_rationale: An implementer following B's literal instruction would not count a reaching-condition failure (e.g. F14's trailer-CRC mismatch under an unimplemented declared major) as an established violation, and so would report cannot-establish rather than nonconforming for that file - the opposite verdict from an implementation built on A or on B's own next sentence.

findings.location_b: §2.3, Conforming verifier bullet; cross-reference at §20.3 (unchanged in B) left dangling
findings.title: B drops 'and updaters' from the one sentence stating both classes inherit every reader obligation

B narrows it to 'Verifiers are readers...'. §20.3, byte-identical in both editions, explicitly attributes this extension to §2.3/R-CNF-11 ('which §2.3 extends to updaters as readers of what they process, [R-CNF-11]') - a citation that, in B, points to a paragraph that no longer says that.
findings.quotation_a: Verifiers and updaters are readers of the files they process and inherit every reader obligation.
findings.quotation_b: Verifiers are readers of the files they process and inherit every reader obligation.
findings.byte_level_rationale: No direct change to a verifier's own accept/reject output; the dropped word concerns updaters, and §20.3 already spells out equivalent updater obligations in full detail elsewhere unchanged, so no implementer's bytes differ, though the cross-reference chain in B is broken.

findings.location_a: §2.3, Conforming verifier bullet, cannot-establish grounds list (5 items)
findings.location_b: §21.6, closing paragraph, cannot-establish grounds list (4 items)
findings.title: B's relocated cannot-establish grounds list omits the 'declines a layer's or tile's decode on resource grounds' ground
