B moves this enumeration to §21.6's closing paragraph but lists only four grounds, omitting that one entirely (confirmed: R-SER-05/08 appear 21 times in A vs 20 in B, the missing hit being exactly this line). §9.7, identical in both editions, separately implies the same substantive rule in prose ('reports that check unmade and cannot certify'), so the rule is not wholly lost from B, only from its canonical enumerated list.
findings.quotation_a: when it declines a layer's or a tile's decode on resource grounds and so cannot check §14's decoded-content obligations ([R-ERR-04], [R-SER-05], [R-SER-08])
findings.quotation_b: as when the file names a format major version it does not implement, a record carries MUST_UNDERSTAND = 1 with a type it does not implement, it cannot execute a codec or filter ([R-COD-11], §17.4), or it declines to decode a user-metadata document ([R-MTA-09])
findings.byte_level_rationale: §9.7 (byte-identical in both editions) independently states the same substantive behavior in prose, so an implementer reading the whole document reaches the same verdict either way; an implementer trusting only B's §21.6 list as exhaustive could under-report this ground by name under R-CNF-11's per-requirement reporting duty - a difference in the report's completeness, not necessarily in the accept/reject/certify verdict.

findings.location_a: §2.3, closing Note to the "reach" paragraph (F14/F5/F15 worked example)
findings.title: B drops A's worked Note illustrating why F14 reaches but F5 and F15 do not, though the operative reaching-row list survives unchanged
findings.detail: A closes the reach paragraph with a Note walking through F14 (reaches, despite reading bytes a future major may redefine), F5 (does not reach, despite its subject being unredefinable), and F15 (does not reach, despite citing R-CNT-24). B has no such Note; its parallel paragraph ends with only 'section 21.2 lists the rows that reach.' Both editions' section 21.2 opening paragraph (byte-identical) still gives the concrete answer (F8, F14, F6, both F1 instances), so the operative list survives in B even though the explanatory worked figure does not.
findings.quotation_a: Note. The test is the invariant a condition violates, not the fields it reads, and three rows show why the distinction carries the weight. §21.2's F14 reaches although the bytes it checksums include fields a future major may redefine ... F5 does not reach although its subject is the physical file size ... F15 does not reach although its Governing rule cell cites [R-CNT-24]
findings.quotation_b: absent (replaced by: "§21.2 lists the rows that reach.")
findings.byte_level_rationale: The operative reaching-row list an implementer would code against (§21.2's opening paragraph, byte-identical in both editions) is unchanged, so no accept/reject/verdict consequence was found; the loss is explanatory/audit value for anyone independently re-deriving F5/F15's classification rather than trusting §21.2's assertion.

findings.title: Each walk's own self-reported finding rests on text confirmed byte-identical in the other edition - neither is B-specific
findings.detail: Walker B's finding that §20.3 step 4 cites R-ERR-01's category where §21.7's own unwitnessed-condition test seems to fit better is argued entirely from §20.3/§21.7 text confirmed byte-identical in edition A - if a real defect, it is A's too, inherited unchanged. Walker A's finding that the pre-trailer pad's minimum-only length makes verifier-reported slack totals non-unique is argued from §6.2/R-CNT-05, confirmed byte-identical in edition B - it applies to B's files identically, though walker B's transcript did not name it as a formal finding.
findings.quotation_a: This bar binds the commit as an actor: no file is nonconforming by virtue of its violation, and no register row records the violation itself, the register enumerating file-conformance violations (§21.1) and the bar stating no condition a file can exhibit (§21.7, [R-ERR-01], [R-CNF-02])
findings.quotation_b: This bar binds the commit as an actor: no file is nonconforming by virtue of its violation, and no register row records the violation itself, the register enumerating file-conformance violations (§21.1) and the bar stating no condition a file can exhibit (§21.7, [R-ERR-01], [R-CNF-02])
findings.byte_level_rationale: Both quoted passages are verbatim-identical between editions, so there is no A-vs-B divergence to test at the byte level; whatever merit either walk's finding has, it is a shared characteristic of the specification predating and surviving edition B's rewrite unchanged.

findings.title: B inverts A's rule that a conduct-only writer violation never makes the file nonconforming
findings.detail: A states that a handful of writer obligations govern the writer's conduct rather than the file's output (naming examples: which registry version a writer targets per §10.3/§18.3, the barriers a commit performs per §9.2, §6.3's ignore-lane-bit rule, §6.2's pre-trailer-gap pad, §20.3 step 4's bar), and says explicitly 'a file is never nonconforming by virtue of one: conduct rules bind the actor, the predicate binds the bytes.' B's rewritten [R-CNF-02] says the opposite: 'a file that breaks one is nonconforming,' and drops the enumerated examples entirely. This is not just a divergence from A -- it self-contradicts B's own unchanged §9.2 text (identical in both editions), which still says of a writer that omits a commit barrier: 'the file it produces is never nonconforming by virtue of it, as [R-CNF-02] says of every conduct rule.' A verifier implemented strictly from B's §2.3 would certify such a file as nonconforming; one implemented from B's own §9.2 (or from A) would certify it as conforming -- a direct byte-level verdict conflict.
findings.quotation_a: A few obligations this specification places on writers govern their *conduct* rather than their output — where a value is published, which registry version a writer targets (§10.3, §18.3), or the barriers a commit performs (§9.2) — and a file is never nonconforming by virtue of one: conduct rules bind the actor, the predicate binds the bytes. [R-CNF-02]
findings.quotation_b: A writer obligation that governs conduct rather than output, or whose violation this specification expressly declares not to be a file-conformance violation, binds the writer, and a file that breaks one is nonconforming. [R-CNF-02]
findings.byte_level_rationale: A verifier built from A (or from B's own untouched §9.2) reports 'conforming' for a file where only a conduct-only obligation was violated (e.g. a missing commit barrier, or a set ignore-lane bit); a verifier built strictly from B's rewritten §2.3 text alone would report 'nonconforming' for the identical bytes -- a different verdict on the same file.

findings.title: B drops the requirement that a conforming reader handle both registered record types
findings.detail: A requires a conforming reader to 'handle ... every user-metadata encoding §18.2 assigns, and both record types §7.3 registers,' and lists 'a registered record type' among the things whose declination disqualifies 'conforming reader' status under the no-subset-profiles rule. B's corresponding sentence ends at 'every user-metadata encoding §18.2 assigns' and the no-subset-profiles sentence is compressed to 'software that declines any of those' -- silently dropping the record-type item from both the requirement and the disqualification list. §7.3 itself (byte-identical in both editions) never independently frames declining a record type as disqualifying conforming-reader status, so this is not restated elsewhere.
findings.quotation_a: and MUST handle every codec and filter that §17 designates as core, both channel layouts (§14), every sample type that §12 designates as core, every user-metadata encoding §18.2 assigns, and both record types §7.3 registers. There are no subset profiles: software that declines to support a core codec, a core filter, either channel layout, a core sample type, an assigned user-metadata encoding, or a registered record type is not a conforming reader, even if it reads all other conforming files correctly.
findings.quotation_b: and MUST handle every codec and filter that §17 designates as core, both channel layouts (§14), every sample type that §12 designates as core, and every user-metadata encoding §18.2 assigns. There are no subset profiles: software that declines any of those is not a conforming reader, even if it reads all other conforming files correctly.
findings.byte_level_rationale: A reader implemented strictly from B's §2.3 alone would not know that declining to support the registered (0x0002) user-metadata record type disqualifies it from 'conforming reader' status; software built to that reading of B could correctly reject that record type entirely while still calling itself conforming, a classification an implementation built from A would refuse.

findings.title: B's replacement for A's five cannot-establish grounds and its experimental-encoding carve-out states only four grounds and drops the carve-out
findings.detail: A enumerates five grounds for a verifier's *cannot establish* verdict: (1) file names an unimplemented format major, (2) a record carries MUST_UNDERSTAND=1 with an unimplemented type, (3) verifier cannot execute a codec or filter, (4) verifier declines a layer's or a tile's decode on resource grounds and so cannot check §14's decoded-content obligations [R-ERR-04, R-SER-05, R-SER-08], (5) verifier declines to decode a user-metadata document [R-MTA-09]; and adds a carve-out that a user-metadata document under an experimental-range encoding is explicitly *not* such a ground (nothing is left unchecked, certification unaffected, R-MTA-10), while encoding 0 and a reserved value are violations (§21.5, R1). B compresses this whole passage in §2.3 to '(§21.6 names the grounds)' and adds a new paragraph to §21.6 that lists only grounds (1),(2),(3),(5) -- omitting ground (4) entirely -- and carries neither the experimental-encoding carve-out nor the R-MTA-10 citation.
findings.quotation_a: ...as when the file names a format major version it does not implement, when a record carries MUST_UNDERSTAND = 1 with a type it does not implement (§21.6), when it cannot execute a codec or filter ([R-COD-11]), when it declines a layer's or a tile's decode on resource grounds and so cannot check §14's decoded-content obligations ([R-ERR-04], [R-SER-05], [R-SER-08]), or when it declines to decode a user-metadata document ([R-MTA-09]). A user-metadata document under an experimental-range encoding — one this specification does not assign and a conforming file can carry (§21.6) — is not such a ground: no content rule attaches there, so nothing is left unchecked, and certification is unaffected ([R-MTA-10]); encoding 0 and a reserved value are violations (§21.5, R1).
findings.quotation_b: ...on a capability or resource ground (§21.6 names the grounds). [in §21.6, B adds:] A verifier is unable to check a requirement on a capability or resource ground, and so reports *cannot establish* ([R-CNF-11]), as when the file names a format major version it does not implement, a record carries MUST_UNDERSTAND = 1 with a type it does not implement, it cannot execute a codec or filter ([R-COD-11], §17.4), or it declines to decode a user-metadata document ([R-MTA-09]).
findings.byte_level_rationale: A verifier implemented strictly from B alone, on declining a layer's or tile's decode on resource grounds, has no textual basis for reporting the distinct *cannot establish* verdict A requires for that case (ground 4) -- it could instead report an ordinary rejection or an unclassified failure, a different reported verdict than one built from A. Separately, a verifier built from B alone could misapply ground (5)'s 'declines to decode a user-metadata document' to an experimental-range-encoded document and report *cannot establish* / decline certification, whereas A explicitly requires it to certify normally in that case (R-MTA-10) -- a different certification outcome for the same file.

findings.location_a: §2.3, reach paragraph (between the class list and §2.4), [R-CNF-13]
findings.title: B inverts the required outcome for a failing reaching condition (reject-file vs. capability refusal)
findings.detail: A requires a reader to treat a failing reaching condition (one asserting an invariant [R-CNT-24] fixes for every format major) as reject-file under the requirement stating it, explicitly 'rather than on capability grounds'; the distinct capability-refusal diagnostic ([R-CNT-07]) is reserved for the separate case where every reaching condition is satisfied but the declared major itself is unimplemented. B's rewrite says the reader must treat such a failure 'as a capability refusal, not as reject-file' -- the exact opposite -- while still going on, in the very next sentence, to describe [R-CNT-07]'s diagnostic as reserved for the 'every reaching condition satisfied' case, which is internally inconsistent with having just called reaching-condition failure itself a capability refusal. This also contradicts B's own unchanged §21.9 text, which names exactly two capability refusals (a foreign format major, and an unimplemented top-level MU=1 type) and does not include a reaching-condition failure as a third.
findings.quotation_a: A reader MUST apply every reaching condition to a file whatever major it declares — an exemption the condition's governing requirement grants on a ground other than the declared major applies unchanged, [R-CNT-04]'s residency exemption among them — and MUST treat its failure as reject-file on the ground of the requirement stating it rather than on capability grounds; the distinct diagnostic [R-CNT-07] asks for is owed where every reaching condition is satisfied and the declared major is one the reader does not implement.
findings.quotation_b: A reader MUST check every reaching condition whatever major the file declares, and MUST treat a failure as a capability refusal, not as reject-file under the requirement that states the condition; an exemption that the condition's own requirement grants for a reason other than the declared major lapses, [R-CNT-04]'s residency exemption among them. [R-CNT-07]'s distinct diagnostic is given where every reaching condition is satisfied and the declared major is one the reader does not implement.
findings.byte_level_rationale: For a file that declares a foreign format major and also fails a reaching condition (e.g. a corrupt trailer CRC, F14, which reaches under [R-CNT-24]), an implementation built from A reports reject-file with a diagnostic tied to the failing requirement; an implementation built strictly from B's rewritten text alone would report a capability refusal instead -- a different outcome class and a different diagnostic for the identical bytes, which §21's conformance vectors (§21.8) would distinguish.

findings.title: B redefines "addressed" as generation-relative where A treats it as an unconditional per-layer property
findings.detail: A's glossary entry says 'every tile of a layer is *addressed*' -- an unconditional, layer-level property -- before separately defining 'stored in a generation' as generation-relative. B's entry instead makes addressing itself generation-relative: 'a tile is *addressed* in a generation if that generation's tile index has an entry for it: the tiles of the layer's grid under the geometry that generation declares.' This introduces the idea that a layer's geometry (and hence its set of addressed tiles) can vary by generation, which the unchanged §11.2 text (defining 'addressed-tile count' as a fixed function N or C·N of the layer's declared grid, with no per-generation variability mentioned) and §15.1 (speaking simply of 'a layer's tile index') do not clearly support either way. I could not fully resolve, from these two files alone, whether layer geometry is in fact fixed for the life of a layer (which would make B's added generation-qualifier an undecided-elsewhere addition) or genuinely variable across generations (which would make A's simpler wording an oversimplification) without re-deriving §20.3/§20.5's full rewriting rules from scratch.
findings.quotation_a: **addressed tile / stored tile** — every tile of a layer is *addressed*. A tile is *stored in a generation* if and only if that generation's tile-index entry for it is not the sentinel (§15); unqualified *stored* means stored in the live generation.
findings.quotation_b: **addressed tile / stored tile** — a tile is *addressed* in a generation if that generation's tile index has an entry for it: the tiles of the layer's grid under the geometry that generation declares (§11.2, §15). It is *stored in a generation* if and only if that entry is not the sentinel (§15); unqualified *stored* means stored in the live generation.
findings.byte_level_rationale: I flag this as an ambiguity rather than a confirmed byte-level divergence because I was not able to determine, within the two-file access rule, whether a layer's declared geometry can ever differ between two generations of the same file; if it cannot, both wordings pick out the identical set of tiles and no implementation would differ; if it can, B's version is the more correct one and A's glossary entry would itself be the imprecise one. Either reading leaves an implementer of the other document with a definition of 'addressed' that does not obviously track the fuller one.

findings.title: Section 3.3, a Note on Part I/Part II independence, is deleted outright in B with no replacement
findings.detail: A carries a short subsection, entirely a `> **Note.**` block, stating that Part I (container) is independent of Part II (array model) by construction, and that this independence is load-bearing for the updater rules of §7 and §20 (i.e. why appenders and rewriters can carry a layer forward without being able to decode its samples). B's outline has no §3.3 at all -- grepping 'Container and array model' and '3.3' across the whole of B returns no match apart from unrelated numeric coincidences (e.g. an RFC version number). Because the block was already non-normative (a `Note`) under [R-CNF-01] in edition A, its outright removal cannot itself change what a strictly-conforming implementation built from B does, so it fails this task's byte-level LOSS test and is reported as an observation rather than a LOSS. It is nonetheless the starkest instance in this pair of content that existed only inside a Note in A now not appearing anywhere in B at all, which the charter asks me to flag.
findings.quotation_a: > **Note.** Part I (container) is independent of Part II (array model) by construction: no Part I structure requires decoding sample payloads, so appenders, and rewriters that carry a layer forward, operate on files whose layers they cannot decode — that independence is load-bearing for the updater rules of §7 and §20.
findings.quotation_b: absent
findings.byte_level_rationale: The removed text was itself non-normative (a Note) in edition A, so no implementation is built from it in either edition and no accept/reject verdict or emitted byte can differ because of its removal.

findings.location_a: §2.3 Conformance classes, "Conforming TARN file" bullet, [R-CNF-02] (edition A lines 166-179)
findings.location_b: §2.3 Conformance classes, "Conforming TARN file" bullet, [R-CNF-02] (edition B lines 210-218)
findings.title: B states the opposite of A on whether a writer conduct-obligation breach makes the file nonconforming
findings.detail: A: a writer obligation that governs conduct rather than output (e.g. which registry version a writer targets, or the barriers a commit performs) never makes the file itself nonconforming - 'conduct rules bind the actor, the predicate binds the bytes.' B, discussing the identical class of obligation under the same requirement ID, states 'a file that breaks one is nonconforming.' An implementation (or a verifier) built from B alone would report such files nonconforming; one built from A alone would not. This is a direct polarity flip, not a paraphrase.
findings.quotation_a: A few obligations this specification places on writers govern their *conduct* rather than their output ... and a file is never nonconforming by virtue of one: conduct rules bind the actor, the predicate binds the bytes.
findings.quotation_b: A writer obligation that governs conduct rather than output, or whose violation this specification expressly declares not to be a file-conformance violation, binds the writer, and a file that breaks one is nonconforming.
findings.byte_level_rationale: A verifier built strictly from B would report *nonconforming* for a file whose writer merely violated a conduct-only obligation (e.g. a registry-version-targeting or commit-barrier rule); a verifier built strictly from A would certify the same file, since file conformance is A's own 'pure predicate on bytes' and conduct rules bind only the actor. Different accept/reject verdict on the same bytes.

findings.location_a: §2.3 Conformance classes, condition/"reaches" paragraph, [R-CNF-13] (edition A lines 260-273)
findings.location_b: §2.3 Conformance classes, condition/"reaches" paragraph, [R-CNF-13] (edition B lines 268-281)
findings.title: B reverses both the diagnostic for a failed reaching condition and whether its governing exemptions still apply
findings.detail: A: a reader MUST treat a reaching condition's failure as an ordinary reject-file violation of the requirement stating it, 'rather than on capability grounds' - the distinct capability diagnostic ([R-CNT-07]) is reserved for the separate case where all reaching conditions pass but the declared major is simply unimplemented; and an exemption a condition's own requirement grants on another ground (R-CNT-04's residency exemption is A's own example) 'applies unchanged' when the file declares a non-1 major. B states a reaching condition's failure must be treated 'as a capability refusal, not as reject-file,' and that the very same exemption 'lapses.' Both clauses are exact opposites of A, using A's own example (R-CNT-04) each time. This also leaves B's own paragraph in tension with itself: B still says a verifier finding such a failure 'reports nonconforming,' yet §21.6 (both editions) defines a capability refusal as one where the file 'can be perfectly conforming' - so B's relabeling as a capability refusal contradicts its own following sentence, not only A.
findings.quotation_a: A reader MUST apply every reaching condition to a file whatever major it declares — an exemption the condition's governing requirement grants on a ground other than the declared major applies unchanged, `[R-CNT-04]`'s residency exemption among them — and MUST treat its failure as reject-file on the ground of the requirement stating it rather than on capability grounds; the distinct diagnostic `[R-CNT-07]` asks for is owed where every reaching condition is satisfied and the declared major is one the reader does not implement.
findings.quotation_b: A reader MUST check every reaching condition whatever major the file declares, and MUST treat a failure as a capability refusal, not as reject-file under the requirement that states the condition; an exemption that the condition's own requirement grants for a reason other than the declared major lapses, `[R-CNT-04]`'s residency exemption among them.
findings.byte_level_rationale: Take a reader relying on R-CNT-04's residency exemption (not holding certain bytes resident) that encounters a file declaring a non-1 major whose reaching condition fails. Per A, the exemption still applies (unchanged) and the failure is reported as an ordinary reject-file violation under the stated requirement. Per B, the exemption lapses (the reader must now perform the check it was previously exempt from) and, if it fails, the outcome is labelled a capability refusal rather than a reject-file violation of that requirement. Different obligations and a different diagnostic/verdict label on the same bytes and the same reader configuration.

findings.location_a: §3.1 Terms, "addressed tile / stored tile" (edition A line ~427); cf. §20.3 step 4 (edition A lines ~3329-3331, unchanged in B)
findings.location_b: §3.1 Terms, "addressed tile / stored tile" (edition B, reordered block near start of §3.1)
findings.title: B makes "addressed" generation-relative where A's Terms entry states it as an unconditional, generation-independent fact
findings.detail: A's Terms definition states flatly 'every tile of a layer is *addressed*,' with no generation qualifier at all. B's definition instead ties address-ness to a specific generation and 'the geometry that generation declares.' A's own §20.3 step 4 (unchanged in both editions) already treats 'the addressed set' as varying with 'the new state' when discussing permitted geometry changes (shrink, re-tiling, rank change) across commits - directly in tension with §3.1's unconditional wording. B's rewrite silently resolves that internal tension in favor of the generation-relative reading; that reading is grounded in A's own §20.3 text, but it is a decision A's own Terms section does not state, and a reader of §3.1 alone in edition A would not learn that address-ness can change across a layer's generations.
findings.quotation_a: **addressed tile / stored tile** — every tile of a layer is *addressed*. A tile is *stored in a generation* if and only if that generation's tile-index entry for it is not the sentinel (§15)...
findings.quotation_b: **addressed tile / stored tile** — a tile is *addressed* in a generation if that generation's tile index has an entry for it: the tiles of the layer's grid under the geometry that generation declares (§11.2, §15). It is *stored in a generation* if and only if that entry is not the sentinel (§15)...
findings.byte_level_rationale: Both editions agree, once §20.3 is read, that a layer's tile set can change across generations via permitted rewrites (shrink, re-tiling, etc.), so an implementation following either edition's full text ends up computing the same addressed set for a given generation. The divergence is confined to what edition A's own Terms section, read on its own, asserts.

findings.location_b: §2.3 Conformance classes, "Conforming reader" bullet, [R-CNF-03] (edition B, same list and sentence)

findings.location_a: §2.3 Conformance classes, "Conforming verifier" bullet, [R-CNF-11] (edition A); cf. §17.4 (unchanged)
findings.location_b: §2.3 Conformance classes, "Conforming verifier" bullet, [R-CNF-11] (edition B) + §21.6 (edition B, new closing paragraph)

findings.detail: A enumerates five specific 'cannot establish' grounds inline in the verifier bullet, including 'when it declines a layer's or a tile's decode on resource grounds and so cannot check §14's decoded-content obligations ([R-ERR-04], [R-SER-05], [R-SER-08]).' findings.quotation_a: ...when it declines a layer's or a tile's decode on resource grounds and so cannot check §14's decoded-content obligations (`[R-ERR-04]`, `[R-SER-05]`, `[R-SER-08]`), or when it declines to decode a user-metadata document (`[R-MTA-09]`).
findings.quotation_b: A verifier is unable to check a requirement on a capability or resource ground, and so reports *cannot establish* (`[R-CNF-11]`), as when the file names a format major version it does not implement, a record carries MUST_UNDERSTAND = 1 with a type it does not implement, it cannot execute a codec or filter (`[R-COD-11]`, §17.4), or it declines to decode a user-metadata document (`[R-MTA-09]`).
findings.byte_level_rationale: The governing rule survives verbatim at §17.4 in both editions, so a verifier implemented from either edition in full still knows it cannot check §14's decoded-content obligations without decoding; only the definitional cross-reference chain is incomplete.

findings.quotation_a: > **Note.** The test is the invariant a condition violates, not the fields it reads, and three rows show why the distinction carries the weight. §21.2's F14 reaches although the bytes it checksums include fields a future major may redefine...
findings.quotation_b: Every other condition concerns a structure this document defines for format major 1 alone... §21.2 lists the rows that reach.

findings.location_a: Front matter, blockquote Note before "## Part 0" (edition A lines 11-23)
findings.location_b: §1 Introduction, "How to read this document" paragraph (edition B)
findings.title: A Note on document conventions is folded into ordinary §1 prose and loses two of its clauses
findings.detail: A's front-matter Note explains the section rubric, layout-table columns, and structural/descriptive field classification, and adds two further clauses: 'a packed variable-length payload has no offsets to give,' and 'Normative requirements carry stable identifiers like [R-IDX-03], and test vectors cite those identifiers rather than prose positions.' B moves a shortened version of this content into §1's 'How to read this document' as ordinary prose (no longer a Note) and drops both extra clauses; grep for their distinguishing phrases ('prose positions', 'no offsets to give') returns zero hits anywhere else in B, so they are not merely relocated. Both are documentation/traceability conventions, not testable technical rules, so this is reported for completeness rather than as a rule loss.
findings.quotation_a: > **Note.** How to read this document. ... On-disk structures are presented as layout tables whose columns suit the structure — §4.7 states what they carry, and a packed variable-length payload has no offsets to give. ... Normative requirements carry stable identifiers like `[R-IDX-03]`, and test vectors cite those identifiers rather than prose positions.
findings.quotation_b: **How to read this document.** Sections follow a fixed rubric where it applies: purpose, byte-layout table, writer rules, reader rules, error handling, worked examples. On-disk structures are presented as layout tables whose columns suit the structure; §4.7 says what the columns carry and classifies every field as structural or descriptive.
findings.byte_level_rationale: Both dropped clauses are about document/test-vector presentation conventions, not decoder or encoder behavior; no implementation would produce different bytes or verdicts based on either.

findings.location_a: §1 Introduction (edition A, goals list and "Reading this document" paragraph)
findings.location_b: §1 Introduction (edition B, goals list and "How to read this document" paragraph)

Part I alone yields a container reader — one that opens files, walks the directory, and lists layers without decoding a sample; returning sample values needs Part II as well, since §19.3's layer validation resolves into Part II's value sets and geometry rules at every step.

Sections follow a fixed rubric where it applies: purpose, byte-layout table, writer rules, reader rules, error handling, worked examples.

findings.location_a: §2.3 Conformance classes, "Conforming TARN file" bullet, [R-CNF-02] (line 156, conduct clause ~168-179)
findings.title: C reverses A's conduct/predicate rule for writer obligations, contradicting C's own §6.3
findings.detail: A states that a writer obligation governing conduct (or one this spec expressly declares not a file-conformance violation) never makes the file nonconforming: 'conduct rules bind the actor, the predicate binds the bytes,' and names §6.3's ignore-lane-bit rule as a worked example. C's rewritten sentence keeps the same category of obligation but flips the conclusion to 'a file that breaks one is nonconforming.' §6.3 is byte-identical in both editions and states outright that a set (undefined) ignore-lane bit 'is not a file-conformance violation' — so edition C's §2.3 now contradicts edition C's own §6.3 on the very case A cites. Concretely: a minimal conforming file with trailer flags bit 16 set (an undefined ignore-lane bit) and a correctly-recomputed trailer CRC is CONFORMING under A (and under C's §6.3), but a verifier applying only C's rewritten §2.3 general rule at face value must call the identical bytes NONCONFORMING, since writing flags=0 is exactly the kind of writer obligation the sentence now says makes the file nonconforming when broken.
findings.quotation_a: a file is never nonconforming by virtue of one: conduct rules bind the actor, the predicate binds the bytes. A writer obligation whose violation this specification expressly declares not to be a file-conformance violation binds the actor in the same way; §6.3's flags rules against a set ignore-lane bit ... are the cases this text states
findings.quotation_b: A writer obligation that governs conduct rather than output, or whose violation this specification expressly declares not to be a file-conformance violation, binds the writer, and a file that breaks one is nonconforming.
findings.byte_level_rationale: A verifier built strictly from edition C's §2.3 sentence classifies the described file (valid trailer, one set undefined ignore-lane bit, correct CRC) as nonconforming; a verifier built from edition A's §2.3 (or from either edition's byte-identical §6.3) classifies the identical byte sequence as conforming. Same bytes, opposite certification verdict depending on which passage of C is applied — and C's two passages disagree with each other on the identical file.

findings.title: Two MUST-level clauses on reaching-condition failures are each flipped to their antonym in C
findings.detail: A: an exemption a condition's own requirement grants on a non-major ground (R-CNT-04's residency exemption is the named example) 'applies unchanged' when the condition reaches a file of another major, and a reader 'MUST treat its failure as reject-file on the ground of the requirement stating it rather than on capability grounds.' C: the same exemption 'lapses,' and the reader 'MUST treat a failure as a capability refusal, not as reject-file under the requirement that states the condition.' Both editions frame these as MUST-level rules; C's wording is the antonym of A's at both points while the surrounding sentence structure and even the R-CNT-04/R-CNT-07 citations are otherwise unchanged — this is not paraphrase or reflow. Concretely, for a remote reader (§6.4-style, not holding the front signature block resident) opening a file that declares an unimplemented major and whose front signature block (a reaching condition per §6.3, byte-identical in both editions: 'the front signature block ... is constant ... permanently') is actually corrupted: under A the exemption still lets that reader skip fetching bytes [0,16) and, having every reaching condition it did check pass, report the case as a capability-only refusal ([R-CNT-07]'s diagnostic), never fetching the corrupted bytes at all. Under C the exemption 'lapses,' so the same reader is now required to fetch and check those bytes for reach purposes — an extra byte range A never requires — and, on finding them corrupted, C's parallel clause tells it to report even that discovered, non-major-specific defect as a mere 'capability refusal' rather than the corruption it is (exactly the misdiagnosis §6.3 itself warns readers against, since no future major fixes an invariant [R-CNT-24] fixes for every major).
findings.quotation_a: an exemption the condition's governing requirement grants on a ground other than the declared major applies unchanged, `[R-CNT-04]`'s residency exemption among them — and MUST treat its failure as reject-file on the ground of the requirement stating it rather than on capability grounds
findings.quotation_b: an exemption that the condition's own requirement grants for a reason other than the declared major lapses, `[R-CNT-04]`'s residency exemption among them ... MUST treat a failure as a capability refusal, not as reject-file under the requirement that states the condition
findings.byte_level_rationale: The two editions require different reader I/O and different mandatory diagnostic categorization for the identical file (declared unimplemented major + corrupted, non-resident front signature block): A permits the remote reader to never fetch bytes [0,16) and to report a pure capability refusal; C requires fetching those bytes for reach purposes and then requires labeling the resulting defect the same way A reserves for the no-defect case. An implementation built from A alone and one built from C alone perform different byte-range fetches and emit different mandatory diagnostic classifications for the same input file.

findings.location_a: §2.3 Conformance classes, "Conforming reader" bullet, [R-CNF-03] (lines 180-196); cf. Appendix H (line 4901)
findings.location_b: §2.3 Conformance classes, "Conforming reader" bullet, [R-CNF-03] (lines 219-227); cf. Appendix H (line 4805, unchanged from A)
findings.title: C drops "both record types §7.3 registers" from the no-subset-profiles list, contradicting C's own Appendix H citation of the same requirement
findings.detail: A's no-subset-profiles list for a conforming reader has five items (core codecs, core filters, both channel layouts, core sample types, assigned user-metadata encodings, and both record types §7.3 registers) and its closing sentence names 'a registered record type' among the things whose non-support disqualifies a reader. C's rewritten list has only four items — record types are gone — and its closing sentence ('software that declines any of those') now only ranges over the shortened list. This is not a glossary trim: C's own Appendix H conformance checklist, byte-identical to A's at that line, still credits `[R-CNF-03]` (citing §2.3 by name) with requiring 'both registered record types.' Edition C therefore disagrees with itself about what its own requirement 03 requires: a reader that fully implements every codec, filter, layout, sample type and metadata encoding but treats the registered user-metadata record type (0x0002) as an unrecognized, ignorable type (permitted for truly-unknown types under §7.2's generic MU=0 rule, byte-identical in both editions) is disqualified as nonconforming under A's §2.3 and under C's own Appendix H, but is not disqualified by C's §2.3 text read on its own.
findings.quotation_a: and MUST handle every codec and filter that §17 designates as core, both channel layouts (§14), every sample type that §12 designates as core, every user-metadata encoding §18.2 assigns, and both record types §7.3 registers. There are no subset profiles: software that declines to support a core codec, a core filter, either channel layout, a core sample type, an assigned user-metadata encoding, or a registered record type is not a conforming reader
findings.quotation_b: and MUST handle every codec and filter that §17 designates as core, both channel layouts (§14), every sample type that §12 designates as core, and every user-metadata encoding §18.2 assigns. There are no subset profiles: software that declines any of those is not a conforming reader
findings.byte_level_rationale: Take a reader that implements every codec/filter/layout/sample-type/metadata-encoding but never surfaces the registered user-metadata record type, treating it as an unrecognized ignorable record. Certifying it against A's §2.3 text (or C's own Appendix H, byte-identical to A's) yields 'not conforming.' Certifying the identical reader against C's §2.3 text alone yields no disqualification, since record types are absent from the enumerated list its closing sentence refers back to. The conformance verdict for the same software differs depending on which passage of the same document is consulted, and the discrepancy is provable entirely within edition C via its own cross-reference.

findings.location_a: §19.1 ("The open algorithm"), step 1, vs. §2.3 ("Conformance classes") and its worked Note on row F5, and [R-CNF-11]'s definition of a verifier's cannot-establish verdict
findings.title: Open-algorithm step 1 applies the 128-byte floor before the major is known; §2.3 says it must not reach a foreign-major file
findings.detail: §19.1 step 1 instructs a reader, as the very first step of opening any file: 'Obtain the transport-authoritative file size F ...; an F below 128 is a validity error at file scope decided from F alone and needing no other byte of the file ([R-CNT-27], F5).' This is unconditional and precedes step 2 (fetching the trailer), so it is applied before version_major -- which lives inside the trailer -- is ever read. Separately, §2.3's format-major 'reach' doctrine ([R-CNF-13]) states a condition reaches a file declaring another major only when it asserts an invariant [R-CNT-24] fixes in every major, and its own worked Note names F5 by row number as a condition that does NOT reach: 'F5 does not reach although its subject is the physical file size, which no major can redefine: the 128-byte floor it asserts is derived from a directory of at least 4 bytes at an offset of at least 16 and a 64-aligned F ([R-CNT-27]), and those are format major 1's.' The accompanying general rule is explicit that a non-reaching condition 'is not assessed against a file declaring another major, no violation of it is established there' -- which can only be honored by first determining (or ruling out) the declared major, an operation §19.1's step ordering forecloses for any file under 128 bytes, since that determination needs trailer bytes step 1 has not yet fetched. Concretely: for a file with, say, 80<=F<128 whose trailer (once read) validates magic, CRC and a version_major the reader does not implement, §19.1 prescribes an immediate, trailer-blind reject-file on F5/[R-CNT-27] grounds, while §2.3 prescribes that F5 must not be established against this file at all, leaving only the capability-refusal ground of [R-CNT-07]. This is not cosmetic: [R-CNF-11] defines a verifier's nonconforming and cannot-establish verdicts as mutually exclusive and priority-ordered ('An established violation takes priority: a verifier that has established any violation reports nonconforming ... and cannot establish is available only to a traversal that established no violation'), and separately names exactly this situation -- 'the file names a format major version it does not implement' -- as a canonical ground for cannot-establish. Whether this file's verdict is nonconforming (F5 established, per §19.1's literal, major-blind ordering) or cannot-establish (F5 does not reach, per §2.3, and only the major is the obstacle) is left genuinely undetermined by the document as written, even though the distinction is MUST-level and consequential.
findings.quotation_a: an F below 128 is a validity error at file scope decided from F alone and needing no other byte of the file (`[R-CNT-27]`, F5)
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: It decides a verifier's MUST-level verdict for one and the same input: nonconforming (an established file-conformance violation, F5) versus cannot-establish (no violation established, only an unimplemented major, per [R-CNF-11]'s own example of that verdict). [R-CNF-11] states these outcomes are mutually exclusive and that an established violation takes strict priority, so an implementer who codes the literal, sequential reading of §19.1 and one who codes §2.3's reach doctrine will certify or refuse to certify the identical bytes differently, and will report different grounds to a caller -- exactly the reader-vs-corruption diagnostic distinction §6.3 itself says SHOULD be kept separate.

findings.location_a: §17.4 ([R-COD-11]) and §2.3 ([R-CNF-03]), read against §21.6's closing paragraph and §21.9 ([R-ERR-04])
findings.title: No outcome class describes a reader that has simply not yet implemented a core codec/filter/type
findings.detail: The document names exactly two licensed cases in which a conforming reader refuses an otherwise-acceptable, possibly-conforming file: an unimplemented format major ([R-CNT-07]) and an experimental-range top-level record type carrying MU=1 ([R-CNT-15]), which §21.6's closing paragraph explicitly enumerates as 'the two capability refusals.' Everything else a conforming reader must be able to do -- every codec, every filter, every sample type, both channel layouts, both user-metadata encodings, both registered record types -- is instead made a precondition of being a 'conforming reader' at all ([R-CNF-03]), and §17.4/[R-COD-11] is explicit that software lacking one of these is simply 'not a conforming reader,' full stop, with no register row, no outcome class, and no described behavior for what such software does when it meets, e.g., a zstd-coded layer. This is a foreseeable situation for anyone using this document as an implementation order (build codec 1 first, add zstd later), yet the conformance vocabulary -- which otherwise gives every other capability boundary (format major, MU=1 record type, resource limits under [R-ERR-04]) an explicit, licensed, reportable disposition -- has nothing to say about it beyond 'that software is out of scope.'
findings.quotation_a: software unable to execute an assigned codec or filter is not a conforming reader (`[R-CNF-03]`)
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: A genuinely conforming reader, by [R-CNF-03]'s own definition, can never be in this state, so resolving the question changes nothing about which bytes a conforming implementation may emit or must accept/reject. The gap is in what the document tells a partial implementation to do while it is still being built, not in what a finished conforming reader does, so it fails the byte-level test and is reported as a documentation-completeness observation rather than a conformance-affecting ambiguity.

findings.title: No register outcome class covers a reader lacking a core (assigned) codec like zstd
findings.detail: R3 posits a reader that does not implement zstd, an assigned core codec (1-4, all core per R-CNF-03). The register's only codec-value reject-layer row (L43) applies to out-of-range codec values, not to a conforming-shaped file with an assigned value a given reader merely can't execute. R-COD-11 states that such software 'is not a conforming reader' at all, so the document's real answer is about the implementation, not a per-layer outcome. An implementer following the register by analogy (treating it like L43) would answer 'reject-layer,' which is not what R-COD-11 actually says.
findings.quotation_a: "software unable to execute an assigned codec or filter is not a conforming reader (`[R-CNF-03]`)"
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: Resolving this does not change any byte a conforming reader may accept, emit or reject, since the scenario describes software the document excludes from 'conforming reader' before any byte-level question is reached; the finding is about the probe's framing not fitting the register, not about divergent reader behavior on conforming bytes.

findings.title: Register row F5 names an 'committed_file_length' instance I could not construct as independently distinguishable from its 'physical file size' instance
findings.detail: F5's Instances column lists 'F (physical file size); committed_file_length' as two instances. But §19.1 step 1 anchors the F<128 check to the transport-authoritative physical size, checked before any trailer byte is read, and F17 (R-CNT-06) independently requires committed_file_length to equal that same transport size — so any file where the two diverge is caught by F17, not F5, and any file where they agree and are both <128 is the identical byte pattern under both labels, which §21.1's own stated methodology says should collapse to one instance ('where a condition is a single predicate over several fields...the fields it reads are not instances, because no two files could differ'). This bears on R-VEC-03's per-instance vector-coverage obligation.
findings.quotation_a: "an F below 128 is a validity error at file scope decided from F alone and needing no other byte of the file (`[R-CNT-27]`, F5)"
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: Does not change accept/reject behavior for any file (both readings reject the same bytes), but does change whether a conformance corpus can satisfy R-VEC-03's 'at least one vector per instance' obligation for this row, since one of the two named instances may not be independently constructible at all.

findings.title: R1's 'list every request' has a stated baseline but not a single conformance-mandated request count
findings.detail: The document explicitly states that a reader MAY instead speculatively fetch a suffix window in one request, and that 'no request count is a conformance property, and nothing here bounds what a reader fetches.' So for the transport R1 describes, the two-request answer is the document's own baseline theory of operation (and the one its worked Appendix A example uses), not the unique conforming answer; a one-request speculative reader is equally conforming.
findings.quotation_a: "This accounting is a theory of operation, not a budget: no request count is a conformance property, and nothing here bounds what a reader fetches."
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: Does not change which bytes are valid or which a reader must accept/reject; it only means the probe's 'list every request' cannot be answered as a single forced sequence without picking one of two explicitly licensed strategies.

findings.title: MU=1 table row is easy to misread as unconditional for an implemented-but-unregistered type
findings.detail: The three-row preservation table's rows are captioned by MU/PE value, and its MU=1 row reads as an unconditional 'retain byte-identical, never drop' rule. But the paragraph immediately following the table states this row 'reaches only a type the updater does not implement,' so for a type the updater implements (even an unregistered one whose private definition fixes MU=1), only the PE bit governs and PE=0 licenses a drop. An implementer reading only the table's row captions, without this connecting sentence, would very plausibly conclude the opposite: that this record must always be retained. This changes which bytes a conforming updater may legitimately emit (record present vs. record dropped) for the identical input state.
findings.quotation_a: "Its MU = 1 row reaches only a type the updater does not implement... so for an implemented type only the PE bit bites."
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: Directly determines whether a conforming updater's output directory may omit this record: reading only the table row, an implementer would forbid the drop; reading the connecting sentence, the drop is licensed. Two implementations could diverge on this exact byte (presence/absence of the record) for identical input and identical operation.

findings.title: An ignore-lane flag bit survives an appender/rewriter but is silently dropped by a plain creator that read the same input
findings.detail: A tool that opens an existing file, decodes its content, and writes a brand-new file from that content is, per §20.1's own taxonomy, a 'creator' unless it either extends the input (appender) or explicitly undertakes §20.4/§20.5's preservation obligations (rewriter). A creator 'undertakes nothing toward its input, whatever it read' and MUST write flags=0. So the identical starting trailer bit (an unknown ignore-lane bit) is preserved byte-for-byte by an appender or a rewriter, but is zeroed by a creator that happens to have read and decoded the very same file — a divergence driven entirely by which of the three named tiers the tool is classified as, not by anything about the bit or the content.
findings.quotation_a: "As a creator it undertakes nothing toward its input, whatever it read: §20.2 binds it, it writes flags = 0, and it answers for every byte of its output."
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: Directly determines one bit's value in the output trailer's flags field for otherwise-identical processing of identical input content, depending solely on which writer tier the tool self-identifies as.

findings.title: Whether an impermissible fill-only change makes the resulting file byte-level nonconforming depends on the layer's own padding geometry, not on the change itself
findings.detail: §20.3 step 4 bars an appender from changing a stored layer's fill, framing the bar as a conduct rule that does not itself make a file nonconforming. But the same passage identifies T4 (padding-position content mismatching the declared fill) as one of the specific register rows such a change CAN trigger. Since padding positions exist only in tiles at the high edge of a dimension whose extent is not a multiple of its tile extent, the very same forbidden fill-only commit produces a byte-level nonconforming file (via T4) for a layer with any padding, and produces a file with no detectable defect at all for a layer with none — an outcome that turns entirely on unrelated geometry fields, not on the fill change's own severity.
findings.quotation_a: "a file such a commit leaves can be nonconforming on its own terms... but for a stored tile's decoded size, a padding position or pad bit, or a boolean byte the register witnesses (T3, T14, T21, T22, T4, T5, T2)... no check any actor owes able to see it."
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: Directly determines whether a conforming verifier must reject the output file (T4, reject-tile) or accept it, for byte-identical fill-declaration edits, depending solely on whether the layer's tile-extent-vs-dimension-extent arithmetic produces any padding position.

findings.location_a: section 20.3 step 4 (fixed-declarations paragraph, governed by R-WRT-04) and section 14.5/R-SER-05 (padding content) and section 21.4 row T4
findings.title: A fill-only commit on a stored-tile layer is a conduct violation that is byte-witnessed only when the layer has edge-tile padding
findings.detail: The document bars an appender from changing a stored-tile-bearing layer's fill value in place, and frames that bar as a pure writer-conduct rule whose violation alone creates no register row and does not by itself make the resulting file nonconforming (R-ERR-01/R-CNF-02: 'no file is nonconforming by virtue of its violation... the bar stating no condition a file can exhibit'). The same passage then says the file such a commit leaves 'can be nonconforming on its own terms.' Tracing that through: if the layer has any edge-tile padding, the already-stored tiles' padding positions were fill-encoded under the layer's old fill value (R-SER-05), so after the commit they no longer match the newly declared fill and a verifier finds a T4 violation (reject-tile) - a genuine byte-level, register-backed consequence. But if the layer has no padding at all (extents exactly divide tile extents) and every addressed tile remains stored, I could find no other rule in the document that a byte-level check could use to detect this specific violation: the stored tile bytes are unchanged, the checksums still verify, and the change is confined to a channel-entry field with no other structural fingerprint. An implementer building a verifier from this document alone, and reasoning that 'the fixed-declaration bar has consequences,' would need to independently discover that those consequences are conditional on padding shape, since the document states the general bar and its unwitnessed classification but does not spell out this particular padding-dependent split explicitly in one place - a reader has to assemble it from R-WRT-04, R-SER-05, and section 21.7's general test. This is not a contradiction (the document's own framework predicts and licenses exactly this kind of split-detectability outcome, and section 21.7 explicitly discusses an analogous case, an undisclosed compression dictionary), but it is a real seam worth naming for an implementer auditing what a verifier can and cannot actually catch here.
findings.quotation_a: This bar binds the commit as an actor: no file is nonconforming by virtue of its violation, and no register row records the violation itself, the register enumerating file-conformance violations (§21.1) and the bar stating no condition a file can exhibit (§21.7, `[R-ERR-01]`, `[R-CNF-02]`); a file such a commit leaves can be nonconforming on its own terms, as the paragraph below sets out.
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: Resolving this does change what a conforming verifier must do with the resulting bytes, but only conditionally: where the layer has edge-tile padding, a verifier MUST reject the affected tiles under T4/R-SER-05 once the fill value changes underneath already-stored tiles: a directly byte-level, testable consequence. Where the layer has no padding, no byte-level check in the document distinguishes the violating file from a legitimate one, so in that instance the condition is unwitnessed and changes nothing any implementation may accept or reject. I flag byte_level=true because the general case does have byte-level teeth (via T4) even though a specific sub-case does not, and I record that split explicitly rather than picking one answer for the whole condition.

findings.title: Pre-trailer pad length is bounded below but not fixed, so verifier-reported slack totals are not unique across conforming writers
findings.detail: §6.2 requires only that the pad reach the next 64-byte boundary, and states 'a longer gap is conforming, and no conforming commit produces one' - i.e. minimal padding is the expected case but any longer, 64-byte-aligned pad remains conforming. An implementer building a writer may therefore legally emit any pad length at or above the minimum for each commit. An implementer building a verifier must accept all such files and, per §9.7/R-CNT-21, report the resulting slack total exactly as it stands in that file - so two conforming writers given the identical layer history can produce files whose reported slack totals differ by any multiple of 64 bytes, purely as a matter of writer discretion the specification declines to pin down, even though nothing else about the files differs.
findings.quotation_a: Writers MUST place the directory so that no structure lies between its end and the trailer. Those bytes — the pre-trailer pad — are slack (§5.2): a writer that ends its directory on a 64-byte boundary leaves none, this specification does not constrain their content, and bounds their number only through step 5 of the commit protocol, which pads to the next 64-byte boundary (`[R-LIF-02]`) — a longer gap is conforming, and no conforming commit produces one.
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: This changes which bytes a conforming implementation may emit (any writer may legally over-pad by additional 64-byte multiples) and, correspondingly, changes the exact numeric slack total a conforming verifier must accept and report for two files with byte-identical layer content and commit history - the divergence is a real difference in accepted file bytes and in the verifier's own reported output, not merely a difference in wording or emphasis.

findings.title: R-COD-11's 'cannot establish' branch for an inexecutable codec/filter is unreachable by a conforming verifier as a final verdict
findings.detail: R-COD-11 opens by saying a verifier that cannot execute a layer's codec or filter 'cannot establish that layer's conformance and MUST NOT certify the file,' fixing the verdict as cannot-establish only where no other violation was established. Its own next sentence confines this, for any conforming reader, to a reserved-or-experimental codec/filter value, since every assigned codec (1-4) and filter (1-2) is core and mandatory (R-CNF-03). But a reserved/experimental codec/filter value is independently and unconditionally a layer-scope violation (register rows L43/L45), detected by an ordinary reader at layer access -- before any decode is attempted. Under R-CNF-11's own priority rule, an established violation forces the verdict to nonconforming regardless of unchecked items, so whenever the premise of R-COD-11's opening sentence is actually true for a conforming verifier, L43/L45 has already fired and the verdict is nonconforming, never cannot-establish. The described consequence is real language in the document but does not correspond to any reachable end state.
findings.quotation_a: "A verifier that cannot execute a layer's codec or filter cannot establish that layer's conformance and MUST NOT certify the file... For a conforming reader that position arises only at a reserved or experimental value, every assigned codec and filter being core: it rejects the layer ([R-COD-03], [R-COD-09]); software unable to execute an assigned codec or filter is not a conforming reader ([R-CNF-03])."
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: Under either reading of R-COD-11, a conforming verifier facing this scenario produces the identical bytes-level result: reject-layer is reported for the offending layer (via L43/L45), and the file's final verdict is nonconforming either way, since L43/L45 alone already forces that outcome regardless of what the verifier says about decode-inability. Only the internal justification differs, not any accept/reject/emit decision.

findings.title: The step-4 no-register-row bar cites R-ERR-01's 'no condition a file can exhibit' category, but fits §21.7's own 'unwitnessed condition' test instead
findings.detail: Section 20.3 step 4 says a commit that changes a fixed declaration of a layer that stored a tile leaves 'no register row' because 'the bar stat[es] no condition a file can exhibit,' citing R-ERR-01 by name. But R-ERR-01/§21.7 defines that category narrowly, via the R-ENC-06 fixed-field-width example: a structure written at the wrong width is not 'the same file with a hidden defect' but simply a different byte sequence evaluated on its own terms. The step-4 case does not fit that shape -- the changed declaration (a new fill value, a new type, etc.) is, taken alone, a perfectly legal value under every structural rule, so there is no 'different file, conforming or not on its own terms' story. What actually makes it a violation is a cross-generation fact (old directory's declaration versus the new live one) that the physical bytes do genuinely encode (the old directory survives as slack) but that no check this specification obliges anyone to perform ever compares, since coverage verification 'walks the live state only' and does not reconstruct history (§9.7's Note). That is precisely the document's own definition of an unwitnessed condition, developed one paragraph earlier in the same section -- yet step 4 invokes the other category.
findings.quotation_a: "This bar binds the commit as an actor: no file is nonconforming by virtue of its violation, and no register row records the violation itself, the register enumerating file-conformance violations (§21.1) and the bar stating no condition a file can exhibit (§21.7, [R-ERR-01], [R-CNF-02])."
findings.quotation_b: "A condition this specification names is unwitnessed where, for every file exhibiting it, some file that does not exhibit it cannot be told apart from it by any check this specification obliges a reader or a verifier to perform... Distinguish an unwitnessed condition from a requirement that states no condition a file can exhibit."
findings.byte_level_rationale: Both categorizations reach the same stated practical conclusion -- no register row is owed and no reader/verifier behavior is prescribed for this act -- so no conforming implementation's accept, reject, or emit behavior differs depending on which category is correct. This is a finding about which of the document's own two named exemption doctrines correctly describes the same underlying fact, not about validity of any bytes.

findings.title: version_minor floor-and-carry rule for appenders is a SHOULD, not a MUST
findings.detail: While drafting a Part I question, I tried to build one around [R-CNT-26]'s appender version_minor rule: given an appender's input trailer version_minor and a commit that needs no new minor-gated feature, what value MUST the output's version_minor carry (the natural candidate answer being max(feature floor, prior minor))? On close reading, the rule is stated as a SHOULD, not a MUST: 'A writer SHOULD emit the lowest version_minor that defines every feature present in the file ... and an appender the maximum of that floor and the prior trailer's minor.' Because writer/updater conformance is semantic ([R-CNF-05]: two conforming writers given identical input MAY produce different conforming files) and this specific sub-rule is advisory, an appender that emits some other version_minor value is not thereby shown nonconforming by anything I can find in the text — there is no register row for it, and it is not listed among [R-ERR-05]'s hard limits. That means a question asking 'what value MUST the output carry' has no single answer this specification actually forces as a file-conformance matter, only a recommended one. I did not include this question in the final slate (I substituted a genuinely MUST-level question about ignore-lane flag carry-forward, [R-CNT-08]) precisely because of this softness. I am not confident this rises to a defect in the document — the SHOULD appears to be a deliberate, clearly-marked choice consistent with the document's general semantic-conformance stance — but it is a real trap for anyone trying to build a determinate byte-level conformance question on this specific rule, so I am reporting it rather than silently discarding it.
findings.quotation_a: A writer SHOULD emit the lowest version_minor that defines every feature present in the file — for a file expressible under this text, 0 — and an appender the maximum of that floor and the prior trailer's minor
findings.quotation_b: absent
findings.byte_level_rationale: This is not a two-edition divergence (I read only one edition) and not itself a byte-level defect in the specification; it is an observation about the difficulty of turning one specific SHOULD-level rule into a determinate byte-level quiz question, made in the course of building the slate.

result.disclosure: I read exactly the two permitted edition files (edition A: scratch/cleanroom/editions/a/tarn.md; edition B: scratch/cleanroom/editions/c/tarn.md) plus the 53 findings supplied verbatim in the computed task text. I did not read any transcript file under fidelity-2/out/ — the findings as given already quote the passages at issue, and I re-verified every disputed quotation myself directly against both edition files using grep/sed/diff (heading-to-heading diffs to get authoritative byte-identical/not verdicts, since the two files differ in total line count). I never listed a directory. No other file (docs/, PLAN.md, AGENTS.md, registry.json, conformance/, git history, web) was read. My scratch directory /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-robertkleffner-Documents-GitHub-tarn-first-draft/fidelity-2/scratch/triage/ was created but unused beyond holding this run; my required output transcript was written to /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-robertkleffner-Documents-GitHub-tarn-first-draft/fidelity-2/triage-correctness/transcript-triage-correctness.md. Material my runtime placed in context before I began (the system reminders, memory file listing, git status) is not evidence and was not used to grade any finding; I disclose it appeared but did not repeat or rely on its content. My lens is correctness only: for every group below I re-opened both editions at the reporters' cited passages and read them myself rather than trusting any reporter's or meta-reporter's claim of accuracy or of byte-identity.

groups.title: R-CNF-02 conduct-rule polarity reversed in B, contradicting B's own §9.2/§20.3, plus the closed list of worked examples dropped
groups.location_b: §2.3 Conforming TARN file bullet, [R-CNF-02] (B lines ~206-218); contradicts B's own §9.2 (~1202-1208) and §20.3 step 4 (~3174-3177), both confirmed byte-identical to A
groups.byte_level_rationale: Confirmed by direct read of both files: A says 'a file is never nonconforming by virtue of one: conduct rules bind the actor, the predicate binds the bytes.' B says 'binds the writer, and a file that breaks one is nonconforming.' A verifier built from B's §2.3 alone reports NONCONFORMING for a file whose only defect is a conduct-only violation (e.g. a set undefined ignore-lane flag bit, a missing commit durability barrier); a verifier built from A, or from B's own unchanged §9.2 ('the file it produces is never nonconforming by virtue of it, as [R-CNF-02] says of every conduct rule') and §20.3 step 4 ('no file is nonconforming by virtue of its violation'), certifies the identical bytes CONFORMING. Different verdict on identical bytes, and B is self-contradictory. cmp-verifier-02 additionally and correctly notes B drops the three-item closed list of worked examples (§6.3's flags rule, §6.2's pad rule, §20.3 step 4's bar) that A names at this sentence; confirmed absent from B's rewrite.
groups.recommended_action: Revert B's §2.3 [R-CNF-02] sentence to state the conduct-rule/predicate-on-bytes distinction (as A does) and restore the three-item worked list; this is a must-fix contradiction, not a style choice — a verifier implementer following only B's §2.3 builds the wrong gate.

groups.title: R-CNF-13 reach-condition-failure disposition reversed in B (reject-file → capability refusal), contradicting B's own §21.2 and its own next sentence
groups.location_b: §2.3 reach paragraph, [R-CNF-13] (B ~276-279); contradicts B's own §21.2 opening paragraph (confirmed byte-identical to A) and B's own following sentence
groups.byte_level_rationale: Confirmed: A: 'MUST treat its failure as reject-file on the ground of the requirement stating it rather than on capability grounds'; exemption 'applies unchanged.' B: 'MUST treat a failure as a capability refusal, not as reject-file under the requirement that states the condition'; exemption 'lapses.' Both clauses are exact opposites, confirmed by direct quotation match. §21.2's opening paragraph is confirmed byte-identical between editions (heading-to-heading diff, empty) and still derives F8, F14, F6 and both F1 instances as reaching rows under 'Outcome: reject-file' — directly contradicting B's own §2.3. result.notes: Correctness-lens re-judgment of 53 findings, grouped into 19 distinct differences/defects. Three groups are genuine, confirmed byte-level CONTRADICTIONS in edition B, each self-contradicting against unchanged text elsewhere in B: (1) the R-CNF-02 conduct-rule polarity flip, (2) the R-CNF-13 reach-condition-failure disposition flip, and (3) the R-CNF-03 dropped record-type clause (contradicted by B's own unchanged Appendix H). These three are the highest-priority items for the maintainer. Two corrections I made relative to the original 53 reports: (a) I upgraded cmp-reader-07's EQUIVALENT grade on the F14/F5/F15 worked-Note drop to LOSS, since the task's own LOSS definition explicitly names a dropped 'worked figure' as a LOSS regardless of whether the bottom-line conclusion survives elsewhere (it does, via byte-identical §21.2 text, which is why this LOSS is not byte-level); this sides with cmp-verifier-06 over cmp-reader-07. (b) I downgraded swab-03's BYTE-LEVEL tag on the cannot-establish-grounds compression to a content-level (non-byte-level) LOSS, because the operative rule it worried about (the resource-decode-decline ground, and the R-MTA-10 experimental-encoding carve-out) is independently and byte-identically restated elsewhere in B's own text (§9.7 and multiple other R-MTA-10 citation sites), so an implementation built from the whole of B does not actually diverge from A, even though B's canonical enumeration passages (§2.3 and the new §21.6 paragraph) are each individually incomplete. Four ids from the original 53 (cmp-verifier-02, swba-07, swba-08, swba-09) were not folded into any of the other passes' apparent groupings in the material I could see; I created dedicated groups for them after independently verifying their citations against both edition files. All 53 input ids are otherwise accounted for as the reconciliation groups above; no id was dropped, and every weak or single-edition-only finding was still grouped and graded (mostly EQUIVALENT, since the great majority of the walk-only findings turned out, on direct heading-to-heading diff, to rest on text that is byte-identical between the two editions — meaning they describe defects of the shared specification, not fidelity differences introduced by edition B's rewrite). I did not independently re-diff every single cited sub-section for the lowest-priority groups (noted explicitly in r2-r5-r6-r7-r8-shared-text and intro-figures-generalized-restated-elsewhere) given the read budget; nothing among the 53 findings or my own reading contradicts those two groups' claims.

Two MUST-level clauses are flipped to their opposites: (1) A says an exemption unrelated to the declared major (R-CNT-04's residency exemption, which lets a reader not holding front-signature bytes [0,16) resident defer or omit that check) "applies unchanged" for a file declaring another major; B says the same exemption "lapses" for such a file.
